questions.text: A point charge situated at a distance $'r'$ from a short electric dipole on its axis, experiences a force $\vec{F}$. If the distance of the charge is $'2r'$, the force on the charge will be :

answer.text: $\dfrac{\vec{F}}{8}$

questions.text: (i) State Coulomb's law in electrostatics and write it in vector form, for two charges. (ii) 'Gauss's law is based on the inverse-square dependence on distance contained in the Coulomb's law.' Explain. (iii) Two charges A (charge q) and B (charge 2q) are located at points $(0, 0)$ and $(a, a)$ respectively. Let $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ be the unit vectors along x-axis and y-axis respectively. Find the force exerted by A on B, in terms of $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$.

answer.text:
(i) Coulomb's law: the force between two point charges varies inversely with the square of the distance between them and is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes, acting along the line joining them.
$\vec{F}_{12} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}^{2}}\,\hat{r}_{12}$
Alternatively: $\vec{F}_{12} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}^{3}}\,\vec{r}_{12}$, where $\vec{r}_{12}$ is the vector from $q_2$ to $q_1$.
(ii) In the derivation of Gauss's law the flux is found using Coulomb's law and the surface area. Coulomb's law contributes a $\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$ factor and the surface area an $r^{2}$ factor; on taking the product the two cancel, so the flux becomes independent of $r$.
(iii) With $A$ (charge $q$) at the origin and $B$ (charge $2q$) at $(a, a)$:
$\vec{r} = \overrightarrow{AB} = a\hat{i} + a\hat{j}, \qquad r = |\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{a^{2}+a^{2}} = \sqrt{2}\,a$
$\vec{F} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q\times 2q}{(\sqrt{2}\,a)^{2}}\times\dfrac{a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}\,a} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2q^{2}}{2a^{2}}\times\dfrac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\vec{F} = \dfrac{q^{2}}{4\sqrt{2}\,\pi\varepsilon_0\,a^{2}}\,(\hat{i}+\hat{j})$.
(If only the magnitude is required: $|\vec{F}| = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q^{2}}{a^{2}}$.)

questions.text: (i) Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the equatorial plane of an electric dipole consisting of charges q and $-q$ separated by a distance 2a. (ii) The distance of a far off point on the equatorial plane of an electric dipole is halved. How will the electric field be affected for the dipole ? (iii) Two identical electric dipoles are placed along the diagonals of a square ABCD of side $\sqrt{2}$ m as shown in the figure. Obtain the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at the centre (O) of the square.

answer.text:
(i) At a point on the equatorial plane, distance $\sqrt{r^{2}+a^{2}}$ from each charge:
$E_{+q} = E_{-q} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}+a^{2}}$.
The components normal to the dipole axis cancel; the components along the axis add up, giving a field opposite to the dipole moment:
$\vec{E} = -(E_{+q}+E_{-q})\cos\theta\,\hat{p} = -\dfrac{2qa}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (r^{2}+a^{2})^{3/2}}\,\hat{p} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (r^{2}+a^{2})^{3/2}}$.
(ii) At a far-off point $r \gg a$:  $\vec{E} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{3}}$.
When the distance is halved ($r \to r/2$):  $\vec{E} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (r/2)^{3}} = -\dfrac{8\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{3}}$, i.e. $\vec{E}$ becomes 8 times.
(iii) For the four charges at the corners of the square (side 2 m), net dipole moment:
$p_1 = p_2 = q\times2\ \text{C m}$, so $p_{net} = \sqrt{p_1^{2}+p_2^{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\,q\ \text{C m}$.
Field at the centre $O$ ($r = 0,\ a = 1$ m):  $E = \dfrac{k\,p_{net}}{(r^{2}+a^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{k\times2\sqrt{2}\,q}{1^{3}} = 2\sqrt{2}\,kq = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$, directed along $DC$.
Alternatively (fields due to point charges): the charges at $B, D$ give $E_1 = \dfrac{kq}{1^{2}}+\dfrac{kq}{1^{2}} = 2kq$ along $OB$, and those at $A, C$ give $E_2 = 2kq$ along $OC$; hence $E_{net} = \sqrt{E_1^{2}+E_2^{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\,kq = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ along $DC$.

questions.text: (i) Use Gauss' law to obtain an expression for the electric field due to an infinitely long thin straight wire with uniform linear charge density $\lambda$. (ii) An infinitely long positively charged straight wire has a linear charge density $\lambda$. An electron is revolving in a circle with a constant speed $v$ such that the wire passes through the centre, and is perpendicular to the plane, of the circle. Find the kinetic energy of the electron in terms of magnitudes of its charge and linear charge density $\lambda$ on the wire. (iii) Draw a graph of kinetic energy as a function of linear charge density $\lambda$.

answer.text:
(i) Consider a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $l$ around the wire. Flux through it: $\phi=E\cdot 2\pi r l$.
By Gauss's law $E\cdot 2\pi r l=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$, and since $q=\lambda l$:
$E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$.
(ii) For an electron moving in a circular path around the wire, the electric force supplies the centripetal force:
$\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}=eE$, so kinetic energy
$K=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}eEr=\dfrac{1}{2}e\cdot\dfrac{\lambda r}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}=\dfrac{e\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$.
(iii) Thus $K=\dfrac{e\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ is independent of $r$; i.e. $K\propto\lambda$ — a straight line through the origin on a $K$-vs-$\lambda$ graph.

questions.text: (i) Consider two identical point charges located at points $(0, 0)$ and $(a, 0)$. (1) Is there a point on the line joining them at which the electric field is zero ? (2) Is there a point on the line joining them at which the electric potential is zero ? Justify your answers for each case. (ii) State the significance of negative value of electrostatic potential energy of a system of charges. Three charges are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle ABC of side 2·0 m as shown in figure. Calculate the electric potential energy of the system of three charges.

answer.text:
(i)(1) Yes — the electric field is zero at the midpoint of the line joining the two identical charges; being a vector, the two equal and opposite field contributions cancel there.
(2) No — the potential cannot be zero anywhere on the line joining them; potential is a scalar and the contributions of two identical charges add and cannot cancel.
(ii) A negative value of the electrostatic potential energy of a system signifies that the system has attractive forces (it is bound / stable).
For the charges $+4{\cdot}0\ \mu\text{C}$ (A), $-4{\cdot}0\ \mu\text{C}$ (B), $+2{\cdot}0\ \mu\text{C}$ (C) at the corners of a triangle of side $2\ \text{m}$:
$U=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{q_Aq_B}{r}+\dfrac{q_Bq_C}{r}+\dfrac{q_Cq_A}{r}\right]=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}}{2}\,[-16-8+8]\times10^{-12}=-7{\cdot}2\times10^{-2}\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: (i) Define electric flux and write its SI unit. (ii) Use Gauss' law to obtain the expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet. (iii) A cube of side L is kept in space, as shown in the figure. An electric field $\vec{E} = (Ax + B)\hat{i}\ \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{C}}$ exists in the region. Find the net charge enclosed by the cube.

answer.text:
(i) Electric flux $\phi=\vec{E}\cdot\vec{A}$ (the number of electric field lines passing normally through an area). Its SI unit is $\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-1}$ (or $\text{V\,m}$).
(ii) For a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet, take a cylindrical (pill-box) Gaussian surface with its two flat faces, each of area $A$, parallel to the sheet. From Gauss's law $\phi=\displaystyle\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$:
$2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.
(iii) The field $\vec{E}=(Ax+B)\hat{i}\ \text{N/C}$ has only an $x$-component, so flux passes only through the two faces perpendicular to the x-axis (side $L$).
Left face: $\phi_L=E\,dS\cos180^{\circ}=-BL^{2}$; right face: $\phi_R=E\,dS\cos0^{\circ}=(AL+B)L^{2}=AL^{3}+BL^{2}$.
Net flux $=\phi_L+\phi_R=(AL^{3}+BL^{2})-BL^{2}=AL^{3}=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$.
$\therefore\ q=AL^{3}\varepsilon_0$.

questions.text: Two identical dipoles are arranged in x-y plane as shown in the figure. Find the magnitude and the direction of net electric field at the origin O.

answer.text:
The four charges lie at $A(+q)$, $B(-q)$, $C(+q)$, $D(-q)$, each at distance $a$ from $O$. Treating $BA$ and $DC$ as two dipoles, the fields $\vec{E}_1$ (along $OB$) and $\vec{E}_2$ (along $OD$) have equal magnitude $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{q}{a^{2}}$.
$|\vec{E}_{net}|=2\sqrt{2}\,E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,q}{a^{2}}$.
The direction of $\vec{E}_{net}$ is at $225^{\circ}$ to the x-axis.
Alternatively, considering $CB$ as a dipole, the equatorial field at $O$ is
$E_1=\dfrac{2kq\times(a/\sqrt{2})}{\left[\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}\right]^{3/2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,kq}{a^{2}}$, and similarly $E_2=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,kq}{a^{2}}$ for $AD$, so $E_{net}=E_1+E_2=\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,kq}{a^{2}}$.

questions.text: A cube of side $0\cdot1$ m is placed, as shown in the figure, in a region where electric field $\vec{E} = 500\,x\,\hat{i}$ exists. Here x is in meters and E in NC$^{-1}$. Calculate : (a) the flux passing through the cube, and (b) the charge within the cube.

answer.text:
(a) Flux through the left face: $\phi_L=\vec{E}_L\cdot\vec{A}=-[500\times0{\cdot}1]\times[(0{\cdot}1)^{2}]=-0{\cdot}5\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$.
Flux through the right face: $\phi_R=\vec{E}_R\cdot\vec{A}=[500\times0{\cdot}2]\times[(0{\cdot}1)^{2}]=1\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$.
Net flux: $\phi=\phi_L+\phi_R=0{\cdot}5\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$.
(b) By Gauss's law $\phi=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$, so
$q=\phi\varepsilon_0=0{\cdot}5\,\varepsilon_0=4{\cdot}4\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}$.

questions.text: Four point charges of 1 $\mu$C, $-2$ $\mu$C, 1 $\mu$C and $-2$ $\mu$C are placed at the corners A, B, C and D respectively, of a square of side 30 cm. Find the net force acting on a charge of 4 $\mu$C placed at the centre of the square.

answer.text:
Four charges are at the corners of a square (side $30\ \text{cm}$) with $Q=4\ \mu\text{C}$ at the centre $O$; $OA=OB=OC=OD=r$.
Net force $\vec{F}=\vec{F}_{OA}+\vec{F}_{OB}+\vec{F}_{OC}+\vec{F}_{OD}$. Since $\vec{F}_{OA}=-\vec{F}_{OC}$ and $\vec{F}_{OB}=-\vec{F}_{OD}$, the pairs cancel, so $\vec{F}=0$.
Alternatively, $F_{OA}=F_{OC}=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times4\times10^{-6}\times1\times10^{-6}}{(15\sqrt{2}\times10^{-2})^{2}}=0{\cdot}8\ \text{N}$ and $F_{OB}=F_{OD}=1{\cdot}6\ \text{N}$; then $F_1=F_{OA}-F_{OC}=0$ and $F_2=F_{OB}-F_{OD}=0$, so the net force $F=0$.

questions.text: Three point charges, 1 $\mu$C each, are kept at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm. Find the net electric field at the centroid of triangle.

answer.text:
Three charges $q_A=q_B=q_C=1\ \text{pC}$ sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle (side $10\ \text{cm}$); the field is required at the centroid $O$, with $AO=BO=CO=r$.
$|\vec{E}_{OA}|=|\vec{E}_{OB}|=|\vec{E}_{OC}|=2{\cdot}7\ \text{N C}^{-1}$. The resultant of $\vec{E}_{OB}$ and $\vec{E}_{OC}$ (at $120^{\circ}$) is $E_{BC}=\sqrt{E_{OB}^{2}+E_{OC}^{2}+2E_{OB}E_{OC}\cos120^{\circ}}=E_{OB}$, directed opposite to $\vec{E}_{OA}$.
Hence $\vec{E}_{BC}+\vec{E}_{OA}=0$, so the net field $\vec{E}_O=0$. (Equivalently, the three equal field vectors at $120^{\circ}$ form a closed polygon, so their vector sum is zero.)

questions.text: (a) Define the term 'electric flux' and write its dimensions. (b) A plane surface, in shape of a square of side 1 cm is placed in an electric field $\vec{E} = \left(100\ \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{C}}\right)\hat{i}$ such that the unit vector normal to the surface is given by $\hat{n} = 0{\cdot}8\hat{i} + 0{\cdot}6\hat{k}$. Find the electric flux through the surface.

answer.text:
(a) Electric flux is the measure of the total number of electric field lines passing normally through a surface (equivalently, the surface integral of the electric field over the surface): $\phi_E=\vec{E}\cdot\vec{A}$. Its dimensional formula is $[ML^{3}T^{-3}A^{-1}]$.
(b) $\phi_E=\vec{E}\cdot\vec{A}=(100\hat{i})\cdot(10^{-4}\hat{n})=(100\hat{i})\cdot(0{\cdot}8\hat{i}+0{\cdot}6\hat{k})\times10^{-4}=8\times10^{-3}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$.

questions.text: (a) Using Gauss's law, deduce an expression for electric field at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet. (b) Two large thin plane sheets, each having surface charge density $\sigma$, are held close and parallel to each other in air. What is the net electric field at a point (i) inside and (ii) outside, the sheets ?

answer.text: Field of a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet (Gauss's law, cylindrical Gaussian surface — only the two flat faces contribute): net flux $= 2EA$, charge enclosed $= \sigma A \Rightarrow 2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}$. For two such parallel sheets each of surface density $\sigma$: (i) net field between them $E_{in} = 0$; (ii) net field outside $E_{out} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.

questions.text: (a) An electric dipole consists of two point charges q and $-$q separated by a distance 2a. Derive an expression for the electric field $\vec{E}$ due to this dipole at a point distant r from the centre of the dipole on the equatorial plane. Write the expression for the electric field at a far off point, i.e. $r \gg a$. (b) A dipole is placed in x-y plane such that charges q and $-$q are located at $x = a$ and $x = b$ respectively. There exists an electric field $\vec{E} = 2\hat{i}\ \dfrac{\text{N}}{\text{C}}$ in the region. Calculate the force $\vec{F}$ and torque $\vec{\tau}$ experienced by the dipole.
questions.topic: Dipole in a Uniform External Field

answer.text: (a) Electric field of a dipole on the equatorial plane: $E_{+q} = E_{-q} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}$; the components perpendicular to the dipole axis cancel and those along the axis add, giving $\vec{E} = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2qa}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}\,\hat{p}$; for $r \gg a$, $\vec{E} = -\dfrac{2qa}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}\,\hat{p} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}$. (b) For the given arrangement, net force $\vec{F} = \vec{F}_{+q} + \vec{F}_{-q} = q(2\hat{i}) - q(2\hat{i}) = 0$; torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p}\times\vec{E} = p(-\hat{i})\times2\hat{i} = 0$ (also $\tau = pE\sin\theta$ with $\theta = \pi \Rightarrow \tau = 0$).

questions.text: A particle of mass m and charge q starts from rest and moves in an electric field $\vec{E} = E_0\,\hat{i}$. After travelling a distance x in the field along x-axis, the kinetic energy of the particle will be :

answer.text: $q E_0 x$

questions.text: An electric dipole consists of two point charges $+1\ \mu$C and $-1\ \mu$C, held 10 cm apart. It is subjected to a uniform electric field of 100 N/C. Calculate the amount of work done in turning the dipole from its position of stable equilibrium to the position of unstable equilibrium, in the field.
questions.topic: Dipole in a Uniform External Field

answer.text: Work done in turning the dipole in an external field $= -pE(\cos\theta_2 - \cos\theta_1)$; with $\theta_1 = 0^\circ$ (stable equilibrium) and $\theta_2 = 180^\circ$ (unstable), net work $= 2pE = 2(2qa)E = 2\times1\times10^{-6}\times10\times10^{-2}\times100 = 2\times10^{-5}\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: (i) State Gauss's Law in electrostatics. Apply this to obtain the electric field $\vec{E}$ at a point near a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet. (ii) Two long straight wires 1 and 2 are kept as shown in the figure. The linear charge density of the two wires are $\lambda_1 = 10\ \mu$C/m and $\lambda_2 = -20\ \mu$C/m. Find the net force $\vec{F}$ experienced by an electron held at point P.

answer.text:
(i) Gauss's law: the electric flux through a closed surface equals $\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$, where $q$ is the total charge enclosed: $\displaystyle\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S}=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$.
For an infinite plane sheet of surface charge density $\sigma$, using a cylindrical Gaussian pillbox (two faces of area $A$ perpendicular to the sheet), the charge enclosed is $\sigma A$:
$2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, i.e. $\vec{E}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}$ (normal to the sheet).
(ii) Field of a long charged wire: $\vec{E}=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\hat{r}$.
At point $P$: $E_1=\dfrac{10\times10^{-6}}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(10\times10^{-2})}$ along $-\hat{j}$ (from wire 1); $E_2=\dfrac{20\times10^{-6}}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(20\times10^{-2})}$ along $-\hat{j}$ (from wire 2).
$E_{net}=\dfrac{10\times10^{-6}}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}1}+\dfrac{2}{0{\cdot}2}\right)(-\hat{j})=3{\cdot}6\times10^{6}(-\hat{j})\ \text{N/C}$.
Force on the electron: $\vec{F}=q\vec{E}_{net}=(-1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19})\times3{\cdot}6\times10^{6}(-\hat{j})=5{\cdot}76\times10^{-13}\ \hat{j}\ \text{N}$.

questions.text: (i) A charge $+Q$ is placed on a thin conducting spherical shell of radius R. Using Gauss's law, derive an expression for the electric field at a point lying (i) inside and (ii) outside the shell. (ii) Show that the electric field for same charge density $(\sigma)$ is twice in case of a conducting plate or surface than in a nonconducting sheet.

answer.text:
(i) Field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell (surface charge density $\sigma$):
Inside the shell ($r<R$): the Gaussian sphere encloses no charge, so $E\times4\pi r^{2}=0\ \Rightarrow\ E=0$.
Outside the shell ($r>R$): the Gaussian sphere encloses the whole charge; $E\times4\pi r^{2}=\dfrac{\sigma\,4\pi R^{2}}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ E=\dfrac{\sigma R^{2}}{\varepsilon_0 r^{2}}=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{2}}$.
(ii) Field of a conducting sheet: $E_c=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$; field of a non-conducting sheet: $E_{nc}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$. For the same surface charge density, $2E_{nc}=E_c$.

questions.text: (i) Using Gauss's law, show that the electric field $\vec{E}$ at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet is given by $\vec{E} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}$, where symbols have their usual meanings. (ii) Electric field $\vec{E}$ in a region is given by $\vec{E} = (5x^2 + 2)\hat{i}$ where E is in N/C and x is in metres. A cube of side 10 cm is placed in the region as shown in figure. Calculate (1) the electric flux through the cube, and (2) the net charge enclosed by the cube.

answer.text:
(i) Field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet: with a cylindrical Gaussian pillbox (two faces of area $A$), $\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S}=2EA$; by Gauss's law $2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, i.e. $\vec{E}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}$ (normally outward).
(ii)(1) Flux through the cube: $\phi=\phi_L+\phi_R=-2\times100\times10^{-4}+[5\times(10\times10^{-2})^{2}+2]\times100\times10^{-4}=5\times10^{-4}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$.
(2) Charge enclosed: $q_{en}=\phi\varepsilon_0=5\times10^{-4}\times8{\cdot}85\times10^{-12}=4{\cdot}43\times10^{-15}\ \text{C}$.

questions.text: (i) A thin spherical shell of radius R has a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. Using Gauss' law, deduce an expression for electric field (i) outside and (ii) inside the shell. (ii) Two long straight thin wires AB and CD have linear charge densities 10 $\mu$C/m and $-20$ $\mu$C/m respectively. They are kept parallel to each other at a distance 1 m. Find magnitude and direction of the net electric field at a point midway between them.

answer.text:
(i) Field of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell (surface charge density $\sigma$):
Outside ($r>R$): flux $\phi=E\times4\pi r^{2}$, enclosed charge $Q=\sigma\times4\pi R^{2}$; by Gauss's law $E\times4\pi r^{2}=\dfrac{\sigma\,4\pi R^{2}}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ E=\dfrac{\sigma R^{2}}{\varepsilon_0 r^{2}}=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{2}}$.
Inside ($r<R$): the Gaussian surface encloses no charge, so $E\times4\pi r^{2}=0\ \Rightarrow\ E=0$.
(ii) Net field at the midpoint between two long straight parallel charged wires (linear densities $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$), each at distance $r$, using $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$:
$E_{net}=E_1+E_2=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}[\lambda_1+\lambda_2]=\dfrac{2\times9\times10^{9}}{0{\cdot}5}[10+20]\times10^{-6}=1{\cdot}08\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$, directed towards $CD$.

questions.text: (i) What is difference between an open surface and a closed surface ? Draw elementary surface vector $\overrightarrow{dS}$ for a spherical surface S. (ii) Define electric flux through a surface. Give the significance of a Gaussian surface. A charge outside a Gaussian surface does not contribute to total electric flux through the surface. Why ? (iii) A small spherical shell $S_1$ has point charges $q_1 = -3\,\mu$C, $q_2 = -2\,\mu$C and $q_3 = 9\,\mu$C inside it. This shell is enclosed by another big spherical shell $S_2$. A point charge Q is placed in between the two surfaces $S_1$ and $S_2$. If the electric flux through the surface $S_2$ is four times the flux through surface $S_1$, find charge Q.

answer.text: (i) Open surface — a surface which does not enclose a volume. Closed surface — a surface which does enclose a volume. Diagram: a point charge $q$ at the centre of a sphere of radius $r$, with an elementary area vector $\Delta\vec{S}$ on the surface and $\vec{E}$ radially outward. (ii) Electric flux is defined as the number of electric field lines crossing an area normally. (Alternatively, $\phi = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A}$, or $\phi = EA\cos\theta$.) Significance of a Gaussian surface: it helps in finding the electric field in a simpler way. Reason: any electric field line from the charge that enters the surface at one point exits at another, resulting in a net zero flux (for a surface enclosing no charge). (iii) Total charge enclosed by $S_1 = (-3-2+9)\ \mu\text{C} = 4\ \mu\text{C}$. Total charge enclosed by $S_2 = Q+4\ \mu\text{C}$. Since $\phi_{S_2} = 4\phi_{S_1}$: $\dfrac{Q+4\ \mu\text{C}}{\varepsilon_0} = 4\left(\dfrac{4\ \mu\text{C}}{\varepsilon_0}\right) \Rightarrow Q = 12\ \mu\text{C}$.

questions.text: (i) Show that Gauss's theorem is consistent with Coulomb's law. Using it, derive an expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius r at a point at a distance y from the centre of the shell such that (I) $y > r$, and (II) $y < r$. (ii) A point charge of $+2$ nC is kept at the origin of a three-dimensional coordinate system. Find the type and magnitude of the charge which should be kept at $(0, 0, -6\text{m})$ so that the potential due to the system becomes zero at $(0, 0, 2\text{m})$.

answer.text: (i) Gauss's theorem is based on the inverse-square dependence on distance contained in Coulomb's law: $\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s} = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{q}{r^2}$. By Coulomb's law, the force on a charge $q_0$ in this field is $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{qq_0}{r^2}$; therefore Gauss's law is consistent with Coulomb's law. For a uniformly charged thin spherical shell (surface charge density $\sigma$): (I) for $y>r$: electric flux through the Gaussian surface $= E\times4\pi y^2$; charge enclosed by the surface $= \sigma\times4\pi r^2$. Using Gauss's theorem, $E(4\pi y^2) = \dfrac{\sigma\,4\pi r^2}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow \vec{E} = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0y^2}\hat{r}$. (II) for $y<r$: the charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface is $0$; using Gauss's theorem, electric flux $= E(4\pi y^2) = 0$, i.e. $E=0$ for $y<r$. (ii) Charge $+2\ \text{nC}$ at the origin O; point A at $(0,0,-6\ \text{m})$ carries an unknown charge $q$; point B is at $(0,0,2\ \text{m})$. Potential at B due to the charge at the origin and the charge $q$ at A: $V = V_1+V_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{2\times10^{-9}}{2}+\dfrac{q}{6+2}\right]$. Setting $V=0$: $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[10^{-9}+\dfrac{q}{8}\right]=0 \Rightarrow q = -8\times10^{-9}\ \text{C}$.

questions.text: Two infinitely long straight wires '1' and '2' are placed d distance apart, parallel to each other, as shown in the figure. They are uniformly charged having charge densities $\lambda$ and $-\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ respectively. Locate the position of the point from wire '1' at which the net electric field is zero and identify the region in which it lies.

answer.text: Two long charged wires/sheets with linear charge densities $\lambda$ (wire 1) and $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ (wire 2), separated by a distance $d$. Electric field due to wire 1 and wire 2 at point P: $E_1 = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0x}$; $E_2 = \dfrac{\lambda/2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(x+d)}$. At P, the net electric field is zero: $E_1=E_2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0x} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\times2\pi\varepsilon_0(x+d)} \Rightarrow x=-2d$. The negative sign indicates that the point lies in region C — at a distance $2d$ from wire 1, the electric field is zero. (Full credit is also given if a student finds the position by taking the point directly in region C.)

questions.text: (i) Obtain an expression for the electric field $\vec{E}$ due to a dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ at a point on its equatorial plane and specify its direction. Hence, find the value of electric field : (I) at the centre of the dipole (r = 0), and (II) at a point $r \gg a$, where 2a is the length of the dipole. (ii) An electric field $\vec{E} = (10x + 5)\hat{i}$ N/C exists in a region in which a cube of side L is kept as shown in the figure. Here x and L are in metres. Calculate the net flux through the cube.

answer.text: (i) Electric field due to a dipole on its equatorial plane: $E_{+q}=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(r^2+a^2)}$, $E_{-q}=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(r^2+a^2)}$; total field $\vec{E} = -(E_{+q}+E_{-q})\cos\theta\,\hat{p} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$ (direction opposite to the dipole moment $\vec{p}$). (I) At the centre of the dipole, $r=0$: $\vec{E}=-\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}$. (II) At a point $r\gg a$: $\vec{E}=-\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$. (ii) $\vec{E}=(10x+5)\hat{i}\ \text{N/C}$. $\phi_L = \displaystyle\int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s} = -E_L(L^2) = -5L^2$. $\phi_R = E_R(L^2) = (10L+5)L^2$. $\phi_{net} = \phi_L+\phi_R = -5L^2+(10L+5)L^2 = 10L^3\ \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}$.

questions.text: (b) (i) Two infinitely long straight wires having linear charge densities $-\lambda$ and $3\lambda$ are held vertically parallel to each other, distance r apart in free space. Find the nature and magnitude of the force/length exerted by one wire on the other. (ii) A small hollow conducting sphere of radius $r_1$ is given a charge Q. It is surrounded by a concentric conducting spherical shell of inner radius $r_2$ and outer radius $r_3$, having charge $-$ 3q. If a point charge 2q were kept at the centre, find : (I) the electric flux through a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius x for (1) $x < r_1$, and (2) $r_1 < x < r_2$. (II) electric field at a point distant x from the centre for (1) $x > r_3$, and (2) $r_1 < x < r_2$. (III) surface charge density on the inner surface of (1) sphere, and (2) shell.

answer.text: (b)(i) Force between the two charged wires (linear densities $\lambda$ and $3\lambda$): attractive; field of wire 1 at wire 2, $E = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$; force per unit length $\dfrac{F}{l} = qE = -\dfrac{3\lambda^2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ (same magnitude acts on the other wire). (ii) Concentric shells: flux — for $x < r_1$, $\phi = \dfrac{2q}{\varepsilon_0}$; for $r_1 < x < r_2$, $\phi = \dfrac{Q+2q}{\varepsilon_0}$. Field — for $x > r_3$, $E = \dfrac{k(Q-q)}{x^2}$; for $r_1 < x < r_2$, $E = \dfrac{k(Q+2q)}{x^2}$. Surface charge density on the inner surfaces — $\sigma = -\dfrac{2q}{4\pi r_1^2}$ and $\sigma = -\dfrac{Q+2q}{4\pi r_2^2}$.

topic_order: Dipole in a Uniform External Field

questions.text: (i) Define electric potential at a point and write its SI unit. (ii) Two capacitors are connected in series. Derive an expression of the equivalent capacitance of the combination. (iii) Two point charges $+q$ and $-q$ are located at points $(3a, 0)$ and $(0, 4a)$ respectively in x-y plane. A third charge Q is kept at the origin. Find the value of Q, in terms of q and a, so that the electrostatic potential energy of the system is zero.

answer.text:
(i) Electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge (without acceleration) from infinity to that point $\left(V=\dfrac{W}{q}=-\displaystyle\int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l}\right)$. Its SI unit is the volt ($\text{J/C}$).
(ii) For two capacitors in series carrying the same charge $Q$: $V=V_1+V_2=\dfrac{Q}{C_1}+\dfrac{Q}{C_2}$, and $\dfrac{Q}{C_{eq}}=Q\left(\dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}\right)$, so
$\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}}=\dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}$.
(iii) With $+q$ at $(3a,0)$, $-q$ at $(0,4a)$ and $Q$ at the origin: the separations are $Q$-to-$q$ $=3a$, $Q$-to-$(-q)$ $=4a$, and $q$-to-$(-q)$ $=5a$.
$U=K\left[\dfrac{Q(-q)}{4a}+\dfrac{Qq}{3a}-\dfrac{q^{2}}{5a}\right]=0\ \Rightarrow\ -\dfrac{Q}{4}+\dfrac{Q}{3}-\dfrac{q}{5}=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{Q}{12}=\dfrac{q}{5}$
$\therefore\ Q=+\dfrac{12q}{5}$.

questions.text: (a) Twelve negative charges of same magnitude are equally spaced and fixed on the circumference of a circle of radius R as shown in Fig. (i). Relative to potential being zero at infinity, find the electric potential and electric field at the centre C of the circle. (b) If the charges are unequally spaced and fixed on an arc of $120^\circ$ of radius R as shown in Fig. (ii), find electric potential at the centre C.

answer.text:
(a) Electric potential due to a point charge: $V = \dfrac{kq}{R}$.
Value of each charge $= -q$, total charge $= -12q$, all at distance $R$ from the centre:
$V = \dfrac{k(-12q)}{R} = \dfrac{-12kq}{R} = \dfrac{-12q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}$.
By symmetry the resultant of all the electric-field vectors is zero, so the electric field at the centre is $\vec{E} = 0$.
(b) Electric potential is a scalar quantity and does not depend on the placement (arrangement) of the charges. Therefore the potential at the centre is unchanged:
$V = \dfrac{-12kq}{R} = \dfrac{-12q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}$.

questions.text: In the following question, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d).
