questions.text: Two charged conducting spheres of radii a and b are connected to each other by a wire. Find the ratio of the electric fields at their surfaces.

answer.text:
When the two spheres are connected by a conducting wire, both are at the same potential:
$k\dfrac{q_1}{a}=k\dfrac{q_2}{b}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{q_1}{q_2}=\dfrac{a}{b}$.
Ratio of the electric fields at their surfaces:
$\dfrac{E_1}{E_2}=\dfrac{k\,q_1/a^{2}}{k\,q_2/b^{2}}=\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\cdot\dfrac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}=\dfrac{a}{b}\cdot\dfrac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}=\dfrac{b}{a}$.

questions.text: A parallel plate capacitor (A) of capacitance C is charged by a battery to voltage V. The battery is disconnected and an uncharged capacitor (B) of capacitance 2C is connected across A. Find the ratio of (i) final charges on A and B. (ii) total electrostatic energy stored in A and B finally and that in A initially.

answer.text:
Initially $Q=CV$. On sharing charge, the two capacitors reach a common voltage $V_1$; finally $q_A=C_A V_1$ and $q_B=C_B V_1$ (with $C_B=2C_A$), so
$\dfrac{q_A}{q_B}=\dfrac{C_A}{C_B}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Since $q_A+q_B=Q$: $q_A=\dfrac{Q}{3}$ and $q_B=\dfrac{2Q}{3}$.
$\dfrac{U_f}{U_i}=\dfrac{\dfrac{q_A^{2}}{2C_A}+\dfrac{q_B^{2}}{2C_B}}{\dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C_A}}=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
Alternatively, common potential $V_1=\dfrac{Q_1+Q_2}{C_1+C_2}=\dfrac{Q}{3C}=\dfrac{V}{3}$, and
$\dfrac{U_f}{U_i}=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}C_{eq}V_1^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}C_A V^{2}}=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}(3C)\left(\frac{V}{3}\right)^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}}=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for electrostatic potential energy of a system of three charges q, 2q and $-3q$ placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side a.
questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

answer.text:
$U=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r}+\dfrac{q_2 q_3}{r}+\dfrac{q_3 q_1}{r}\right]$
With charges $q,\ 2q,\ -3q$ at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a$:
$U=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{(q)(2q)}{a}+\dfrac{(2q)(-3q)}{a}+\dfrac{(-3q)(q)}{a}\right]=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{2q^{2}-6q^{2}-3q^{2}}{a}\right]$
$U=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{-7q^{2}}{a}$.

questions.text: Two small conducting balls A and B of radius $r_1$ and $r_2$ have charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ respectively. They are connected by a wire. Obtain the expression for charges on A and B, in equilibrium.

answer.text:
By conservation of charge, $q_1+q_2=q_1'+q_2'=Q$.
When the two balls are connected by a wire they reach the same potential:
$\dfrac{kq_1'}{r_1}=\dfrac{kq_2'}{r_2}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{q_1'}{r_1}=\dfrac{q_2'}{r_2}$, i.e. $q_1' r_2=q_2' r_1=(Q-q_1')r_1$.
Solving, $q_1'(r_1+r_2)=Qr_1$, so
$q_1'=\dfrac{Qr_1}{r_1+r_2}=\dfrac{(q_1+q_2)r_1}{r_1+r_2}$ and $q_2'=Q-q_1'=\dfrac{(q_1+q_2)r_2}{r_1+r_2}$.

questions.text: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges. Force and electric field, due to a point charge is basically determined by Coulomb's law. For symmetric charge configurations, Gauss's law, which is also based on Coulomb's law, helps us to find the electric field. A charge/a system of charges like a dipole experience a force/torque in an electric field. Work is required to be done to provide a specific orientation to a dipole with respect to an electric field. Answer the following questions based on the above : (a) Consider a uniformly charged thin conducting shell of radius R. Plot a graph showing the variation of $|\vec{E}|$ with distance r from the centre, for points $0 \leq r \leq 3R$. (b) The figure shows the variation of potential V with $\dfrac{1}{r}$ for two point charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, where V is the potential at a distance r due to a point charge. Find $\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2}$. (c) An electric dipole of dipole moment of $6 \times 10^{-7}$ C-m is kept in a uniform electric field of $10^4$ N/C such that the dipole moment and the electric field are parallel. Calculate the potential energy of the dipole.  OR  (c) An electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is initially kept in a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$ such that $\vec{p}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{E}$. Find the amount of work done in rotating the dipole to a position at which $\vec{p}$ becomes antiparallel to $\vec{E}$.
questions.topic: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

answer.text:
(a) For a charged conducting shell, the field is zero inside up to $r=R$ and then varies as $E\propto\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$, decreasing beyond $r=R$.
(b) Since $V=\dfrac{kQ}{r}$, the slope of the graph is proportional to $Q$:
$\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2}=\dfrac{\tan60^{\circ}}{\tan30^{\circ}}=3$.
(c) $U=-pE\cos\theta$; for $\theta=0^{\circ}$:
$U=-(6\times10^{-7})\times(10^{4})=-6\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}$.
OR — Work done: $W=-pE(\cos\theta_2-\cos\theta_1)$ with $\theta_1=90^{\circ},\ \theta_2=180^{\circ}$:
$W=-pE(\cos180^{\circ}-\cos90^{\circ})=+pE$.

questions.text: The capacitors, each of 4 $\mu$F are to be connected in such a way that the effective capacitance of the combination is 6 $\mu$F. This can be achieved by connecting
options: Two of them connected in series and the combination in parallel to the third.
Two of them connected in parallel and the combination in series to the third.

answer.text: Two of them connected in series and the combination in parallel to the third.

questions.text: Depict the orientation of an electric dipole in (a) stable and (b) unstable equilibrium in an external uniform electric field. Write the potential energy of the dipole in each case.
questions.topic: Potential Energy in an External Field

answer.text:
(a) Stable equilibrium: the dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is aligned with the field $\vec{E}$ ($\theta=0^{\circ}$). Potential energy $U=-pE$ (minimum).
(b) Unstable equilibrium: the dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{E}$ ($\theta=180^{\circ}$). Potential energy $U=+pE$ (maximum).

questions.text: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. The two conductors have equal and opposite charges with a potential difference between them. The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the geometrical configuration (shape, size and separation) of the system and also on the nature of the insulator separating the two conductors. They are used to store charges. Like resistors, capacitors can be arranged in series or parallel or a combination of both to obtain desired value of capacitance. (i) Find the equivalent capacitance between points A and B in the given diagram. (ii) A dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor. The electric field between the plates decreases. Explain. (iii) A capacitor A of capacitance C, having charge Q is connected across another uncharged capacitor B of capacitance 2C. Find an expression for (a) the potential difference across the combination and (b) the charge lost by capacitor A.  OR  (iii) Two slabs of dielectric constants 2K and K fill the space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A and plate separation d as shown in figure. Find an expression for capacitance of the system.

answer.text:
(i) The bridge is balanced, so the middle capacitor carries no charge; each arm (two $C$ in series) gives $C$, and the two arms in parallel give
$C_{net}=C+C=2C$.
(ii) Within the dielectric slab, the induced electric field due to polarization reduces the net electric field:
$E=E_0-E_p=\dfrac{E_0}{K}$.
(iii) $V'=\dfrac{Q_{total}}{C_{eq}}=\dfrac{Q}{3C}=\dfrac{V}{3}$.
Charge on A now: $Q_A'=C\times\dfrac{V}{3}=\dfrac{Q}{3}$; originally $Q_A=CV=Q$. Charge lost by A: $\Delta Q=Q-\dfrac{Q}{3}=\dfrac{2Q}{3}$.
OR — Capacitance of the left portion $C_1=\dfrac{6K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ and of the right portion $C_2=\dfrac{3K\varepsilon_0 A}{2d}$; as they are in series,
$\dfrac{1}{C_{eq}}=\dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}=\dfrac{d}{6K\varepsilon_0 A}+\dfrac{2d}{3K\varepsilon_0 A}=\dfrac{5d}{6K\varepsilon_0 A}$, so $C_{eq}=\dfrac{6KA\varepsilon_0}{5d}$.

questions.text: Ten capacitors, each of capacitance 1 $\mu$F, are connected in parallel to a source of 100 V. The total energy stored in the system is equal to :

answer.text: $5\cdot0 \times 10^{-2}$ J

questions.text: (i) Derive an expression for potential energy of an electric dipole $\vec{p}$ in an external uniform electric field $\vec{E}$. When is the potential energy of the dipole (1) maximum, and (2) minimum ? (ii) An electric dipole consists of point charges $-1\cdot0$ pC and $+1\cdot0$ pC located at $(0, 0)$ and $(3\ \text{mm}, 4\ \text{mm})$ respectively in x $-$ y plane. An electric field $\vec{E} = 1000\ \dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\,\hat{i}$ is switched on in the region. Find the torque $\vec{\tau}$ acting on the dipole.

answer.text:
(i) Work done in rotating a dipole from $\theta_0$ to $\theta_1$ against the restoring torque $\tau_{ext}=pE\sin\theta$:
$W=\displaystyle\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_1}\tau_{ext}\,d\theta=\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_1}pE\sin\theta\,d\theta=pE(\cos\theta_0-\cos\theta_1)$.
Taking $\theta_0=90^{\circ}$ (reference) and $\theta_1=\theta$: $W=pE\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\cos\theta\right)$, so the potential energy is
$U(\theta)=-pE\cos\theta=-\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E}$.
(1) $U$ is maximum when $\vec{p}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{E}$ ($\theta=180^{\circ}$).
(2) $U$ is minimum when $\vec{p}$ is parallel to $\vec{E}$ ($\theta=0^{\circ}$).
(ii) Dipole moment magnitude $p=2aq$. Torque $\tau=pE\sin\theta=(2aq)E\sin\theta$; with the charge separation vector at $(3\ \text{mm},4\ \text{mm})$ and $E=1000\ \text{V/m}$ along $\hat{i}$, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}$:
$\tau=(5\times10^{-3}\times1\times10^{-12})\times10^{3}\times\dfrac{4}{5}=4\times10^{-12}\ \text{N m}$, directed along $-\hat{k}$.

questions.text: (i) An electric dipole (dipole moment $\vec{p} = p\hat{i}$), consisting of charges $-q$ and $q$, separated by distance 2a, is placed along the x-axis, with its centre at the origin. Show that the potential V, due to this dipole, at a point x, $(x \gg a)$ is equal to $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{\vec{p}\cdot\hat{i}}{x^2}$. (ii) Two isolated metallic spheres $S_1$ and $S_2$ of radii 1 cm and 3 cm respectively are charged such that both have the same charge density $\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{C}}{m^2}$. They are placed far away from each other and connected by a thin wire. Calculate the new charge on sphere $S_1$.

answer.text:
(i) For charges $-q$ at $(-a,0)$ and $+q$ at $(a,0)$, the potential at a point $P$ on the x-axis at distance $x$ from the origin is
$V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{q}{x-a}-\dfrac{q}{x+a}\right]=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{2a}{x^{2}-a^{2}}\right]=\dfrac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(x^{2}-a^{2})}$, since $p=2qa$ and $\vec p$ is along the x-axis:
$V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{\vec{p}\cdot\hat{i}}{x^{2}-a^{2}}$.
For $x\gg a$, $x^{2}-a^{2}\approx x^{2}$, so $V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{\vec{p}\cdot\hat{i}}{x^{2}}$.
(ii) Charge on each sphere: $Q_1=\sigma\times4\pi r_1^{2}=\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\times10^{-9}\right)\times4\pi(1\times10^{-2})^{2}=8\times10^{-13}\ \text{C}$; $Q_2=\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\times10^{-9}\right)\times4\pi(3\times10^{-2})^{2}=72\times10^{-13}\ \text{C}$.
When connected, charge is conserved and they reach a common potential $V$: $Q_1+Q_2=(C_1+C_2)V$, with $C_1=4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_1=\dfrac{1}{9}\times10^{-11}\ \text{F}$ and $C_2=4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_2=\dfrac{1}{3}\times10^{-11}\ \text{F}$:
$V=\dfrac{80\times10^{-13}}{\left(\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\times10^{-11}}=1{\cdot}8\ \text{V}$, so the new charge on $S_1$ is
$Q_1'=C_1V=\dfrac{1}{9}\times10^{-11}\times1{\cdot}8=2\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}$.

questions.text: (i) Obtain an expression for the electric potential due to a small dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$, at a point $\vec{r}$ from its centre, for much larger distances compared to the size of the dipole. (ii) Three point charges q, 2q and nq are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. If the potential energy of the system is zero, find the value of n.
questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

answer.text:
(i) At a point $P(r,\theta)$ due to a dipole ($\pm q$ separated by $2a$), $V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{q}{r_1}-\dfrac{q}{r_2}\right)$, with $r_1^{2}=r^{2}+a^{2}-2ar\cos\theta$ and $r_2^{2}=r^{2}+a^{2}+2ar\cos\theta$.
For $r\gg a$, retaining terms to first order in $\dfrac{a}{r}$ (using the binomial theorem):
$\dfrac{1}{r_1}\approx\dfrac{1}{r}\left(1+\dfrac{a\cos\theta}{r}\right),\qquad\dfrac{1}{r_2}\approx\dfrac{1}{r}\left(1-\dfrac{a\cos\theta}{r}\right)$.
$\therefore\ V=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2a\cos\theta}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{2}}$ (using $p=2qa$).
(ii) For charges $q,2q,nq$ at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $a$, potential energy
$U=\dfrac{k(q)(2q)}{a}+\dfrac{k(2q)(nq)}{a}+\dfrac{k(q)(nq)}{a}=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2q^{2}+2nq^{2}+nq^{2}=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2+3n=0$
$\therefore\ n=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.text: Consider a group of charges $q_1, q_2, q_3 \ldots$ such that $\Sigma q \neq 0$. Then equipotentials at a large distance, due to this group are approximately :

answer.text: Spherical surface

questions.text: A proton is taken from point $P_1$ to point $P_2$, both located in an electric field. The potentials at points $P_1$ and $P_2$ are $-5$ V and $+5$ V respectively. Assuming that kinetic energies of the proton at points $P_1$ and $P_2$ are zero, the work done on the proton is :

answer.text: $1\cdot6 \times 10^{-18}$ J

questions.text: The figure shows four pairs of parallel identical conducting plates, separated by the same distance $2.0$ cm and arranged perpendicular to x-axis. The electric potential of each plate is mentioned. The electric field between a pair of plates is uniform and normal to the plates. (i) For which pair of the plates is the electric field $\vec{E}$ along $\hat{i}$ ? (A) I (B) II (C) III (D) IV (ii) An electron is released midway between the plates of pair IV. It will : (A) move along $\hat{i}$ at constant speed (B) move along $-\hat{i}$ at constant speed (C) accelerate along $\hat{i}$ (D) accelerate along $-\hat{i}$ (iii) Let $V_0$ be the potential at the left plate of any set, taken to be at $x = 0$ m. Then potential V at any point $(0 \leq x \leq 2\ \text{cm})$ between the plates of that set can be expressed as : (A) $V = V_0 + \alpha x$ (B) $V = V_0 + \alpha x^2$ (C) $V = V_0 + \alpha x^{1/2}$ (D) $V = V_0 + \alpha x^{3/2}$ where $\alpha$ is a constant, positive or negative. (iv)(a) Let $E_1, E_2, E_3$ and $E_4$ be the magnitudes of the electric field between the pairs of plates, I, II, III and IV respectively. Then : (A) $E_1 > E_2 > E_3 > E_4$ (B) $E_3 > E_4 > E_1 > E_2$ (C) $E_4 > E_3 > E_2 > E_1$ (D) $E_2 > E_3 > E_4 > E_1$  OR  (iv)(b) An electron is projected from the right plate of set I directly towards its left plate. It just comes to rest at the plate. The speed with which it was projected is about : (Take $(e/m) = 1.76 \times 10^{11}$ C/kg) (A) $1.3 \times 10^5$ m/s (B) $2.6 \times 10^6$ m/s (C) $6.5 \times 10^5$ m/s (D) $5.2 \times 10^7$ m/s

answer.text:
(i) (D) IV.
(ii) (D) accelerate along $-\hat{i}$.
(iii) (A) $V=V_0+\alpha x$.
(iv)(a) (C) $E_4>E_3>E_2>E_1$.
OR (iv)(b) (B) $2{\cdot}6\times10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.text: (i) Obtain the expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric medium between its plates. (ii) A charge of 6 $\mu$C is given to a hollow metallic sphere of radius $0.2$ m. Find the potential at (i) the surface and (ii) the centre of the sphere.

answer.text:
(i) When a dielectric slab (constant $K$) is inserted between the plates, an induced (bound) charge density $\sigma_P$ appears which opposes the free charge density $\sigma$. The field in the dielectric is $E=\dfrac{\sigma-\sigma_P}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $V=Ed=\dfrac{(\sigma-\sigma_P)}{\varepsilon_0}d$.
Since $(\sigma-\sigma_P)=\dfrac{\sigma}{K}$: $V=\dfrac{\sigma d}{\varepsilon_0 K}=\dfrac{Qd}{A\varepsilon_0 K}$, hence $C=\dfrac{Q}{V}=\dfrac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$.
(ii) Potential due to a point charge: $V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r}$.
At the surface ($r=0{\cdot}2\ \text{m},\ q=6\ \mu\text{C}$): $V=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times6\times10^{-6}}{0{\cdot}2}=2{\cdot}7\times10^{5}\ \text{V}$.
Since the electric field inside the hollow sphere is zero, the potential is constant throughout the volume and equals the surface value: $V=2{\cdot}7\times10^{5}\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: Two charges $+q$ each are kept $2a$ distance apart. A third charge $-2q$ is placed midway between them. The potential energy of the system is :
questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

answer.text: $-\dfrac{7q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 a}$

questions.text: The electric field in a region is given by $\vec{E} = (10x + 4)\hat{i}$ where x is in m and E is in N/C. Calculate the amount of work done in taking a unit charge from (i) (5 m, 0) to (10 m, 0) (ii) (5 m, 0) to (5 m, 10 m).

answer.text:
(i) $\Delta V=-\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}E\,dx=-\int_{5}^{10}(10x+4)\,dx=-\left[\dfrac{10x^{2}}{2}+4x\right]_{5}^{10}=-395\ \text{V}$.
Work done: $W=q\Delta V=-395\times1=-395\ \text{J}$.
(ii) Moving from $(5\ \text{m},0)$ to $(5\ \text{m},10\ \text{m})$ is perpendicular to $\vec{E}$ (which is along $x$), so $\Delta V=-\displaystyle\int_{5}^{5}(10x+4)\,dx=0$ and $W=q\Delta V=0$.

questions.text: (i) A dielectric slab of dielectric constant 'K' and thickness 't' is inserted between plates of a parallel plate capacitor of plate separation d and plate area A. Obtain an expression for its capacitance. (ii) Two capacitors of different capacitances are connected first (1) in series and then (2) in parallel across a dc source of 100 V. If the total energy stored in the combination in the two cases are 40 mJ and 250 mJ respectively, find the capacitance of the capacitors.

answer.text:
(i) Field in the air gap between the plates $E_0=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$; field inside the dielectric slab (thickness $t$, constant $K$) $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0 K}$.
Potential difference $V=E_0(d-t)+Et=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\left[d-t+\dfrac{t}{K}\right]=\dfrac{q}{A\varepsilon_0}\left[d-t+\dfrac{t}{K}\right]$.
Hence $C=\dfrac{q}{V}=\dfrac{A\varepsilon_0}{d-t+\frac{t}{K}}=\dfrac{A\varepsilon_0}{d-t\left(1-\frac{1}{K}\right)}$.
(ii) Energy stored in series: $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{C_1 C_2}{C_1+C_2}\right)V^{2}=40\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}$  ...(1); energy stored in parallel: $\dfrac{1}{2}(C_1+C_2)V^{2}=250\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}$  ...(2).
With $V=100\ \text{V}$, solving (1) and (2): $C_1=4\times10^{-5}\ \text{F}=40\ \mu\text{F}$ and $C_2=1\times10^{-5}\ \text{F}=10\ \mu\text{F}$.

questions.text: Dielectrics play an important role in design of capacitors. The molecules of a dielectric may be polar or non-polar. When a dielectric slab is placed in an external electric field, opposite charges appear on the two surfaces of the slab perpendicular to electric field. Due to this an electric field is established inside the dielectric. The capacitance of a capacitor is determined by the dielectric constant of the material that fills the space between the plates. Consequently, the energy storage capacity of a capacitor is also affected. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series and parallel. (i) Which of the following is a polar molecule ? (A) $\text{O}_2$ (B) $\text{H}_2$ (C) $\text{N}_2$ (D) HC$l$ (ii) Which of the following statements about dielectrics is correct ? (A) A polar dielectric has a net dipole moment in absence of an external electric field which gets modified due to the induced dipoles. (B) The net dipole moment of induced dipoles is along the direction of the applied electric field. (C) Dielectrics contain free charges. (D) The electric field produced due to induced surface charges inside a dielectric is along the external electric field. (iii) When a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor, the energy stored in it : (A) increases and the electric field inside it also increases. (B) decreases and the electric field also decreases. (C) decreases and the electric field increases. (D) increases and the electric field decreases. (iv)(a) An air-filled capacitor with plate area A and plate separation d has capacitance $C_0$. A slab of dielectric constant K, area A and thickness $\left(\dfrac{d}{5}\right)$ is inserted between the plates. The capacitance of the capacitor will become : (A) $\left[\dfrac{4K}{5K+1}\right]C_0$ (B) $\left[\dfrac{K+5}{4}\right]C_0$ (C) $\left[\dfrac{5K}{4K+1}\right]C_0$ (D) $\left[\dfrac{K+4}{5K}\right]C_0$  OR  (iv)(b) Two capacitors of capacitances $2C_0$ and $6C_0$ are first connected in series and then in parallel across the same battery. The ratio of energies stored in series combination to that in parallel is : (A) $\dfrac{1}{4}$ (B) $\dfrac{1}{6}$ (C) $\dfrac{2}{15}$ (D) $\dfrac{3}{16}$

answer.text:
(i) (D) HCl.
(ii) (B) The net dipole moment of the induced dipoles is along the direction of the applied electric field.
(iii) (B) decreases, and the electric field also decreases.
(iv)(a) (C) $\left[\dfrac{5K}{4K+1}\right]C_0$.
OR (iv)(b) (D) $\dfrac{3}{16}$.

questions.text: (i) Draw equipotential surfaces for an electric dipole. (ii) Two point charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ are located at $\vec{r}_1$ and $\vec{r}_2$ respectively in an external electric field $\vec{E}$. Obtain an expression for the potential energy of the system. (iii) The dipole moment of a molecule is $10^{-30}$ Cm. It is placed in an electric field $\vec{E}$ of $10^5$ V/m such that its axis is along the electric field. The direction of $\vec{E}$ is suddenly changed by $60^\circ$ at an instant. Find the change in the potential energy of the dipole, at that instant.
questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

answer.text:
(i) The equipotential surfaces of an electric dipole are shown (they are everywhere perpendicular to the field lines; the plane bisecting the dipole is the zero-potential surface).
(ii) Work in bringing $q_1$ from infinity to $\vec{r}_1$: $W_1=q_1V(\vec{r}_1)$  ...(1). Work in bringing $q_2$ from infinity to $\vec{r}_2$ against the external field: $W_2=q_2V(\vec{r}_2)$  ...(2). Work done on $q_2$ against the field of $q_1$: $W_{12}=\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_{12}}$  ...(3).
Total potential energy of the system $U=q_1V(\vec{r}_1)+q_2V(\vec{r}_2)+\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_{12}}$.
(iii) Change in potential energy of a dipole rotated in a field: $W=pE[\cos\theta_0-\cos\theta_1]=10^{-30}\times10^{5}[\cos0^{\circ}-\cos60^{\circ}]=5{\cdot}0\times10^{-26}\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: (i) Two point charges 5 $\mu$C and $-1$ $\mu$C are placed at points $(-3$ cm, 0, 0$)$ and $(3$ cm, 0, 0$)$ respectively. An external electric field $\vec{E} = \dfrac{A}{r^2}\hat{r}$ where A $= 3 \times 10^5$ Vm is switched on in the region. Calculate the change in electrostatic energy of the system due to the electric field. (ii) A system of two conductors is placed in air and they have net charge of $+80\,\mu$C and $-80\,\mu$C which causes a potential difference of 16 V between them. (1) Find the capacitance of the system. (2) If the air between the capacitor is replaced by a dielectric medium of dielectric constant 3, what will be the potential difference between the two conductors ? (3) If the charges on two conductors are changed to $+160\,\mu$C and $-160\,\mu$C, will the capacitance of the system change ? Give reason for your answer.

answer.text: $\vec{E} = \dfrac{3\times10^{5}}{r^2}\hat{r}$ (given), $dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} \Rightarrow V = \dfrac{3\times10^{5}}{r}$. Electrostatic energy of the system in the absence of the field: $U_i = \dfrac{Kq_1q_2}{r_{12}}$. In the presence of the field: $U_f = \dfrac{Kq_1q_2}{r_{12}} + q_1V(\vec{r}_1) + q_2V(\vec{r}_2)$, so $\Delta U = U_f-U_i = q_1V(\vec{r}_1)+q_2V(\vec{r}_2) = \dfrac{5\times10^{-6}\times3\times10^{5}}{3\times10^{-2}} - \dfrac{1\times10^{-6}\times3\times10^{5}}{3\times10^{-2}} = 40\ \text{J}$. (ii)(1) $C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{80}{16} = 5\ \mu\text{F}$. (2) $C' = KC = 3\times5\ \mu\text{F} = 15\ \mu\text{F}$; $V' = \dfrac{Q}{C'} = \dfrac{80\ \mu\text{C}}{15\ \mu\text{F}} = 5{\cdot}33\ \text{V}$. (3) No — the capacitance of the system depends on its geometry.

questions.text: (i) Consider three metal spherical shells A, B and C, each of radius R. Each shell is having a concentric metal ball of radius R/10. The spherical shells A, B and C are given charges $+6q$, $-4q$, and $14q$ respectively. Their inner metal balls are also given charges $-2q$, $+8q$ and $-10q$ respectively. Compare the magnitude of the electric fields due to shells A, B and C at a distance 3R from their centres. (ii) A charge $-6$ $\mu$C is placed at the centre B of a semicircle of radius 5 cm, as shown in the figure. An equal and opposite charge is placed at point D at a distance of 10 cm from B. A charge $+5$ $\mu$C is moved from point 'C' to point 'A' along the circumference. Calculate the work done on the charge.

answer.text: Total charge for A = total charge for B = total charge for C $= +4q$. Using $E=\dfrac{kQ}{r^2}$: since $Q=4q$ and $r=3R$, $E = \dfrac{k(4q)}{9R^2} = \dfrac{4kq}{9R^2} \Rightarrow E_A=E_B=E_C$. (ii) $V_C = \left[\dfrac{k\times6\times10^{-6}}{5\times10^{-2}} - \dfrac{k\times6\times10^{-6}}{5\times10^{-2}}\right] = 0$. $V_A = \left[\dfrac{k\times6\times10^{-6}}{15\times10^{-2}} - \dfrac{k\times6\times10^{-6}}{5\times10^{-2}}\right] = \dfrac{k\times6\times10^{-6}}{10^{-2}}\left[\dfrac{1-3}{15}\right] = -\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times6\times10^{-6}\times2}{15\times10^{-2}} = -7{\cdot}2\times10^{5}\ \text{V}$. $W = q[V_A-V_C] = 5\times10^{-6}[-7{\cdot}2\times10^{5}-0] = -3{\cdot}6\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: A parallel plate capacitor has two parallel plates which are separated by an insulating medium like air, mica, etc. When the plates are connected to the terminals of a battery, they get equal and opposite charges and an electric field is set up in between them. This electric field between the two plates depends upon the potential difference applied, the separation of the plates and nature of the medium between the plates. (i) The electric field between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is E. Now the separation between the plates is doubled and simultaneously the applied potential difference between the plates is reduced to half of its initial value. The new value of the electric field between the plates will be : (A) E (B) 2E (C) $\dfrac{E}{4}$ (D) $\dfrac{E}{2}$ (ii) A constant electric field is to be maintained between the two plates of a capacitor whose separation d changes with time. Which of the graphs correctly depict the potential difference (V) to be applied between the plates as a function of separation between the plates (d) to maintain the constant electric field ? (options A, B, C, D shown in first figure) (iii) In the above figure P, Q are the two parallel plates of a capacitor. Plate Q is at positive potential with respect to plate P. MN is an imaginary line drawn perpendicular to the plates. Which of the graphs correctly shows the variations of the magnitude of electric field strength E along the line MN ? (options A, B, C, D shown in second figure) (iv)(a) Three parallel plates are placed above each other with equal displacement $\vec{d}$ between neighbouring plates. The electric field between the first pair of the plates is $\vec{E}_1$ and the electric field between the second pair of the plates is $\vec{E}_2$. The potential difference between the third and the first plate is : (A) $(\vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2)\cdot\vec{d}$ (B) $(\vec{E}_1 - \vec{E}_2)\cdot\vec{d}$ (C) $(\vec{E}_2 - \vec{E}_1)\cdot\vec{d}$ (D) $\dfrac{d(\vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2)}{2}$  OR  (iv)(b) A material of dielectric constant K is filled in a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C. The new value of its capacitance becomes : (A) C (B) $\dfrac{C}{K}$ (C) CK (D) $C\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{K}\right)$

answer.text: (i) (C) $\dfrac{E}{4}$. (ii) (D) [graph: $V$ rises linearly with $d$]. (iii) (C) [graph: field $E$ constant from M to N]. (iv) (A) $(\vec{E}_1+\vec{E}_2)\cdot\vec{d}$ [OR (C) $CK$].

questions.text: (i) A small conducting sphere A of radius r charged to a potential V, is enclosed by a spherical conducting shell B of radius R. If A and B are connected by a thin wire, calculate the final potential on sphere A and shell B. (ii) Write two characteristics of equipotential surfaces. A uniform electric field of 50 NC$^{-1}$ is set up in a region along $+$x axis. If the potential at the origin (0, 0) is 220 V, find the potential at a point (4m, 3m).

answer.text: (i) Potential on sphere A: $V = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, so charge on sphere A $= 4\pi\varepsilon_0 rV$. This charge is transferred to shell B, so potential on shell B $= \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\times\dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 rV}{R} = \dfrac{rV}{R}$. Hence potential on sphere A = potential on shell B. (ii) Characteristics of equipotential surfaces (any two): the potential at all points on the surface is the same; an equipotential surface is normal to the direction of the electric field; the work done in moving a charge on an equipotential surface is zero. $V_0 - V = Ed = 50\times4 \Rightarrow V_0-V = 200\ \text{V} \Rightarrow V = 220\ \text{V}-200\ \text{V} = 20\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: A parallel plate capacitor consists of two conducting plates kept generally parallel to each other at a distance. When the capacitor is charged, the charge resides on the inner surfaces of the plates and an electric field is set up between them. Thus, electrostatic energy is stored in the capacitor. The figure shows three large square metallic plates, each of side 'L' held parallel and equidistant from each other. The space between $P_1$ and $P_2$ and $P_2$ and $P_3$ is completely filled with mica sheets of dielectric constant 'K'. The plate $P_2$ is connected to point A and other plates $P_1$ and $P_3$ are connected to point B. Point A is maintained at a positive potential with respect to point B and the potential difference between A and B is V. (i) The capacitance of the system between A and B will be : (A) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 KL^2}{d}$ (B) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 KL^2}{2d}$ (C) $\dfrac{2\varepsilon_0 KL^2}{d}$ (D) $\dfrac{2\varepsilon_0 Kd}{L^2}$ (ii) The charge on plate $P_1$ is : (A) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 VKL^2}{2d}$ (B) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 VKL^2}{d}$ (C) $\dfrac{2\varepsilon_0 VKL^2}{d}$ (D) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 VKL^2}{4d}$ (iii) The electric field in the region between $P_1$ and $P_2$ is : (A) $\dfrac{V}{d}$ (B) $\dfrac{2V}{d}$ (C) $\dfrac{V}{2d}$ (D) $\dfrac{d}{V}$ (iv)(a) The separation between the plates of same area $(L^2)$ of a parallel plate air capacitor having capacitance equal to that of this system, will be : (A) $\dfrac{d}{K}$ (B) $\dfrac{2d}{K}$ (C) $\dfrac{d}{2K}$ (D) $\dfrac{d}{4K}$  OR  (iv)(b) If the source of potential difference applied between A and B is removed, and then A and B are connected by a conducting wire, the net charge on the system will be : (A) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 VKL^2}{4d}$ (B) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 VKL^2}{2d}$ (C) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 VKL^2}{d}$ (D) Zero

answer.text: (i) (C) $\dfrac{2\varepsilon_0KL^2}{d}$. (ii) (B) $\dfrac{\varepsilon_0VKL^2}{d}$. (iii) (A) $\dfrac{V}{d}$. (iv)(a) (C) $\dfrac{d}{2K}$ [OR (b) (D) Zero].

questions.text: (i) Two point charges $+q$ and $-q$ are held at $(a, 0)$ and $(-a, 0)$ in x-y plane. Obtain an expression for the net electric field due to the charges at a point $(0, y)$. Hence, find electric field at a far off point $(y \gg a)$. (ii) Three point charges of $-2$ nC, $-1$ nC, and $+5$ nC are kept at the vertices A, B and C of an equilateral triangle of side $0{\cdot}2$ m. Find the total amount of work done in shifting the charges from A to $A_1$, B to $B_1$ and C to $C_1$. Here $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ are the midpoints of sides AB, BC and CA, respectively.

answer.text: (i) Magnitude of the electric field due to the two charges $+q$ and $-q$: $E_{+q} = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{1}{y^2+a^2}$, $E_{-q} = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{1}{y^2+a^2}$. The components normal to the dipole axis cancel out; the components along the axis add up. The total electric field, opposite to the dipole moment, is $\vec{E} = -(E_{+q}+E_{-q})\cos\theta\,\hat{p} = -\dfrac{2qa}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(y^2+a^2)^{3/2}}\,\hat{p}$ ($\hat{p}$ is a unit vector along the dipole moment). At large distance ($y\gg a$): $\vec{E} = -\dfrac{2qa}{4\pi\varepsilon_0y^3}\,\hat{p}$. (ii) Triangle ABC with charges $q_A=-2\ \text{nC}$, $q_B=-1\ \text{nC}$, $q_C=5\ \text{nC}$ and midpoint triangle $A_1B_1C_1$. Initial electrostatic potential energy: $U_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{q_Aq_B}{AB}+\dfrac{q_Cq_A}{AC}+\dfrac{q_Cq_B}{BC}\right) = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}}{0{\cdot}2}\big[(-2\times-1)+(-2\times5)+(-1\times5)\big]\times10^{-18} = -5{\cdot}85\times10^{-7}\ \text{J}$. For the midpoint triangle (half the side length): $U_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{q_{A_1}q_{B_1}}{A_1B_1}+\dfrac{q_{C_1}q_{A_1}}{A_1C_1}+\dfrac{q_{C_1}q_{B_1}}{B_1C_1}\right) = -11{\cdot}7\times10^{-7}\ \text{J}$. Work done, $W = U_2-U_1 = -5{\cdot}85\times10^{-7}\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: A metal sheet is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C. If the sheet partly occupies the space between the plates, the capacitance :

answer.text: becomes greater than C

questions.text: The electric field at a point in a region is given by $\vec{E} = \alpha\,\dfrac{\vec{r}}{|\vec{r}|^3}$, where $\alpha$ is a constant and r is the distance of the point from the origin. The magnitude of potential of the point is :

answer.text: $\dfrac{\alpha}{r}$

questions.text: A parallel plate capacitor has plate area A and plate separation d. Half of the space between the plates is filled with a material of dielectric constant K in two ways as shown in the figure. Find the values of the capacitance of the capacitors in the two cases.

answer.text: (a) $\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{K\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d/2}\right)} + \dfrac{1}{\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d/2}} = \dfrac{d}{2K\varepsilon_0A}+\dfrac{d}{2\varepsilon_0A} = \left(\dfrac{1}{K}+1\right)\dfrac{d}{2\varepsilon_0A} \Rightarrow C = \left(\dfrac{2K}{K+1}\right)\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$. (b) $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0AK}{2d}+\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{2d} = \left(\dfrac{K+1}{2}\right)\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$.

questions.text: Two small solid metal balls A and B of radii R and 2R having charge densities $2\sigma$ and $3\sigma$ respectively are kept far apart. Find the charge densities on A and B after they are connected by a conducting wire.

answer.text: For ball A: $q_1 = 2\sigma\times4\pi R^2 = 8\pi R^2\sigma$. For ball B: $q_2 = 3\sigma\times4\pi(2R)^2 = 48\pi R^2\sigma$. Total charge $Q = q_1+q_2 = 56\pi R^2\sigma$. When balls A and B are connected by a wire, their potentials become equal. Let $q$ be the charge on ball A and $(Q-q)$ the charge on ball B after connecting: $\dfrac{Kq}{R} = \dfrac{K(Q-q)}{2R} \Rightarrow 2q = Q-q \Rightarrow q = \dfrac{Q}{3} = \dfrac{56\pi R^2\sigma}{3}$; $Q-\dfrac{Q}{3} = \dfrac{112\pi R^2\sigma}{3}$. $\sigma_A = \dfrac{56\pi R^2\sigma/3}{4\pi R^2} = \dfrac{14}{3}\sigma$. $\sigma_B = \dfrac{112\pi R^2\sigma/3}{4\pi(2R)^2} = \dfrac{7}{3}\sigma$.

questions.text: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. In practice, the two conductors have charges Q and $-$Q with potential difference $V = V_1 - V_2$ between them. The ratio $\dfrac{Q}{V}$ is a constant, denoted by C and is called the capacitance of the capacitor. It is independent of Q or V. It depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the two conductors and the medium separating the conductors. When a parallel plate capacitor is charged, the electric field $E_0$ is localised between the plates and is uniform throughout. When a slab of a dielectric is inserted between the charged plates (charge density $\sigma$), the dielectric is polarised by the field. Consequently opposite charges appear on the faces of the slab, near the plates, with surface charge density of magnitude $\sigma_p$. For a linear dielectric $\sigma_p$ is proportional to $E_0$. Introduction of a dielectric changes the electric field, and hence, the capacitance of a capacitor, and hence, the energy stored in the capacitor. Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series or in parallel or in a combination of series and parallel. (i) Consider a capacitor of capacitance C, with plate area A and plate separation d, filled with air [Fig. (a)]. The distance between the plates is increased to 2d and one of the plates is shifted as shown in Fig. (b). The capacitance of the new system now is : (A) $\dfrac{C}{4}$ (B) $\dfrac{C}{2}$ (C) 2C (D) 4C (ii) A slab (area A and thickness $d_1$) of a linear dielectric of dielectric constant K is inserted between charged plates (charge density $\sigma$) of a parallel plate capacitor [plate area A and plate separation d ($> d_1$)] and opposite charges with surface charge density of magnitude $\sigma_p$ appear on the faces of the slab. The dielectric constant K is given by : (A) $\dfrac{\sigma + \sigma_p}{\sigma}$ (B) $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sigma - \sigma_p}$ (C) $\dfrac{\sigma + \sigma_p}{\sigma_p}$ (D) $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sigma_p}$ (iii) An electric field E is established between the plates of an air filled parallel plate capacitor, with charges Q and $-$Q. V is the volume of the space enclosed between the plates. The energy stored in the capacitor is : (A) $\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$ (B) $\varepsilon_0 Q^2 E$ (C) $\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 V$ (D) $\varepsilon_0 E Q V$ (iv)(a) Three capacitors A, B and M, each of capacitance C are connected to a capacitor N of capacitance 2C and a battery as shown in the figure. If the charges on A and N are Q and Q$'$ respectively, then $\dfrac{Q'}{Q}$ is : (A) $\dfrac{1}{6}$ (B) $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (C) 3 (D) 6  OR  (iv)(b) A slab (area A and thickness $\dfrac{d}{2}$) of dielectric constant K is inserted in a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A and plate separation d. If C and $C_0$ are the capacitances of the capacitors with and without the dielectric, then $\dfrac{C}{C_0}$ is : (A) $\dfrac{K+1}{2K}$ (B) $\dfrac{2K}{K+1}$ (C) $\dfrac{K}{K-1}$ (D) $\dfrac{K-1}{K}$

answer.text: (i) (A) $\dfrac{C}{4}$. (ii) (B) $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sigma-\sigma_p}$. (iii) (C) $\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E^2V$. (iv)(a) (D) $6$ [OR (b) (B) $\dfrac{2K}{K+1}$].

questions.text: (i) The electric field in a region is given by $\vec{E} = 40x\,\hat{i}$ N/C. Find the amount of work done in taking a unit positive charge from the point (0, 3m) to the point (5m, 0). (ii) A charge Q is distributed over two concentric hollow spheres of radii r and R ($R > r$) such that their surface charge densities are equal. Find : (I) the electric field, and (II) the potential at their common centre.

answer.text: (i) $V = -\displaystyle\int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = -\int40x\,dx = -20x^2$. Potential at A$(0,3\text{m})$: $V_A=0$. Potential at B$(5\text{m},0)$: $V_B=-500\ \text{V}$. Work done in taking a unit positive charge from A to B: $W=q(V_B-V_A)=1(-500-0)=-500\ \text{J}$. (ii)(I) The electric field at the common centre will be zero, as the charge enclosed by the inner sphere is zero. (Alternatively: $q_{en}=0 \Rightarrow \phi_E=0 \Rightarrow \oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}=0 \Rightarrow E=0$.) (II) Since the surface charge densities are equal: $\dfrac{q}{4\pi r^2}=\dfrac{Q-q}{4\pi R^2} \Rightarrow q=\dfrac{Qr^2}{R^2+r^2}$. Potential at the common centre: $V = \dfrac{kq}{r}+\dfrac{k(Q-q)}{R} = \dfrac{k}{r}\cdot\dfrac{Qr^2}{R^2+r^2}+\dfrac{k}{R}\left[Q-\dfrac{Qr^2}{R^2+r^2}\right] = \dfrac{kQ(R+r)}{R^2+r^2}$.

questions.text: Two horizontal plates, separated by 1 cm, are arranged one above the other. A particle of mass 5 mg and charge 2 nC is released in air between the plates. The potential difference that should be applied to the plates so that the particle remains suspended between them, is :

(i) A parallel plate capacitor with plate area A and plate separation d has a capacitance $C_0$. A slab of dielectric constant K having area A and thickness $\left(\dfrac{d}{4}\right)$ is inserted in the capacitor, parallel to the plates. Find the new value of its capacitance. (ii) You are provided with a large number of 1 $\mu$F identical capacitors and a power supply of 1200 V. The dielectric medium used in each capacitor can withstand up to 200 V only. Find the minimum number of capacitors and their arrangement, required to build a capacitor system of equivalent capacitance of 2 $\mu$F for use with this supply.

answer.text: (i) $C_0=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$; $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{(d-t)+\frac{t}{K}}$; with $t=\dfrac{d}{4}$: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{\left(d-\frac{d}{4}\right)+\frac{d}{4K}} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d\left(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4K}\right)} = C_0\dfrac{4K}{3K+1}$. (Alternatively: when the dielectric is inserted, the field between the plates $E=\dfrac{E_0}{K}$; potential difference $V=E_0\left(\dfrac{3d}{4}\right)+E\left(\dfrac{d}{4}\right)=E_0\left(\dfrac{3d}{4}\right)+\dfrac{E_0}{K}\left(\dfrac{d}{4}\right)=V_0\left(\dfrac{3}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4K}\right)$; $V=V_0\dfrac{3K+1}{4K}$; $C=\dfrac{Q_0}{V}=\left(\dfrac{4K}{3K+1}\right)\dfrac{Q_0}{V_0}=C_0\left(\dfrac{4K}{3K+1}\right)$.) (ii) Each capacitor can withstand $200\ \text{V}$; number of capacitors in each row $=\dfrac{1200}{200}=6$; net capacitance of each row $=\dfrac{1}{6}\ \mu\text{F}$. Let the number of rows be $n$: $C_{eq}=\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{6}+\cdots(n\text{ terms}) \Rightarrow 2=\dfrac{n}{6} \Rightarrow n=12$. Total number of capacitors in the arrangement $=6\times12=72$.

questions.text: (i) An electric dipole of dipole moment p consists of point charges q and $-$ q, separated by 2a. Derive an expression for electric potential in terms of its dipole moment at a point at a distance x ($\gg$ a) from its centre and lying (I) along its axis, and (II) along its bisector line. (ii) An electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p} = (0{\cdot}8\hat{i} + 0{\cdot}6\hat{j}) \times 10^{-29}$ Cm is placed in an electric field $\vec{E} = 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^7\,\hat{k}\ \dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}$. Calculate the magnitude of the torque acting on it and the angle it makes with the x-axis, at this instant.
questions.topic: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

answer.text: I. Along the dipole axis: $V_- = -\dfrac{kq}{x+a}$; $V_+ = \dfrac{kq}{x-a}$; $V=V_-+V_+ = kq\left(-\dfrac{1}{x+a}+\dfrac{1}{x-a}\right) = \dfrac{kq\cdot2a}{x^2-a^2} = \dfrac{kp}{x^2-a^2}$; for $x\gg a$, $V=\dfrac{kp}{x^2}$. II. Along the bisector line: $V_- = \dfrac{kq}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}$; $V_+ = -\dfrac{kq}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}$; $V=V_-+V_+=0$. (ii) $\vec{\tau}=\vec{p}\times\vec{E} = (0{\cdot}8\hat{i}+0{\cdot}6\hat{j})\times10^{-29}\times(1\times10^{7})\hat{k} = [0{\cdot}8(-\hat{j})+0{\cdot}6\hat{i}]\times10^{-22}$; $\tau = \left[\sqrt{(0{\cdot}8)^2+(0{\cdot}6)^2}\right]\times10^{-22} = 10^{-22}\ \text{Nm}$; $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{|0{\cdot}8|}{0{\cdot}6} \Rightarrow \alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)=53^\circ$.

questions.text: In a region, the electric potential varies as $V = 10 - 50x$, where V is in volts and x in meters. The electric field in the region is :

answer.text: 50 N/C along $+$x

questions.text: A conducting wire connects two charged metallic spheres A and B of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively. The distance between the spheres is very large compared to their radii. The ratio of electric fields, $(E_A/E_B)$ at the surfaces of spheres A and B will be :

A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C has a dielectric slab between its plates. It is charged to a potential difference V by connecting it across a battery. The battery is then disconnected. If the dielectric slab is now withdrawn from the capacitor, how will the following be affected ? (a) Capacitance of the capacitor, (b) Energy stored in the capacitor, and (c) The potential difference between the plates of the capacitor. Justify your answer in each case.

answer.text: Effect of removing the dielectric slab (charge $Q$ kept constant): (a) Capacitance decreases: $C = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ becomes $C' = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \dfrac{C}{K}$. (b) Energy stored increases: $U = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C}$ becomes $U' = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C'} = KU$. (c) Potential difference increases: $V = \dfrac{Q}{C}$ becomes $V' = \dfrac{Q}{C'} = KV$.

questions.text: Figure shows a narrow beam of electrons entering with a velocity of $3 \times 10^7$ m/s, symmetrically through the space between two parallel horizontal plates $P_1 P_1'$ and $P_2 P_2'$ kept 2 cm apart. If each plate is 3 cm long, calculate the potential difference V applied between the plates so that the beam just strikes the end $P_2'$.

answer.text: For an electron deflected in the field between the plates: acceleration $a = \dfrac{qE}{m} = \dfrac{qV}{mL}$; time to cross the plates $t = \dfrac{x}{u_x}$; deflection $y = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{qV}{mL}\right)\left(\dfrac{x}{u_x}\right)^2$. Hence $V = \dfrac{2ymLu_x^2}{ex^2} = \dfrac{2\times1\times10^{-2}\times9{\cdot}1\times10^{-31}\times2\times10^{-2}\times(3\times10^{7})^2}{1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}\times(3\times10^{-2})^2} = 2275\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: Three point charges 2q, $-$2q and q are kept at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $l$. The potential energy of the system is
questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

answer.text: $\dfrac{-q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 l}$

questions.text: Two metal spheres of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ ($r_2 > r_1$) having charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ respectively kept in air, are brought in contact. Which of the following statements is $\underline{\text{not}}$ correct ?
options: The total charge of the two spheres is conserved.
Both spheres attain the same potential.
The final potential of the system equals $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(q_1+q_2)}{(r_1+r_2)}$
The final potential of the system equals $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(q_1+q_2)(r_1+r_2)}{r_1 r_2}$

answer.text: The final potential of the system equals $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(q_1+q_2)(r_1+r_2)}{r_1 r_2}$

questions.text: (a) An electric field $\vec{E} = E_0\,\hat{j}$ exists in a region of space. Draw three equipotential surfaces in the region. (b) Two point charges $-$q and $+$q are located at points $(-a, 0, 0)$ and $(a, 0, 0)$ respectively. Find the electrostatic potential at point $(x, 0, 0)$ where $x \gg a$.

answer.text: (a) Three equipotential surfaces for a uniform field (planes perpendicular to $\vec{E}$). (b) Potential at $P(x,0,0)$ for a dipole with $-q$ at $(-a,0,0)$ and $+q$ at $(+a,0,0)$: $V_{-q} = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{q}{x+a}$, $V_{+q} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{q}{x-a}$; net $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2qa}{x^2-a^2}$; for $x \gg a$, $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2qa}{x^2} = \dfrac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2}$.

questions.text: (a) Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A and plate separation d with air present between the plates. (b) Two air-filled capacitors of capacitances $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected in parallel with a dc battery. After the capacitors are fully charged, a slab of dielectric constant K is inserted between the plates of each capacitor. How will the (i) charge on each capacitor and (ii) energy stored in the capacitor affected after the slab is introduced.

answer.text: (a) Parallel-plate capacitor: field between the plates $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{q}{A\varepsilon_0}$; potential difference $V = Ed = \dfrac{qd}{A\varepsilon_0}$; capacitance $C = \dfrac{q}{V} = \dfrac{A\varepsilon_0}{d}$. (b) On inserting a dielectric slab (capacitors in parallel, same $V$): (i) each capacitance becomes $K$ times ($C' = KC$), so the charge on each becomes $K$ times: $q' = C'V = KCV = Kq$ (i.e. $q_1' = Kq_1$, $q_2' = Kq_2$). (ii) Energy stored $U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$ also becomes $K$ times: $U' = KU$.

questions.text: Capacitors are manufactured with certain standard capacitances and working voltages. However, these standard values may not be the ones that are actually needed in a particular application. Two or more capacitors can be grouped in series or in parallel to achieve desired capacitance and voltage. When connected in series, the total capacitance decreases while the voltage rating increases, whereas in parallel connections, the total capacitance increases and maintains the same voltage rating. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and stored energy is proportional to the square of the voltage and capacitance $U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$, where symbols have their usual meanings. Two capacitors, one of 3 $\mu$F and the other of 6 $\mu$F, are connected in series in the circuit as shown in the figure, for a long time. (i) The total capacitance of the circuit is : (A) 6 $\mu$F (B) 3 $\mu$F (C) 9 $\mu$F (D) 2 $\mu$F (ii) The current in the 10 $\Omega$ resistor is : (A) $0{\cdot}3$ A (B) $0{\cdot}6$ A (C) $0{\cdot}2$ A (D) 0 (iii) The potential difference between point A and B is : (A) 2 V (B) $0{\cdot}3$ V (C) $0{\cdot}2$ V (D) 3 V (iv)(a) The value of charge on the plates of the 6 $\mu$F capacitor is : (A) 6 $\mu$C (B) 4 $\mu$C (C) 12 $\mu$C (D) 8 $\mu$C  OR  (iv)(b) The wire between two capacitors is cut at point P. The current in the circuit will : (A) increase (B) decrease (C) remain the same (D) first increase then become stable

answer.text: (i) (D) $2\ \mu\text{F}$. (ii) (C) $0{\cdot}2\ \text{A}$. (iii) (A) $2\ \text{V}$. (iv) (B) $4\ \mu\text{C}$ [OR (C) remain the same].

questions.text: (a) (i) In the figure, OA and OB show the variation of electric potential V at a point due to two point charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ with $\dfrac{1}{r}$ respectively. Here r represents the distance of the point from the two point charges. (I) Identify the nature of the two charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$. (II) What is the value of $\left(\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2}\right)$ ? Justify your answer. (ii) Two point charges $-$ 2 $\mu$C and 5 $\mu$C are placed at $(-30$ cm, 0$)$ and $(30$ cm, 0$)$ respectively in an external electric field $\vec{E} = \dfrac{A}{x^2}\,\hat{i}$, where A $= 9 \times 10^5$ Nm$^2$ C$^{-1}$. Find the electrostatic potential energy of this configuration.
questions.topic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

answer.text: (a)(i)(I) From the $V$ vs $\dfrac{1}{r}$ graph, $Q_1$ is positive and $Q_2$ is negative. (II) $\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \dfrac{\text{slope of A}}{\text{slope of B}} = \dfrac{\tan60^\circ}{\tan30^\circ} = 3$. (ii) Potential $V(r) = -\displaystyle\int E\,dx = -\int\dfrac{A}{x^2}dx = \dfrac{A}{x}$; potential energy $U = q_1V(x_1) + q_2V(x_2) + \dfrac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x_{12}}$; substituting the given values $= (-6 + 15 - 0{\cdot}15)\ \text{J} = 8{\cdot}85\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain the following statements giving reason : (I) An equipotential surface through a point is normal to the electric field at that point. (II) When a dielectric is placed in an external electric field, the electric field inside the dielectric is less than that outside it. (III) The potential difference between the plates of a charged parallel plate capacitor decreases when its plates are brought closer. (ii) Obtain an expression for the work done to dissociate the system of three charges q, $-$ 4q and 2q placed at the vertices A, B and C respectively of an equilateral triangle of side 'a'.

answer.text: (a)(i)(I) The field is normal to an equipotential surface because otherwise it would have a component along the surface, and moving a charge along that surface against the field would need work — contradicting the definition of an equipotential surface ($\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 90^\circ$). (II) A dielectric placed in an external field gets polarised; the induced field opposes the external one, so the net field inside is reduced. (III) $V = \dfrac{Q}{C} = \dfrac{Qd}{A\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow V \propto d$, so bringing the plates closer (smaller $d$) decreases the potential difference. (ii) Interaction energy $W = k\left[\dfrac{q_1q_2}{a} + \dfrac{q_1q_3}{a} + \dfrac{q_2q_3}{a}\right] = \dfrac{k}{a}\big[(q)(-4q) + (q)(2q) + (-4q)(2q)\big] = -\dfrac{10kq^2}{a}$; hence work needed to dissociate $= +\dfrac{10kq^2}{a}$.

questions.text: The figure represents the variation of the electric potential V at a point in a region of space as a function of its position along the x-axis. A charged particle will experience the maximum force at :

answer.text: S

questions.text: Two parallel plate capacitors X and Y are connected in series to a 6 V battery. They have the same plate area and same plate separation but capacitor X has air between its plates, whereas capacitor Y contains a material of dielectric constant 4. (a) Calculate the capacitances of X and Y, if the equivalent capacitance of the combination of X and Y is 4 $\mu$F. (b) Calculate the potential difference across the plates of X and Y.

answer.text: $C_X = C$ and $C_Y = KC = 4C$ in series: $C_{eq} = \dfrac{C_XC_Y}{C_X+C_Y} = \dfrac{C\cdot4C}{5C} = 4\ \mu\text{F} \Rightarrow C = 5\ \mu\text{F}$, so $C_X = 5\ \mu\text{F}$ and $C_Y = 20\ \mu\text{F}$. Charge $Q = C_{eq}V = 4\times10^{-6}\times6 = 24\ \mu\text{C}$. Voltages $V_X = \dfrac{Q}{C_X} = \dfrac{24}{5} = 4{\cdot}8\ \text{V}$ and $V_Y = \dfrac{Q}{C_Y} = \dfrac{24}{20} = 1{\cdot}2\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: The electric potential (V) and electric field (E) are closely related concepts in electrostatics. The electric field is a vector quantity that represents the force per unit charge at a given point in space, whereas electric potential is a scalar quantity that represents the potential energy per unit charge at a given point in space. Electric field and electric potential are related by the equations $E_r = \dfrac{-dV}{dr}$ and $\vec{E} = E_r\,\hat{r}$, i.e., electric field is the negative gradient of the electric potential. A pair of square conducting plates having sides of length $0{\cdot}05$ m are arranged parallel to each other in x-y plane. They are $0{\cdot}01$ m apart along z-axis and are connected to a 200 V power supply as shown in the figure. An electron enters with a speed of $3 \times 10^7$ ms$^{-1}$ horizontally and symmetrically in the space between the two plates. Neglect the effect of gravity on the electron. (i) The electric field $\vec{E}$ in the region between the plates is : (A) $\left(2 \times 10^2\ \dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\right)\hat{k}$ (B) $-\left(2 \times 10^2\ \dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\right)\hat{k}$ (C) $\left(2 \times 10^4\ \dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\right)\hat{k}$ (D) $-\left(2 \times 10^4\ \dfrac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\right)\hat{k}$ (ii) In the region between the plates, the electron moves with an acceleration $\vec{a}$ given by : (A) $-(3{\cdot}5 \times 10^{15}\ \text{ms}^{-2})\hat{k}$ (B) $(3{\cdot}5 \times 10^{15}\ \text{ms}^{-2})\hat{k}$ (C) $(3{\cdot}5 \times 10^{13}\ \text{ms}^{-2})\hat{k}$ (D) $-(3{\cdot}5 \times 10^{13}\ \text{ms}^{-2})\hat{i}$ (iii)(a) Time interval during which an electron moves through the region between the plates is : (A) $9{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-9}$ s (B) $1{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-8}$ s (C) $1{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-9}$ s (D) $2{\cdot}17 \times 10^{-9}$ s  OR  (iii)(b) The vertical displacement of the electron which travels through the region between the plates is : (A) 10 mm (B) $4{\cdot}9$ mm (C) $5{\cdot}9$ mm (D) $3{\cdot}0$ mm (iv) Which one of the following is the path traced by the electron in between the two plates ? (A) a (B) b (C) c (D) d

answer.text: (i) (D) $(-2\times10^{4}\ \text{V/m})\hat{k}$. (ii) (B) $(3{\cdot}5\times10^{15}\ \text{m/s}^2)\hat{k}$. (iii)(a) (C) $1{\cdot}67\times10^{-9}\ \text{s}$ [OR (b) (B) $4{\cdot}9\ \text{mm}$]. (iv) (B) $b$.

questions.text: (a) Obtain the condition of balance of a Wheatstone bridge. (b) Find net resistance of the network of resistors connected between A and B, as shown in figure.

answer.text: Balanced Wheatstone-bridge condition, using Kirchhoff's rules with $I_g = 0$: loop ADBA gives $-I_1R_1 + I_2R_2 = 0$ and loop CBDC gives $I_4R_4 - I_3R_3 = 0$; with $I_1 = I_3$ and $I_2 = I_4$, this gives $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \dfrac{R_4}{R_3}$. (b) Net resistance of the network (the bridge is balanced $\Rightarrow R_{MN} = R$): $R_{AB} = R_{AM} + R_{MN} + R_{NB} = 2R + R + 3R = 6R\ \Omega$.

questions.text: (a) Two cells of emf $E_1$ and $E_2$ with internal resistances $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively, are connected in parallel by connecting their positive terminals together and negative terminals together. Deduce an expression for equivalent emf and equivalent internal resistance of the combination. (b) A parallel combination, as stated in (a) above, of two cells of emfs E and 3E and internal resistances R each is connected across a resistance 2R. Find the current that flows through resistance 2R.
questions.topic: Cells in Series and in Parallel

answer.text: (a) Two cells $(\varepsilon_1, r_1)$ and $(\varepsilon_2, r_2)$ in parallel: with $I = I_1 + I_2$ and $V = \varepsilon_1 - I_1r_1 = \varepsilon_2 - I_2r_2$, $V = \dfrac{\varepsilon_1 r_2+\varepsilon_2 r_1}{r_1+r_2} - I\cdot\dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2}$; so the equivalent emf $\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_1 r_2+\varepsilon_2 r_1}{r_1+r_2}$ and equivalent internal resistance $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2}$. (b) For cells $(E, R)$ and $(3E, R)$: $E_{eq} = \dfrac{ER + 3ER}{R+R} = 2E$, $r_{eq} = \dfrac{R}{2}$; current through the external resistance $2R$: $I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{2R + r_{eq}} = \dfrac{2E}{2R + R/2} = \dfrac{4E}{5R}$.

questions.text: (a) An electric field $\vec{E}$ is established across the ends of a cylindrical conductor of length L and area of cross-section A. Discuss how electrons attain an average velocity, independent of time. Hence, obtain a relation between current in the conductor and this 'average velocity' of electrons. (b) (i) This 'average velocity' is found be few mm/s for currents in range of a few amperes. How then is current established almost the instant a circuit is closed ? (ii) Two copper wires having their radii in the ratio of 3 : 2 are connected in series across a battery. Find the ratio of the drift velocities of the electrons in the wires.
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text: (a) Drift velocity $v_d = -\dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$ is independent of time because $\tau$ (average time between collisions) is constant; for $n$ free electrons per unit volume, the charge crossing a cross-section $A$ in time $\Delta t$ is $q = neA|v_d|\Delta t$, so current $I = neA|v_d|$. (b)(i) Current is established almost instantly because the electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, producing a local drift everywhere. (ii) $v_d = \dfrac{I}{ne\pi r^2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{v_{d1}}{v_{d2}} = \left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}$.

questions.text: (b) (i) Answer the following giving reason : (I) The electron drift speed is estimated to be only a few mm/s for currents in the range of a few amperes. How, then, is the current established almost the instant a circuit is closed ? (II) A low voltage supply from which one needs high currents must have very low internal resistance. Why ? (III) The assertion that V $=$ IR is a statement of Ohm's law is not true. Why ?

answer.text: (b)(i)(I) The current is established almost instantly because the electric field is set up throughout the circuit at nearly the speed of light, causing a local electron drift everywhere. (II) The maximum current from a cell, $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R+r}$, is largest when $R=0$ ($I_{max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}$), so it needs a low internal resistance. (III) Ohm's law requires the $I$–$V$ plot to be linear ($R$ independent of $V$); a diode does not obey this, so the assertion is not true. (ii) Two cells $(12\ \text{V}, 1\ \Omega)$ and $(6\ \text{V}, 0{\cdot}5\ \Omega)$ in parallel: $\varepsilon_{AB} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_1r_2+\varepsilon_2r_1}{r_1+r_2} = \dfrac{12\times0{\cdot}5+6\times1}{1{\cdot}5} = 8\ \text{V}$; internal resistance $r = \dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5\times1}{1{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{1}{3}\ \Omega$.

questions.text: For a metallic conductor, the correct representation of variation of resistance R with temperature T is :
The potential difference across a cell in an open circuit is 8 V. It falls to 4 V when a current of 4 A is drawn from it. The internal resistance of the cell is :

answer.text: $1\ \Omega$

questions.text: A steady current flows through a metallic wire whose area of cross-section (A) increases continuously from one end of the wire to the other. The magnitude of drift velocity ($v_d$) of the free electrons as a function of $'A'$ can be shown by :

questions.text: The following figure shows a circuit diagram. We can find the currents through and potential differences across different resistors using Kirchhoff's rules. Answer the following questions based on the above : (a) Which points are at the same potential in the circuit ? (b) What is the current through arm bg ? (c) Find the potential difference across resistance $R_3$.  OR  (c) What is the power dissipated in resistance $R_2$ ?

answer.text:
(a) The points $(a, b, c)$, $(d, e)$ and $(j, f, g, h)$ are each at the same potential (any two such points may be named).
(b) Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule:
Closed loop $abgha$:  $-6 + 10 I_2 + I_1 = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ I_1 + 10 I_2 = 6$  ...(i)
Closed loop $acfha$:  $-6 + 10(I_1 - I_2) + I_1 = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ 11 I_1 - 10 I_2 = 6$  ...(ii)
Adding (i) and (ii):  $12 I_1 = 12 \ \Rightarrow\ I_1 = 1\ \text{A}$, and hence $I_2 = 0{\cdot}5\ \text{A}$, which is the current through arm $bg$.
(c) Potential difference across $R_3$:  $V_{R_3} = (I_1 - I_2)R_3 = 0{\cdot}5\times5 = 2{\cdot}5\ \text{V}$.
OR — Power dissipated in $R_2$:  $P = (I_1 - I_2)^{2}R_2 = (0{\cdot}5)^{2}\times5 = 1{\cdot}25\ \text{W}$.

questions.text: Define current density and relaxation time. Derive an expression for resistivity of a conductor in terms of number density of charge carriers in the conductor and relaxation time.
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text:
Current density is the current flowing per unit area of cross-section of a conductor $\left(j=\dfrac{I}{A}\right)$.
Relaxation time is the average time interval between two successive collisions of the drifting electrons in a conductor.
From $I=nAe\,v_d$ and $v_d=\dfrac{eE}{m}\tau$:
$I=nAe\cdot\dfrac{eE}{m}\tau\ \Rightarrow\ j=\dfrac{I}{A}=\dfrac{ne^{2}E\tau}{m}$.
But $j=\dfrac{E}{\rho}$, therefore $\rho=\dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}$.

questions.text: A potential difference V is applied across a conductor of length $l$ and uniform cross-section area A. How will the (i) electric field E, (ii) drift velocity $v_d$, and (iii) current density $j$ be affected when (a) V is doubled and (b) $l$ is halved (keeping other factors constant) ?
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text:
(a) When $V$ is doubled:
(i) $E=\dfrac{V}{l}\ \Rightarrow\ E'=2E$ (electric field is doubled).
(ii) $v_d=\left(\dfrac{eE}{m}\right)\tau=\dfrac{e\tau}{m}\left(\dfrac{V}{l}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ v_d'=2v_d$ (drift velocity is doubled).
(iii) $J=\dfrac{I}{A}=\dfrac{V}{RA}\ \Rightarrow\ J$ is doubled.
(b) When $l$ is halved:
(i) $E=\dfrac{V}{l}\ \Rightarrow\ E'=2E$ (electric field is doubled).
(ii) $v_d=\left(\dfrac{eE}{m}\right)\tau=\dfrac{e}{m}\left(\dfrac{V}{l}\right)\tau\ \Rightarrow\ v_d'=2v_d$.
(iii) $J=\dfrac{I}{A}=\dfrac{V}{RA}=\dfrac{V}{A}\left(\dfrac{A}{\rho l}\right)=\dfrac{V}{\rho l}\ \Rightarrow\ J$ is doubled.

questions.text: Write two differences between the emf and terminal potential difference of a cell. What is the most important precaution that one should take while drawing current from a cell ?

answer.text:
Two differences between emf and terminal potential difference:
1. The potential difference across the electrodes in an open circuit is the emf $\varepsilon$, whereas in a closed circuit it is the terminal potential difference $V$.
2. $V$ depends on the internal resistance $r$, whereas $\varepsilon$ is independent of $r$.
Most important precaution: some external resistance should be connected in series with the cell (short-circuiting must be avoided).

questions.text: (i) Define mobility of electrons. Give its SI units. (ii) A steady current flows through a wire AB, as shown in the figure. What happens to the electric field and the drift velocity along the wire ? Justify your answer. (iii) Consider the circuit shown in the figure. Find the effective resistance of the circuit and the current drawn from the battery.
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text:
(i) Mobility is defined as the magnitude of the drift velocity per unit electric field, $\mu=\dfrac{|v_d|}{E}$. Its SI unit is $\dfrac{\text{m}^{2}}{\text{V s}}$ (or $\dfrac{\text{C s}}{\text{kg}}$).
(ii) As the cross-section of the wire increases along $AB$, both the electric field and the drift velocity decrease. Justification: from $v_d=\dfrac{I}{neA}$, as $A$ increases $v_d$ decreases; and from $v_d=\dfrac{eE}{m}\tau$, as $v_d$ decreases $E$ decreases (since $e,m,\tau$ are constant).
(iii) $10\ \Omega$ and $14\ \Omega$ are in series: $R_1=24\ \Omega$; $10\ \Omega$ and $10\ \Omega$ are in series: $R_2=20\ \Omega$. Then $24\ \Omega,\ 20\ \Omega,\ 30\ \Omega$ are in parallel:
$\dfrac{1}{R}=\dfrac{1}{24}+\dfrac{1}{20}+\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{5+6+4}{120}=\dfrac{15}{120}\ \Rightarrow\ R=8\ \Omega$.
Current: $I=\dfrac{V}{R}=\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}\ \text{A}$.

questions.text: (i) Define electrical conductivity of a wire. Give its SI unit. (ii) High current is to be drawn safely from (1) a low-voltage battery, and (2) a high-voltage battery. What can you say about the internal resistance of the two batteries ? (iii) Calculate the total energy supplied by the batteries to the circuit shown in the figure, in one minute.

answer.text:
(i) Electrical conductivity is the measure of a material's ability to carry a current through it (the reciprocal of resistivity; equivalently, the current density per unit electric field). Its SI unit is $\Omega^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}$ (or $\text{S m}^{-1}$).
(ii) For a low-voltage battery the internal resistance should be low; for a high-voltage battery the internal resistance should be high.
(iii) Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule: $10-I(1)-4-2I-6I-3I=0\ \Rightarrow\ 12I=6\ \Rightarrow\ I=0{\cdot}5\ \text{A}$.
Heat energy: $H=I^{2}Rt=0{\cdot}25\times12\times60=180\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: The potential difference applied across a given conductor is doubled. How will this affect (i) the mobility of electrons and (ii) the current density in the conductor ? Justify your answers.
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text:
(i) No effect on the mobility of the electrons. Justification: $\mu=\dfrac{v_d}{E}=\dfrac{e\tau}{m}$, which is a constant (independent of the applied potential difference).
(ii) The current density gets doubled. Justification: $J=\dfrac{I}{A}=\dfrac{V}{RA}$, so $J\propto V$; doubling $V$ doubles $J$.

questions.text: (i) Explain how free electrons in a metal at constant temperature attain an average velocity under the action of an electric field. Hence obtain an expression for it. (ii) Consider two conducting wires A and B of the same diameter but made of different materials joined in series across a battery. The number density of electrons in A is $1\cdot5$ times that in B. Find the ratio of drift velocity of electrons in wire A to that in wire B.

answer.text:
(i) Under an external field each electron experiences a force $\vec{F}=-e\vec{E}$ between collisions, so it accelerates with $\vec{a}=-\dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}$.
Velocity at any instant: $\vec{V}_i=\vec{v}_i-\dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}t_i$.
The drift velocity is the average of $\vec{V}_i$; since $(\vec{v}_i)_{avg}=0$ (random thermal motion),
$\vec{v}_d=-\dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}\tau$.
(ii) $v_d=\dfrac{I}{enA}=\left(\dfrac{4I}{en\pi D^{2}}\right)$, so for the same diameter and current $v_d\propto\dfrac{1}{n}$.
Given $n_A=1{\cdot}5\,n_B$: $\dfrac{v_{dA}}{v_{dB}}=\dfrac{n_B}{n_A}=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.text: (i) A cell of emf (E) and internal resistance (r) is connected across a variable load resistance (R). Draw plots showing the variation of terminal voltage V with (i) R and (ii) the current (I) in the load. (ii) Three cells, each of emf E but internal resistances 2r, 3r and 6r are connected in parallel across a resistor R. Obtain expressions for (i) current flowing in the circuit, and (ii) the terminal potential difference across the equivalent cell.
questions.topic: Cells in Series and in Parallel

answer.text:
(i) The plot of terminal voltage $V$ against external resistance $R$ rises from $0$ and saturates towards $E$; the plot of $V$ against current $I$ is a straight line from $(0,E)$ down to $(E/r,0)$.
(ii) For the three cells (of equal emf $E$ and internal resistances $2r,3r,6r$) in parallel:
$\dfrac{1}{r_{eq}}=\dfrac{1}{2r}+\dfrac{1}{3r}+\dfrac{1}{6r}=\dfrac{1}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ r_{eq}=r$, and $E_{eq}=E$.
Current: $I=\dfrac{E_{eq}}{R+r_{eq}}=\dfrac{E}{R+r}$.
Terminal potential difference: $V=E_{eq}-I r_{eq}=E-\dfrac{E}{R+r}\times r=\dfrac{ER}{R+r}$.

questions.text: Find the temperature at which the resistance of a wire made of silver will be twice its resistance at $20^\circ$C. Take $20^\circ$C as the reference temperature and temperature coefficient of resistance of silver at $20^\circ$C = $4\cdot0 \times 10^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$.

answer.text:
$R=R_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]$; given $R=2R_0$:
$2R_0=R_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]\ \Rightarrow\ 1=\alpha(T-T_0)$.
For silver, $\alpha\approx4\times10^{-3}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, so $T-T_0=\dfrac{1}{\alpha}=250$.
$\therefore\ T=T_0+250=270^{\circ}\text{C}$ or $543\ \text{K}$ (taking $T_0=20^{\circ}\text{C}$).

questions.text: Define current density. Is it a scalar or a vector ? An electric field $\vec{E}$ is maintained in a metallic conductor. If n be the number of electrons (mass m, charge $-e$) per unit volume in the conductor and $\tau$ its relaxation time, show that the current density $\vec{j} = \sigma\vec{E}$, where $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$.
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text:
Current density is the amount of charge flowing per second per unit area normal to the flow $\left(j=\dfrac{I}{A}\right)$; it is a vector quantity.
The charge crossing area $A$ in time $\Delta t$ is $I\Delta t$, where $I$ is the magnitude of the current, so
$I\Delta t=neA|v_d|\Delta t$.
With $|v_d|=\dfrac{e\tau}{m}|E|$: $I\Delta t=\dfrac{e^{2}A}{m}\tau n\Delta t|E|$, so $I=|j|A$ with
$|j|=\dfrac{ne^{2}}{m}\tau|E|$, i.e. $\vec{j}=\sigma\vec{E}$ (where $\sigma=\dfrac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}$ is the conductivity).

questions.text: What is a Wheatstone bridge ? Obtain the necessary conditions under which the Wheatstone bridge is balanced.

answer.text:
A Wheatstone bridge is an arrangement of four resistances $R_1,R_2,R_3,R_4$ forming a closed network (with a galvanometer $G$ across $BD$ and a battery across $AC$), used to determine an unknown resistance.
For loop $ADBA$: $-I_1R_1+I_2R_2+I_gG=0$  ...(1).
For loop $CBDC$: $I_4R_4-I_3R_3-I_gG=0$  ...(2).
For a balanced bridge $I_g=0$; applying Kirchhoff's junction rule at $B$ and $D$: $I_1=I_3$ and $I_2=I_4$.
From (1) and (2): $\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}$ and $\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\dfrac{R_4}{R_3}$,
$\therefore\ \dfrac{R_2}{R_1}=\dfrac{R_4}{R_3}$ (balance condition).

questions.text: Define resistivity of a conductor. How does the resistivity of a conductor depend upon the following : (a) Number density of free electrons in the conductor (n) (b) Their relaxation time ($\tau$)
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text:
Resistivity is the resistance offered by a material of unit length and unit cross-sectional area:
$\rho=\dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}$.
(a) $\rho\propto\dfrac{1}{n}$ (inversely proportional to the number density of free electrons).
(b) $\rho\propto\dfrac{1}{\tau}$ (inversely proportional to the relaxation time).

questions.text: The figure shows a circuit with three ideal batteries. Find the magnitude and direction of currents in the branches AG, BF and CD.

answer.text:
Applying Kirchhoff's rules to the given circuit (currents $I_1$ in CD, $I_2$ in BF, $I_3$ in AG, with $I_1+I_2=I_3$ at junction B):
Loop AGFBA: $3+2I_3-6+4I_2+2I_3=0\ \Rightarrow\ I_2+I_3=\dfrac{3}{4}$  ...(1).
Using $I_3=2I_1+I_2$: $2I_1+I_2=\dfrac{3}{4}$  ...(2).
Loop BFDCB: $-4I_2+6+2I_1-6+2I_1=0\ \Rightarrow\ I_2=I_1$  ...(3).
From (2) and (3): $I_1=I_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\ \text{A}$, and from (1): $I_3=\dfrac{1}{2}\ \text{A}$.

questions.text: When the terminals of a cell are connected to a conductor of resistance R, an electric current flows through the circuit. The electrolyte of the cell also offers some resistance in the path of the current, like the conductor. This resistance offered by the electrolyte is called internal resistance of the cell (r). It depends upon the nature of the electrolyte, the area of the electrodes immersed in the electrolyte and the temperature. Due to internal resistance, a part of the energy supplied by the cell is wasted in the form of heat. When no current is drawn from the cell, the potential difference between the two electrodes in known as emf of the cell ($\varepsilon$). With a current drawn from the cell, the potential difference between the two electrodes is termed as terminal potential difference (V). (i) Choose the incorrect statement : (A) The potential difference (V) between the two terminals of a cell in a closed circuit is always less than its emf ($\varepsilon$), during discharge of the cell. (B) The internal resistance of a cell decreases with the decrease in temperature of the electrolyte. (C) When current is drawn from the cell then $V = \varepsilon - Ir$. (D) The graph between potential difference between the two terminals of the cell (V) and the current (I) through it is a straight line with a negative slope. (ii) Two cells of emfs $2\cdot0$ V and $6\cdot0$ V and internal resistances $0\cdot1\ \Omega$ and $0\cdot4\ \Omega$ respectively, are connected in parallel. The equivalent emf of the combination will be : (A) $2\cdot0$ V (B) $2\cdot8$ V (C) $6\cdot0$ V (D) $8\cdot0$ V (iii) Dipped in the solution, the electrode exchanges charges with the electrolyte. The positive electrode develops a potential $+V_+$ $(V_+ > 0)$, and the negative electrode develops a potential $-(V_-)$ $(V_- \geq 0)$, relative to the electrolyte adjacent to it. When no current is drawn from the cell then : (A) $\varepsilon = V_+ + V_- > 0$ (B) $\varepsilon = V_+ - V_- > 0$ (C) $\varepsilon = V_+ + V_- < 0$ (D) $\varepsilon = V_+ + V_- = 0$ (iv)(a) Five identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance $0\cdot1\ \Omega$ are connected in parallel. This combination in turn is connected to an external resistor of $9\cdot98\ \Omega$. The current flowing through the resistor is : (A) $0\cdot05$ A (B) $0\cdot1$ A (C) $0\cdot15$ A (D) $0\cdot2$ A  OR  (iv)(b) Potential difference across a cell in the open circuit is 6 V. It becomes 4 V when a current of 2 A is drawn from it. The internal resistance of the cell is : (A) $1\cdot0\ \Omega$ (B) $1\cdot5\ \Omega$ (C) $2\cdot0\ \Omega$ (D) $2\cdot5\ \Omega$
questions.topic: Cells in Series and in Parallel

answer.text:
(i) The incorrect statement is: \"The internal resistance of a cell decreases with the decrease in temperature of the electrolyte\" — in fact internal resistance increases as the electrolyte's temperature decreases.
(ii) For two cells in parallel ($\varepsilon_1=2{\cdot}0\ \text{V},r_1=0{\cdot}1\ \Omega$; $\varepsilon_2=6{\cdot}0\ \text{V},r_2=0{\cdot}4\ \Omega$), the equivalent emf is
$\varepsilon_{eq}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_1/r_1+\varepsilon_2/r_2}{1/r_1+1/r_2}=\dfrac{20+15}{10+2{\cdot}5}=2{\cdot}8\ \text{V}$.
(iii) With no current drawn, $\varepsilon=V_++V_->0$.
(iv)(a) For 5 identical cells ($\varepsilon=2\ \text{V},\ r=0{\cdot}1\ \Omega$) in parallel, equivalent internal resistance $=\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{5}=0{\cdot}02\ \Omega$; total resistance $=9{\cdot}98+0{\cdot}02=10\ \Omega$, so
$I=\dfrac{2}{10}=0{\cdot}2\ \text{A}$.
OR (iv)(b) $V=\varepsilon-Ir\ \Rightarrow\ 4=6-2r\ \Rightarrow\ r=1{\cdot}0\ \Omega$.

questions.text: What is meant by relaxation time $\tau$ of free electrons in a conductor ? Show that the resistance of a conductor can be expressed by $R = \dfrac{m\,l}{ne^2\tau\,A}$, where symbols have their usual meanings.
questions.topic: Drift of Electrons and the Origin of Resistivity

answer.text:
Relaxation time $\tau$ is the average time between two successive collisions of an electron in the presence of an electric field.
Drift velocity of an electron: $v_d = \dfrac{eE}{m}\tau$   ...(i)
Current flowing through a conductor of length $l$ and area of cross-section $A$: $I = neAv_d$   ...(ii)
From (i) and (ii): $I = \dfrac{ne^2AE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{ne^2A\tau V}{ml}$
Therefore $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{ml}{ne^2\tau A}$.

questions.text: Draw the circuit diagram of a Wheatstone bridge. Obtain the condition when no current flows through the galvanometer in it.

answer.text:
For a balanced Wheatstone bridge the galvanometer current is zero ($I_g=0$). Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule to the closed loops $ADBA$ and $CBDC$:
$-I_1R_1+I_2R_2=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}$  ...(i).
$I_2R_4-I_1R_3=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\dfrac{R_4}{R_3}$  ...(ii).
Comparing (i) and (ii), the balance condition is $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}=\dfrac{R_4}{R_3}$.

questions.text: Determine the current in branches AB, AC and BC of the network shown in figure.

answer.text:
Applying Kirchhoff's rules to the network:
Loop $ADCA$: $10-4(I_1-I_2)+2(I_2+I_3-I_1)-I_1=0\ \Rightarrow\ 7I_1-6I_2-2I_3=10$  ...(i).
Loop $ABCA$: $10-4I_2-2(I_2+I_3)-I_1=0\ \Rightarrow\ I_1+6I_2+2I_3=10$  ...(ii).
Loop $BCDED$: $5-2(I_2+I_3)-2(I_2+I_3-I_1)=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2I_1-4I_2-4I_3=-5$  ...(iii).
Solving: current in branch $AB=I_2=\dfrac{5}{8}\ \text{A}$; current in branch $AC=I_1=2{\cdot}5\ \text{A}$; current in branch $BC=I_2+I_3=2{\cdot}5\ \text{A}$.

questions.text: Two electric heaters have power ratings $P_1$ and $P_2$, at voltage V. They are connected in series to a dc source of voltage V. Find the power consumed by the combination. Will they consume the same power if connected in parallel across the same source ?

answer.text:
For each heater, $R_1=\dfrac{V^{2}}{P_1}$ and $R_2=\dfrac{V^{2}}{P_2}$.
In series, $R_{eq}=R_1+R_2=V^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{P_1}+\dfrac{1}{P_2}\right)$, so $P_{series}=\dfrac{V^{2}}{R_{eq}}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{P_{series}}=\dfrac{1}{P_1}+\dfrac{1}{P_2}$.
For the parallel combination the total power is $P_{parallel}=P_1+P_2$; hence the power consumed is not the same in the two cases (No).

questions.text: What is the difference between 'emf' and 'terminal voltage' of a cell ? Two cells of emfs $E_1$ and $E_2$ and internal resistances $r_1$ and $r_2$ are connected in parallel. Derive an expression for the emf and internal resistance of the equivalent cell.

answer.text: (Any one difference) The potential difference between the terminals of a cell in open circuit is the emf, while in a closed circuit it is the terminal voltage. (Alternatively: emf does not depend on external resistance, while terminal voltage does; emf is the cause and terminal voltage is the effect.) Derivation: $V=E_1-I_1r_1$; $V=E_2-I_2r_2$; $I=I_1+I_2=\left(\dfrac{E_1-V}{r_1}\right)+\left(\dfrac{E_2-V}{r_2}\right)$. Comparing with $I=\dfrac{E_{eq}-V}{r_{eq}}$: $E_{eq}=\dfrac{E_1r_2+E_2r_1}{r_1+r_2}$; $r_{eq}=\dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2}$.
