questions.text: In a metallic conductor, an electron, moving due to thermal motion, suffers collisions with the heavy fixed ions but after collision, it will emerge out with the same speed but in random directions. If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be zero. When an electric field is applied, electrons move with an average velocity, known as drift velocity ($v_d$). The average time between successive collisions is known as relaxation time ($\tau$). The magnitude of drift velocity per unit electric field is called mobility ($\mu$). An expression for current through the conductor can be obtained in terms of drift velocity, number of electrons per unit volume (n), electronic charge ($-$e), and the cross-sectional area (A) of the conductor. This expression leads to an expression between current density ($\vec{j}$) and the electric field ($\vec{E}$). Hence, an expression for resistivity ($\rho$) of a metal is obtained. This expression helps us to understand increase in resistivity of a metal with increase in its temperature, in terms of change in the relaxation time ($\tau$) and change in the number density of electrons (n). The conductivity of the material of the wire (in $\Omega^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$) is : (A) $2{\cdot}5 \times 10^4$ (B) $3{\cdot}0 \times 10^5$ (C) $3{\cdot}75 \times 10^6$ (D) $5{\cdot}0 \times 10^7$ (iii) The temperature coefficient of resistance of nichrome is $1{\cdot}70 \times 10^{-4}\ ^\circ$C$^{-1}$. In order to increase resistance of a nichrome wire by $8{\cdot}5\%$, the temperature of the wire should be increased by : (A) $250^\circ$C (B) $500^\circ$C (C) $850^\circ$C (D) $1000^\circ$C (iv)(a) Consider the contribution of the following two factors I and II in resistivity of a metal : I. Relaxation time of electrons  II. Number of electrons per unit volume. The resistivity of a metal increases with increase in its temperature because : (A) I decreases and II increases. (B) I increases and II is almost constant. (C) Both I and II increase. (D) I decreases and II is almost constant.  OR  (iv)(b) A steady current flows in a copper wire of non-uniform cross-section. Consider the following three physical quantities : I. Electric field  II. Current density  III. Drift speed. Then at the different points along the wire : (A) II and III change, but I is constant. (B) I and II change, but III is constant. (C) I and III change, but II is constant. (D) All I, II and III change.

answer.text: (i) (D) $1$. (ii) (C) $3{\cdot}75\times10^{6}$. (iii) (B) $500^\circ\text{C}$. (iv)(a) (D) I decreases and II is almost constant [OR (b) (D) all I, II and III change].

questions.text: State Kirchhoff's rules. Using these rules, find the current flowing through branch FC in the given circuit.

answer.text: (a) Kirchhoff's rules: Junction rule — the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it (conservation of charge). Loop rule — the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero (conservation of energy). (b) Current through branch FC: loop AFCBA gives $4i_1 - i_2 = 0 \Rightarrow 4i_1 = i_2\ \ldots(i)$; loop FEDCF gives $4i_1 + 5i_2 = 2\ \ldots(ii)$; solving (i) and (ii), $i_1 = \dfrac{1}{12}\ \text{A}$ and $i_2 = \dfrac{1}{3}\ \text{A}$ (current through FC $= \dfrac{1}{3}\ \text{A}$).

questions.text: (a) An electric iron rated $2{\cdot}2$ kW, 220 V is operated at 110 V supply. Find : (i) its resistance, and (ii) heat produced by it in 10 minutes.

answer.text: Resistance of the heater $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{(220)^2}{2{\cdot}2\times10^{3}} = 22\ \Omega$. Operated at $110\ \text{V}$ for $10\ \text{min}$, current $I = \dfrac{110}{22} = 5\ \text{A}$ and heat produced $H = I^2Rt = 5^2\times22\times600 = 3{\cdot}3\times10^{5}\ \text{J}$.

questions.text: (b) A current of $4{\cdot}0$ A flows through a wire of length 1 m and cross-sectional area $1{\cdot}0$ mm$^2$, when potential difference of 2 V is applied across its ends. Calculate the resistivity of the material of the wire.

answer.text: Resistivity of the wire $\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l}$, with $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{2}{4} = 0{\cdot}5\ \Omega$, $A = 1\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$ and $l = 1\ \text{m} \Rightarrow \rho = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5\times1\times10^{-6}}{1} = 5\times10^{-7}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}$.

questions.text: (a) (i) Derive the condition for which a Wheatstone Bridge is balanced. (ii) Determine the current in 3 $\Omega$ branch of a Wheatstone Bridge in the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text: (a)(i) Balanced Wheatstone bridge (galvanometer current $I_g = 0$): Kirchhoff's loop rule for ADBA gives $-I_1R_1 + I_2R_2 = 0$ and for CBDC gives $I_2R_4 - I_1R_3 = 0$; dividing, $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \dfrac{R_4}{R_3}$ (the balance condition). (ii) Current in the $3\ \Omega$ branch of the given network, using Kirchhoff's rules: loop ABDA gives $-20I_1 - 3I_2 + 12(I-I_1) = 0$; loop BCDB gives $-2(I_1-I_2) + 1(I-I_1+I_2) + 3I_2 = 0$; loop EADCE gives $-12(I-I_1) - 1(I-I_1+I_2) = -6$; solving these, $I_2 = \dfrac{12}{821} \approx 0{\cdot}014\ \text{A}$.

questions.text: (b) (i) Consider a cylindrical conductor of length $l$ and area of cross-section A. Current I is maintained in the conductor and electrons drift with velocity $v_d$ $\left(|\vec{v}_d| = \dfrac{e|\vec{E}|}{m}\,\tau\right)$, (where symbols have their usual meanings). Show that the conductivity $\sigma$ of the material of the conductor is given by $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2}{m}\,\tau$. (ii) The resistance of a metal wire at $20^\circ$C is $1{\cdot}05\ \Omega$ and at $100^\circ$C is $1{\cdot}38\ \Omega$. Determine the temperature coefficient of resistivity of this metal.

answer.text: (b)(i) Conductivity $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$: with $n$ free electrons per unit volume, the charge crossing a cross-section $A$ in time $\Delta t$ is $Q = neAv_d\Delta t$, so $I = neAv_d$; using drift velocity $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, current density $J = \dfrac{I}{A} = ne\cdot\dfrac{eE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}E$; comparing with $J = \sigma E \Rightarrow \sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$. (ii) Temperature coefficient of resistance $\alpha = \dfrac{R_2-R_1}{R_1(T_2-T_1)} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}38-1{\cdot}05}{1{\cdot}05\times(100-20)} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}33}{84} \approx 0{\cdot}0039\ {}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$.

questions.text: An alpha particle is projected with velocity $\vec{v} = (3{\cdot}0 \times 10^5\ \text{m/s})\,\hat{i}$ into a region in which magnetic field $\vec{B} = [(0{\cdot}4\ \text{T})\hat{i} + (0{\cdot}3\ \text{T})\hat{j}]$ exists. Calculate the acceleration of the particle in the region. $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ are unit vectors along x, y and z axis respectively and charge to mass ratio for alpha particle is $4{\cdot}8 \times 10^7$ C/kg.

answer.text:
$\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = q\,(3\times10^{5}\,\hat{i})\times(0{\cdot}4\,\hat{i}+0{\cdot}3\,\hat{j})$
$= q\,(3\times10^{5})(0{\cdot}3)(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}) = q\,(0{\cdot}9\times10^{5}\,\hat{k})\ \text{N}$
Since $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$,  $\vec{a} = \dfrac{q}{m}\,(0{\cdot}9\times10^{5}\,\hat{k})$.
For an $\alpha$-particle $\dfrac{q}{m} = 4{\cdot}8\times10^{7}\ \text{C/kg}$, so
$\vec{a} = (4{\cdot}8\times10^{7})(0{\cdot}9\times10^{5})\,\hat{k} = 4{\cdot}32\times10^{12}\,\hat{k}\ \text{ms}^{-2}$
(the acceleration is directed along $+\hat{k}$).

questions.text: (i) State Biot-Savart's law for the magnetic field due to a current carrying element. Use this law to obtain an expression for the magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop of radius $'a'$ and carrying a current $'I'$. Draw the magnetic field lines for a current loop indicating the direction of magnetic field. (ii) An electron is revolving around the nucleus in a circular orbit with a speed of $10^7$ m s$^{-1}$. If the radius of the orbit is $10^{-10}$ m, find the current constituted by the revolving electron in the orbit.
questions.topic: Magnetic Field due to a Current Element, Biot-Savart Law

answer.text:
(i) Biot-Savart law: the magnetic field due to a current element $I\,d\vec{l}$ is
$d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{a^{2}}$.
At the centre of a circular loop of radius $a$, $d\vec{l}\perp\hat{r}$, so $\theta = 90^{\circ},\ \sin 90^{\circ} = 1$ and
$dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{a^{2}}$.
Magnetic field at the centre (integrating over the loop, $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi a} dl = 2\pi a$):
$B = \displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi a}\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{a^{2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{a^{2}}\,(2\pi a) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2a}$.
(ii) For the orbiting electron ($q = e,\ v = 10^{7}\ \text{ms}^{-1},\ r = 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$), the equivalent current is
$i = \dfrac{q}{T} = \dfrac{qv}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}\times10^{7}}{2\times\pi\times10^{-10}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}8}{\pi}\times10^{-2}\ \text{A}$
$i = 0{\cdot}255\times10^{-2}\ \text{A} = 2{\cdot}55\ \text{mA}$.

questions.text: (i) Derive an expression for the force acting on a current carrying straight conductor kept in a magnetic field. State the rule which is used to find the direction of this force. Give the condition under which this force is (1) maximum, and (2) minimum. (ii) Two long parallel straight wires A and B are $2{\cdot}5$ cm apart in air. They carry $5{\cdot}0$ A and $2{\cdot}5$ A currents respectively in opposite directions. Calculate the magnitude of the force exerted by wire A on a 10 cm length of wire B.

answer.text:
(i) Consider a rod of area $A$, length $l$, with $n$ mobile charge carriers per unit volume, so total carriers $= n l A$. For a steady current $I$ with drift velocity $\vec{v}_d$, the force in an external field $\vec{B}$ is
$\vec{F} = n l A\,q\,(\vec{v}_d\times\vec{B}) = [\vec{j}\,A l]\times\vec{B} = I(\vec{l}\times\vec{B})$,
where $\vec{j} = nq\vec{v}_d$ is the current density and $|\vec{j}|A = I$ is the current.
Fleming's left-hand rule: if the forefinger, middle finger and thumb are stretched mutually perpendicular so that the forefinger points along $\vec{B}$ and the middle finger along the current, the thumb points along the force on the conductor.
Condition for maximum force: $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, $|\vec{F}| = BIl\sin\theta = BIl$.
Condition for minimum force: $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$, $|\vec{F}| = 0$.
(ii) Force between the two parallel wires:
$F = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2 I_1 I_2}{d}\,l = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times2\times5\times2{\cdot}5}{2{\cdot}5\times10^{-2}}\times10\times10^{-2}\ \text{N} = 10^{-5}\ \text{N}$.

questions.text: A wire of length $l$ is in the form of a circular loop A of one turn. This loop is reshaped into loop B of three turns. Find the ratio of the magnetic fields at the centres of loop A and loop B for the same current through them.

answer.text:
For a circular loop, $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2r}$, and its length is $l=2\pi r$.
Loop A (1 turn): $l=2\pi r_A$. Loop B (3 turns): $l=3(2\pi r_B)$, so $r_B=\dfrac{r_A}{3}$.
$\dfrac{B_A}{B_B}=\dfrac{\mu_0 N_A I/(2r_A)}{\mu_0 N_B I/(2r_B)}=\dfrac{N_A}{N_B}\cdot\dfrac{r_B}{r_A}=\dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}$
$\therefore\ \dfrac{B_A}{B_B}=\dfrac{1}{9}$.

questions.text: (i) Write the principle and explain the working of a moving coil galvanometer. A galvanometer as such cannot be used to measure the current in a circuit. Why ? (ii) Why is the magnetic field made radial in a moving coil galvanometer ? How is it achieved ?

answer.text:
(i) Principle: when a rectangular coil carrying current $I$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field, it experiences a torque.
Working: the torque on the coil is $\tau=NiAB\sin\theta$; for a radial field $\sin\theta=1$, so $\tau=NiAB$. The spring provides a restoring torque $k\phi$. In equilibrium $k\phi=NiAB$, giving
$\phi=\left(\dfrac{NAB}{k}\right)i$ (the deflection is proportional to the current).
A galvanometer cannot be used as such to measure current because it has a large resistance (it would change the circuit current) and is a very sensitive device.
(ii) The field is made radial so that the coil's magnetic moment $\vec{m}$ is always perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ (i.e. $\sin\theta=1$ always), which makes the scale linear. This is achieved by using concave (curved) pole pieces along with a soft-iron cylindrical core.

questions.text: (i) Derive an expression for magnetic field on the axis of a current carrying circular loop. (ii) Write any two points of difference between a diamagnetic and a paramagnetic substance.
questions.topic: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop

answer.text:
(i) By the Biot-Savart law, $d\vec{B}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,|d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}|}{r^{3}}$; for a point on the axis, $dB=\dfrac{\mu_0 I\,dl\sin90^{\circ}}{4\pi(x^{2}+R^{2})}$.
The perpendicular components $dB_\perp$ cancel; the axial components add:
$B=\displaystyle\int dB\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\dfrac{I\,dl}{(x^{2}+R^{2})}\cdot\dfrac{R}{(x^{2}+R^{2})^{1/2}}=\dfrac{\mu_0 IR}{4\pi(x^{2}+R^{2})^{3/2}}(2\pi R)$
$\vec{B}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I R^{2}}{2(x^{2}+R^{2})^{3/2}}\,\hat{i}$.
(ii) Differences between diamagnetic and paramagnetic substances (any two):

rows: Susceptibility is a small positive number.
Relative permeability is slightly greater than $1$.
Tends to move from a stronger to a weaker field; repelled by a magnet.
Tends to move from a weaker to a stronger field; weakly attracted by a magnet.
Field inside the material is reduced (field lines are expelled).
Field inside the material is slightly enhanced (field lines crowd in).

questions.text: A beam of electrons moving horizontally with a velocity of $3 \times 10^7$ m/s enters a region between two plates as shown in the figure. A suitable potential difference is applied across the plates such that the electron beam just strikes the edge of the lower plate. Answer the following questions based on the above : (a) How long does an electron take to strike the edge ? (b) What is the shape of the path followed by the electron and why ? (c) Find the potential difference applied.  OR  (c) Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field which should be created in the space between the plates so that the electron beam goes straight undeviated.

answer.text:
(a) The electron strikes the edge after travelling $3\ \text{cm}$ horizontally (along the x-axis):
$S_x=v_x\,t\ \Rightarrow\ 3\times10^{-2}=(3\times10^{7})\,t\ \Rightarrow\ t=10^{-9}\ \text{s}$.
(b) The path is a parabola, because the force (acceleration) is constant and acts in a fixed direction perpendicular to the initial velocity.
(c) Along the y-direction, $S_y=u_y t+\dfrac{1}{2}a_y t^{2}$:
$-0{\cdot}5\times10^{-2}=0+\dfrac{1}{2}a_y(10^{-9})^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ a_y=-10^{16}\ \text{m/s}^{2}$.
Since $a_y=\dfrac{eE}{m}=\dfrac{e}{m}\left(\dfrac{V}{l}\right)$:
$V=\dfrac{10^{16}\times9{\cdot}1\times10^{-31}\times1\times10^{-2}}{1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}}=568{\cdot}75\ \text{V}$.
OR — For a magnetic field balancing the electric force, $|qE|=|qvB|$, so $B=\dfrac{E}{v}=\left(\dfrac{ma_y}{e}\right)\dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{9{\cdot}1\times10^{-31}\times10^{16}}{1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}}\times\dfrac{1}{3\times10^{7}}=1{\cdot}9\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}$, directed out of the plane of the paper.

questions.text: Two circular loops A and B, each of radius 3 m, are placed coaxially at a distance of 4 m. They carry currents of 3 A and 2 A in opposite directions respectively. Find the net magnetic field at the centre of loop A.
questions.topic: Magnetic Field due to a Current Element, Biot-Savart Law

answer.text:
For loop A (at its centre): $B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3}{2\times3}=2\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}=6{\cdot}28\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}$.
For loop B (on the axis of A, at $x=4\ \text{m}$): $B_2=\dfrac{\mu_0 I R^{2}}{2(R^{2}+x^{2})^{3/2}}=\dfrac{2\pi\times10^{-7}\times2\times9}{(3^{2}+4^{2})^{3/2}}=\dfrac{36\pi\times10^{-7}}{125}=0{\cdot}9\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}$, directed opposite to $B_1$.
Net field: $B_{net}=B_1-B_2=6{\cdot}28\times10^{-7}-0{\cdot}9\times10^{-7}=5{\cdot}38\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}$.

questions.text: Write the expression for the Lorentz force on a particle of charge q moving with a velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. When is the magnitude of this force minimum ? Show that no work is done by this force on the particle during its motion from a point $\vec{r}_1$ to a point $\vec{r}_2$.

answer.text:
Lorentz (magnetic) force: $\vec{F}_m=q\,(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$, with magnitude $F_m=qvB\sin\theta$.
The magnitude is maximum for $\theta=90^{\circ}$ ($F_m=qvB$).
Since the magnetic force always acts perpendicular to the velocity, no work is done by it on the particle.
Alternatively, $W=\vec{F}\cdot(\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1)=F\,|\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1|\cos90^{\circ}=0$.

questions.text: A straight wire AB carries a current I. A particle (mass m and charge q) moves with a velocity $\vec{v}$, parallel to the wire, at a distance d from it as shown in the figure. Obtain the expression for the force experienced by the particle and mention its directions.

answer.text:
The magnetic field produced by the current-carrying conductor $AB$ at the particle is $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$, directed into the plane of the paper.
Force experienced by the charged particle: $\vec{F}_m=q\,(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$; since $\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}$,
$F_m=qvB\sin90^{\circ}=qv\cdot\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$.
The force is repulsive — it acts away from the conductor (towards the right).

questions.text: Two long, straight, parallel conductors carry steady currents in opposite directions. Explain the nature of the force of interaction between them. Obtain an expression for the magnitude of the force between the two conductors. Hence define one ampere.
questions.topic: Force between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

answer.text:
The nature of the force between the two parallel current-carrying conductors is repulsive (for currents in opposite directions).
The field due to $I_a$ at conductor $b$ is $B_{ab}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_a}{2\pi d}$ (directed downwards); the force on a length $l$ of $b$ is
$F_{ab}=I_b l B_{ab}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_a I_b}{2\pi d}l$ (directed towards $b$, i.e. attractive/repulsive per the current directions).
By Newton's third law, $F_{ba}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_a I_b}{2\pi d}l$ acts on $a$ in the opposite direction.
One ampere is the steady current which, when maintained in each of two very long straight parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed $1\ \text{m}$ apart in vacuum, produces a force of $2\times10^{-7}\ \text{N/m}$ on each conductor.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the torque $\vec{\tau}$ acting on a current carrying loop in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. Draw the necessary diagram.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text:
For a rectangular current loop $ABCD$ (sides $a,b$, current $I$) in a uniform field $B$: the forces on arms $BC$ and $DA$ are equal, opposite, and collinear (along the axis), so they cancel. The forces on arms $AB$ and $CD$, $F_1=F_2=IbB$, are equal, opposite, but not collinear — they form a couple.
Torque: $\tau=F_1\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta+F_2\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta=IabB\sin\theta=IAB\sin\theta$ (where $A=ab$).
With magnetic moment $\vec{m}=I\vec{A}$: $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$.

questions.text: (i) A particle of mass m and charge q is moving with a velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ as shown in the figure. Show that it follows a helical path. Hence, obtain its frequency of revolution. (ii) In a hydrogen atom, the electron moves in an orbit of radius 2 Å making $8 \times 10^{14}$ revolutions per second. Find the magnetic moment associated with the orbital motion of the electron.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text:
(i) The velocity components are $v_\perp=v\sin\theta$ (perpendicular to $\vec{B}$) and $v_\parallel=v\cos\theta$ (parallel to $\vec{B}$). $v_\perp$ makes the charge trace a circular path, while $v_\parallel$ carries it steadily along $\vec{B}$ — combined, the charge traces a helical path.
Centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv_\perp^{2}}{r}=Bqv_\perp\ \Rightarrow\ v_\perp=\dfrac{Bqr}{m}$.
Time period $T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v_\perp}=\dfrac{2\pi m}{Bq}$, so the frequency of revolution is
$\nu=\dfrac{1}{T}=\dfrac{Bq}{2\pi m}$.
(ii) Magnetic moment $M=IA$, with $I=e\nu=1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}\times8\times10^{14}=1{\cdot}28\times10^{-4}\ \text{A}$:
$M=1{\cdot}28\times10^{-4}\times3{\cdot}14\times(2\times10^{-10})^{2}=1{\cdot}6\times10^{-23}\ \text{A m}^{2}$.

questions.text: (i) What is current sensitivity of a galvanometer ? Show how the current sensitivity of a galvanometer may be increased. 'Increasing the current sensitivity of a galvanometer may not necessarily increase its voltage sensitivity.' Explain. (ii) A moving coil galvanometer has a resistance $15\ \Omega$ and takes 20 mA to produce full scale deflection. How can this galvanometer be converted into a voltmeter of range 0 to 100 V ?

answer.text:
(i) Current sensitivity of a galvanometer is the deflection produced per unit current: $I_S=\dfrac{\theta}{I}=\dfrac{NBA}{K}$.
It can be increased by (any one): increasing the number of turns $N$; increasing the area $A$ of the coil; decreasing the torsional constant $K$.
Voltage sensitivity is $V_S=\dfrac{\theta}{V}=\dfrac{NBA}{KR}$; if current sensitivity is increased by increasing $N$, the resistance $R$ of the coil also increases proportionally, so voltage sensitivity may not increase.
(ii) To convert to a voltmeter of range $0$–$100\ \text{V}$: $V=I_G(R+G)\ \Rightarrow\ R=\dfrac{V}{I_G}-G=\dfrac{100}{20\times10^{-3}}-15=4985\ \Omega$.
A resistance of $4985\ \Omega$ is connected in series with the galvanometer.

questions.text: Two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents, exert a force on each other. Why ? Derive an expression for the force per unit length between two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents in opposite directions. Explain the nature of the force between these conductors.
questions.topic: Force between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

answer.text:
Each conductor experiences a force due to the magnetic field produced by the other. The field due to conductor $a$ at all points along conductor $b$ is $B_a=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_a}{2\pi d}$.
Force on a length $L$ of conductor $b$: $F_{ba}=I_b L B_a=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_a I_b L}{2\pi d}$.
Force per unit length: $f_{ba}=\dfrac{F_{ba}}{L}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_a I_b}{2\pi d}$ (directed away from $a$); similarly $f_{ab}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_a I_b}{2\pi d}$ (directed away from $b$).
For currents in opposite directions the forces act away from each other, i.e. the force is repulsive.

questions.text: (i) (1) What is meant by current sensitivity of a galvanometer ? Mention the factors on which it depends. (2) A galvanometer of resistance G is converted into a voltmeter of range $(0 - V)$ by using a resistance R. Find the resistance, in terms of R and G, required to convert it into a voltmeter of range $\left(0 - \dfrac{V}{2}\right)$. (ii) The magnetic flux through a coil of resistance $5\ \Omega$ increases with time as : $\phi = (2.0\,t^3 + 5.0\,t^2 + 6.0\,t)$ mWb. Find the magnitude of induced current through the coil at $t = 2$ s.

answer.text:
(i)(1) Current sensitivity of a galvanometer is the deflection produced per unit current: $\dfrac{\phi}{I}=\dfrac{NBA}{K}$. It depends on the number of turns $N$, the magnetic field $B$, the area $A$ of the coil and the torsional constant $K$ (any two).
(2) For a voltmeter of range $(0\text{–}V)$: $R=\dfrac{V}{I}-G$; for range $\left(0\text{–}\dfrac{V}{2}\right)$: $R_1=\dfrac{V}{2I}-G$. Using $\dfrac{V}{I}=R+G$: $R_1=\dfrac{R+G}{2}-G=\dfrac{R-G}{2}$.
(ii) $\phi=(2{\cdot}0t^{3}+5{\cdot}0t^{2}+6{\cdot}0t)\ \text{mWb}$; the induced emf is $|\varepsilon|=\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}=50\times10^{-3}\ \text{V}$, so $I=\dfrac{|\varepsilon|}{R}=\dfrac{50\times10^{-3}}{5}=10\ \text{mA}$.

questions.text: A circular loop of radius 10 cm carrying current of $1{\cdot}0$ A lies in x-y plane. answer.text:
Magnetic field due to the circular current loop at its centre $O$: $B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2r}=\dfrac{\mu_0\times1}{2\times0{\cdot}1}=5\mu_0\ \text{T}$, perpendicular to the plane of the loop and directed inwards.

For the net field at $O$ to be zero, $B_1=B_2$: $5\mu_0=\dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{0{\cdot}4\pi}\ \Rightarrow\ I_2=2\pi\ \text{A}=6{\cdot}28\ \text{A}$.

questions.text: Derive an expression for magnetic force $\vec{F}$ acting on a straight conductor of length L carrying current I in an external magnetic field $\vec{B}$. Is it valid when the conductor is in zig-zag form ? Justify.

answer.text:
The total number of mobile charge carriers in a conductor of length $L$, cross-sectional area $A$ and number density $n$ is $nLA$.
Force on these carriers in an external field $\vec{B}$: $\vec{F}=(nAL)q\vec{v}_d\times\vec{B}$  ...(1).
Since the current $I=v_d qnA$, i.e. $I\vec{L}=\vec{v}_d qnAL$  ...(2), from (1) and (2): $\vec{F}=I(\vec{L}\times\vec{B})$.
Yes, this is valid for a zig-zag conductor too, since it can be treated as a collection of short linear strips $d\vec{l}$ whose contributions are summed vectorially.

questions.text: An electron moving with a velocity $\vec{v} = (1{\cdot}0 \times 10^7\ \text{m/s})\hat{i} + (0{\cdot}5 \times 10^7\ \text{m/s})\hat{j}$ enters a region of uniform magnetic field $\vec{B} = (0{\cdot}5\ \text{mT})\hat{j}$. Find the radius of the circular path described by it. While rotating; does the electron trace a linear path too ? If so, calculate the linear distance covered by it during the period of one revolution.

answer.text:
Radius of the circular path (from the perpendicular velocity component $v_x$): $r=\dfrac{mv_x}{eB}=\dfrac{9{\cdot}1\times10^{-31}\times1\times10^{7}}{1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}\times0{\cdot}5\times10^{-3}}=11{\cdot}38\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}$.
Yes, it also traces a linear path (due to the parallel component $v_y$).
Linear distance covered in one revolution (the pitch): $y=\dfrac{2\pi m}{eB}\times v_y=\dfrac{2\times\pi\times9{\cdot}1\times10^{-31}\times0{\cdot}5\times10^{7}}{1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}\times0{\cdot}5\times10^{-3}}=0{\cdot}357\ \text{m}\approx0{\cdot}36\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: Using Biot-Savart law, derive expression for the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ due to a circular current carrying loop at a point on its axis and hence at its centre.
questions.topic: Magnetic Field due to a Current Element, Biot-Savart Law

answer.text: Magnetic field on the axis of a circular loop, from the Biot–Savart law: $|d\vec{B}| = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{I|d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}|}{r^3}$. With $r^2 = x^2+R^2$ and $|d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}| = r\,dl$: $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{i\,dl}{x^2+R^2}$. $d\vec{B}$ has two components; those perpendicular to the axis cancel around the loop, only the axial components add: $dB_x = dB\cos\theta$, with $\cos\theta = \dfrac{R}{(R^2+x^2)^{1/2}}$, so $dB_x = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi}\,dl\cdot\dfrac{R}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$. Summing over the entire loop ($\oint dl = 2\pi R$): $\vec{B} = B_x\hat{i} = \dfrac{\mu_0 iR^2}{2(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}}\hat{i}$. At the centre of the loop ($x=0$): $\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2R}\hat{i}$.

questions.text: (i) A proton moving with velocity $\vec{V}$ in a non-uniform magnetic field traces a path as shown in the figure. The path followed by the proton is always in the plane of the paper. What is the direction of the magnetic field in the region near points P, Q and R ? What can you say about relative magnitude of magnetic fields at these points ? (ii) A current carrying circular loop of area A produces a magnetic field B at its centre. Show that the magnetic moment of the loop is $\dfrac{2BA}{\mu_0}\sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text: (i) Near point P: magnetic field acts into the plane of the paper (as the force acts upwards). Near point Q: magnetic field is into the plane of the paper (as the force acts upwards). Near point R: magnetic field acts out of the plane of the paper (as $\vec{F}$ acts downwards). Relative magnitude of the field: since $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$, the magnitude of $B$ is small near P, relatively smaller near Q than at P, and relatively larger near R than at P, i.e. $B_Q < B_P < B_R$. (ii) Let $r$ be the radius of the circular coil and $I$ the current in it: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$ or $I = \dfrac{2Br}{\mu_0}$; with $A=\pi r^2$, $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$. $M = IA = \dfrac{2Br}{\mu_0}A = \dfrac{2BA}{\mu_0}\sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$.

questions.text: (i) Derive an expression for the torque acting on a rectangular current loop suspended in a uniform magnetic field. (ii) A charged particle is moving in a circular path with velocity $\vec{V}$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. It is made to pass through a sheet of lead and as a consequence, it loses one half of its kinetic energy without change in its direction. How will (1) the radius of its path (2) its time period of revolution change ?
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text: (i) $\vec{F}_1$ and $\vec{F}_2$ are the forces acting on two arms (sides $a$ and $b$) of a rectangular current loop. $|\vec{F}_1| = |\vec{F}_2| = IbB$ ($b$ = length of the arm); these forces constitute a couple, so the magnitude of torque on the loop is $\tau = F_1\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta + F_2\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta = IabB\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau} = I\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$. (Alternatively, if the plane of the coil makes an angle $\alpha$ with the field: $\vec{F}_{DA}=-\vec{F}_{BC}$ cancel; force on arm DC is into the plane, $|\vec{F}_{DC}|=IbB$; force on arm AB is out of the plane, $|\vec{F}_{AB}|=IbB$; these form a couple with $\tau = IbB\times a\cos\alpha = IabB\cos\alpha = IAB\cos\alpha$. With $\hat{n}$ the outward normal and $\theta+\alpha=90^\circ$: $\tau = IAB\cos(90^\circ-\theta) = IAB\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau}=I\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$.) (ii)(1) $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB} \Rightarrow r\propto\sqrt{K}$; $\dfrac{r'}{r} = \dfrac{\sqrt{K/2}}{\sqrt{K}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \Rightarrow r' = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt2}$. (2) $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ — the time period does not depend on kinetic energy, so the time period will not change.

questions.text: Two infinitely long conductors kept along XX$'$ and YY$'$ axes are carrying current $I_1$ and $I_2$ along $-$X axis and $-$Y axis respectively. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field produced at point P(X, Y).

answer.text: Reason — the source of the force is the interaction between the field produced by the current-carrying conductor and the external field in which it is placed. (i) Two long parallel conductors $a$ and $b$, separated by a distance $d$, carrying currents $I_a$ and $I_b$ respectively. The magnetic field due to $a$: $B_a = \dfrac{\mu_0I_a}{2\pi d}$. The force $F_{ba}$ on a segment $L$ of $b$ due to $a$: $F_{ba} = I_bLB_a = \dfrac{\mu_0I_aI_b}{2\pi d}L$. Definition — the 'ampere' is that value of steady current which, when maintained in each of two very long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section, placed one metre apart in vacuum, would produce on each of these conductors a force equal to $2\times10^{-7}$ newton per metre of length. questions.text: (i) A current carrying loop can be considered as a magnetic dipole placed along its axis. Explain. (ii) Obtain the relation for magnetic dipole moment $\vec{M}$ of current carrying coil. Give the direction of $\vec{M}$. (iii) A current carrying coil is placed in an external magnetic field. The coil is free to turn in the magnetic field. What is the net force acting on the coil ? Obtain the orientation of the coil in stable equilibrium. Show that in this orientation the flux of the total field (field produced by the loop $+$ external field) through the coil is maximum.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text: (i) The two faces of a current-carrying loop behave like two poles of a magnet, so it can be considered a magnetic dipole placed along its axis. (ii) Magnetic moment $M \propto$ current $I$ and $M \propto$ area $A$, so $\vec{M} = I\vec{A}$; its direction is the same as the area vector. (Alternatively: the magnetic moment is perpendicular to the plane of the coil.) (iii) The net force acting on the coil is zero. The potential energy $U_B$ of a current-carrying loop in an external magnetic field is $U_B = -\vec{M}\cdot\vec{B}$. For the coil to be in stable equilibrium, $U_B$ should be minimum, so $\theta=0^\circ$. Therefore the magnetic flux due to the total field $= (B_{coil}+B_{ext})A$, which is its maximum value. (Alternatively: the orientation of stable equilibrium is one where the area vector $\vec{A}$ of the loop is in the direction of the external field; in this orientation the magnetic field produced by the loop is in the same direction as the external field, both normal to the plane of the loop, giving rise to the maximum flux of the total field.)

answer.text: (a) $d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{I(d\vec{l}\times\vec{r})}{r^3}$. (b) Using $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{2I}{a}$: magnetic field due to the current-carrying wire along $XX'$: $\vec{B}_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{2I}{a} = \dfrac{2\times2\times10^{-7}}{5} = (8\times10^{-8}\ \text{T})(\hat{k})$. Magnetic field due to the current-carrying wire along $YY'$: $\vec{B}_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{2I}{a} = \dfrac{2\times2\times10^{-7}}{4} = 10\times10^{-8}\ \text{T}(-\hat{k})$. $\vec{B}_{net} = \vec{B}_2+\vec{B}_1 = 2\times10^{-8}\ \text{T}(-\hat{k})$. The direction of the resultant magnetic field is along the $-Z$ axis.

questions.text: A voltmeter of resistance 1000 $\Omega$ can measure up to 25 V. How will you convert it so that it can read up to 250 V ?

answer.text: $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{25}{1000} = 25\times10^{-3}\ \text{A}$. Resistance to be connected, $R' = \dfrac{V'}{I} - R = \dfrac{250}{25\times10^{-3}} - 1000 = 9000\ \Omega$. This $9000\ \Omega$ is connected in series with the voltmeter.

questions.text: An electron of mass m and charge $-e$ is revolving anticlockwise around the nucleus of an atom. (a) Obtain the expression for the magnetic dipole moment ($\mu$) of the atom. (b) If $\vec{L}$ is the angular momentum of electron, show that $\vec{\mu} = -\left(\dfrac{e}{2m}\right)\vec{L}$.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text: (a) $\mu = IA = \dfrac{e}{T}\times A = \dfrac{e}{2\pi r/v}\times\pi r^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}evr$. (b) $L = mvr$; $\mu = \dfrac{evr\times m}{2\times m} = \left(\dfrac{e}{2m}\right)L$. The direction of $\vec{\mu}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{L}$, so $\vec{\mu} = -\left(\dfrac{e}{2m}\right)\vec{L}$.

questions.text: A galvanometer is an instrument used to show the direction and strength of the current passing through it. In a galvanometer, a coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque and hence gets deflected when a current passes through it. The name is derived from the surname of Italian scientist L. Galvani, who in 1791 discovered that electric current makes a dead frog's leg jerk. A spring attached with the coil provides a counter torque. In equilibrium, the deflecting torque is balanced by the restoring torque of the spring and we have : NBAI = k$\phi$, where N is the total number of turns in the coil, A is the area of cross-section of each turn, B is the radial magnetic field, k is the torsional constant of the spring, $\phi$ is the angular deflection of the coil. (i) The value of the current sensitivity of a galvanometer is given by : (A) $\dfrac{k}{NBA}$ (B) $\dfrac{NBA}{k}$ (C) $\dfrac{kBA}{N}$ (D) $\dfrac{kNB}{A}$ (ii) A galvanometer of resistance 6 $\Omega$ shows full scale deflection for a current of $0{\cdot}2$ A. The value of shunt to be used with this galvanometer to convert it into an ammeter of range $(0-5$ A$)$ is : (A) $0{\cdot}25\ \Omega$ (B) $0{\cdot}30\ \Omega$ (C) $0{\cdot}50\ \Omega$ (D) $6{\cdot}0\ \Omega$ (iii) The value of resistance of the ammeter in case (ii) will be : (A) $0{\cdot}20\ \Omega$ (B) $0{\cdot}24\ \Omega$ (C) $6{\cdot}0\ \Omega$ (D) $6{\cdot}25\ \Omega$ (iv)(a) A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter of range $(0-V)$ by connecting with it, a resistance $R_1$. If $R_1$ is replaced by $R_2$, the range becomes $(0-2V)$. The resistance of the galvanometer is : (A) $(R_2 - 2R_1)$ (B) $(R_2 - R_1)$ (C) $(R_1 + R_2)$ (D) $(R_1 - 2R_2)$  OR  (iv)(b) A current of 5 mA flows through a galvanometer. Its coil has 100 turns, each of area of cross-section 18 cm$^2$ and is suspended in a magnetic field $0{\cdot}20$ T. The deflecting torque acting on the coil will be : (A) $3{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}$ Nm (B) $1{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-4}$ Nm (C) $2{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3}$ Nm (D) $1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-4}$ Nm

answer.text: (i) (B) $\dfrac{NBA}{K}$. (ii) (A) $0{\cdot}25\ \Omega$. (iii) (B) $0{\cdot}24\ \Omega$. (iv)(a) (A) $(R_2-2R_1)$ [OR (b) (B) $1{\cdot}8\times10^{-4}\ \text{Nm}$].

questions.text: (i) Write Biot-Savart's law in vector form. (ii) Two identical circular coils A and B, each of radius R, carrying currents I and $\sqrt{3}$I respectively, are placed concentrically in XY and YZ planes respectively. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at their common centre.
questions.topic: Magnetic Field due to a Current Element, Biot-Savart Law

answer.text: (i) $d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{I(d\vec{l}\times\vec{r})}{r^3}$. (ii) $B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}$; $B_2=\dfrac{\mu_0\sqrt3I}{2R}$; $B=\sqrt{B_1^2+B_2^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\sqrt{1+3}$. $\tan\theta = \dfrac{B_1}{B_2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$. The direction of the net magnetic field is $30^\circ$ with the direction of $B_2$ (equivalently $60^\circ$ with the direction of $B_1$).

questions.text: (i) A rectangular loop of sides $l$ and b carries a current I clockwise. Write the magnetic moment $\vec{m}$ of the loop and show its direction in a diagram. (ii) The loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ and is free to rotate about an axis which is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$. Prove that the loop experiences no net force, but a torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}$.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text: (i) $\vec{m}=I\vec{A}$. (ii) $F_1=F_2=IbB$; $F_1$ = force on arm AB, into the plane; $F_2$ = force on arm CD, out of the plane. Since the forces are equal and opposite, the net force is zero. Both forces form a couple; the magnitude of the torque acting on the coil is $\tau = F_1\dfrac{l}{2}\sin\theta+F_2\dfrac{l}{2}\sin\theta = IbBl\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta = mB\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$. (Alternatively, if the plane of the coil makes an angle $\alpha$ with the field: $\vec{F}_{DA}=-\vec{F}_{BC}$ cancel; force on arm DC is into the plane, $|F_{DC}|=IbB$; force on arm AB is out of the plane, $|F_{AB}|=IbB$; net force is zero; both form a couple with torque $\tau = IbB\times l\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau}=I\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$.)

questions.text: (i) With the help of a labelled diagram, explain the principle of working of a moving coil galvanometer. Write the purpose of using (i) radial magnetic field, and (ii) soft iron core, in it. (ii) Define current sensitivity of a galvanometer. \"Increasing the current sensitivity may not necessarily increase the voltage sensitivity.\" Give reason.

answer.text: Principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque. (Labelled diagram: scale, pointer, permanent magnet N-S, coil with soft-iron core on a pivot, in a uniform radial magnetic field.) (i) A radial magnetic field makes the scale linear. (Alternatively: a radial field provides maximum torque.) (ii) The soft-iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field / increases the sensitivity of the galvanometer. Current sensitivity is defined as the deflection per unit current: $I_s = \dfrac{\Phi}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k}$. Voltage sensitivity $V_s = \dfrac{\Phi}{V} = \left(\dfrac{NAB}{k}\right)\dfrac{I}{V} = \left(\dfrac{NAB}{k}\right)\dfrac{1}{R}$. Increasing the number of turns increases the current sensitivity and the resistance of the galvanometer in the same proportion, so the voltage sensitivity remains unchanged.

questions.text: (i) (I) Write Ampere's circuital law in mathematical form and explain the terms used. (II) As the current carrying solenoid is made longer, the magnetic field produced outside it approaches zero. Why ? (III) A flexible loop of irregular shape carrying current when located in an external magnetic field, changes to a circular shape. Give reason. (ii) A galvanometer of resistance G is converted into a voltmeter to measure up to V volts, by connecting a resistance $R_1$ with the coil. If $R_1$ is replaced by $R_2$, then it can only measure up to $\dfrac{V}{2}$ volt. Find the value of the resistance $R_3$ (in terms of $R_1$ and $R_2$) needed to convert it into a voltmeter that can read up to 2 V.

answer.text: (i)(I) Ampere's circuital law: $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_0I_e$; $I_e$ = total current through the surface, $B$ = magnetic field, $dl$ = length of a small element. (II) As the length of the solenoid increases, it appears like a long cylindrical metal sheet, so the field outside approaches zero. (III) For a given perimeter, a circle encloses a greater area than any other shape, which maximises the flux. (ii) $R_1=\dfrac{V}{I_g}-G \Rightarrow \dfrac{V}{I_g}=R_1+G\ \ldots(1)$; $R_2=\dfrac{V}{2I_g}-G \Rightarrow \dfrac{V}{2I_g}=R_2+G\ \ldots(2)$. Solving (1) and (2): $G=R_1-2R_2$. $R_3=\dfrac{2V}{I_g}-G\ \ldots(3)$; solving using (1) and (3): $R_3=3R_1-2R_2$.

questions.text: A wire of length L is bent round into (i) a square coil having N turns and (ii) a circular coil having N turns. The coil in both cases is free to turn about a vertical axis coinciding with the plane of the coil, in a uniform, horizontal magnetic field and carry the same currents. Find the ratio of the maximum value of the torque acting on the square coil to that on the circular coil.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text: Side of the square coil $a = \dfrac{L}{4N}$, radius of the circular coil $r = \dfrac{L}{2\pi N}$. Since $\tau = NIBA$, $\dfrac{\tau_1}{\tau_2} = \dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{(L/4N)^2}{\pi (L/2\pi N)^2} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Hence $\tau_1 : \tau_2 = \pi : 4$.

questions.text: A galvanometer is used to detect or/and measure small currents in an electrical circuit. It essentially works on the fact that a current-carrying coil experiences a deflecting torque when placed in a magnetic field. This deflection in the coil can be measured and it is related to the current flowing in the coil, the number of turns in the coil, area of the coil and the magnetic field. A hair spring attached to the coil provides a counter torque and helps in measuring the deflection. A galvanometer can be converted to an ammeter or a voltmeter of desired range by using suitable resistances. (I) The torque on the coil remains constant irrespective of the coil's orientation during rotation due to (A) use of soft iron core which increases the magnetic field. (B) radial magnetic field. (C) hair spring which provides the counter torque. (D) eddy current in the iron core which causes damping. (II) The best way to increase current sensitivity of a galvanometer is by (A) increasing number of turns of the coil (B) increasing area of coil and magnetic field strength (C) decreasing area of coil and magnetic field strength (D) increasing torsional constant of the hair spring. (III)(a) A moving coil galvanometer has a coil with area of cross-section $4{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-2}$ m$^2$ and number of turns 50. The coil is rotating in a magnetic field of $0{\cdot}25$ T. The torque acting on the coil when a current of 5 A passes through it is (A) $1{\cdot}0$ N m (B) $2{\cdot}0$ N m (C) $0{\cdot}50$ N m (D) $0{\cdot}25$ N m.  OR  (III)(b) A galvanometer coil has a resistance of 15 $\Omega$ and the meter shows full scale deflection for a current of 3 mA. The value of resistance required to convert it into a voltmeter of range $(0 - 12$ V$)$ is (A) 4015 $\Omega$ (B) 3985 $\Omega$ (C) 415 $\Omega$ (D) 385 $\Omega$. (IV) A galvanometer with coil of resistance 20 $\Omega$ shows full scale deflection for a current of 5 mA. To convert it into an ammeter of range $(0 - 10$ A$)$, a resistance of (A) $0{\cdot}05\ \Omega$ should be connected in series with it. (B) $0{\cdot}05\ \Omega$ should be connected in parallel with it. (C) $0{\cdot}01\ \Omega$ should be connected in parallel with it. (D) $0{\cdot}01\ \Omega$ should be connected in series with it.

answer.text: (I) (B) radial magnetic field. (II) (A) increasing the number of turns of the coil. (III) (D) $0{\cdot}25\ \text{N}{\cdot}\text{m}$ [OR (B) $3985\ \Omega$]. (IV) (C) $0{\cdot}01\ \Omega$ should be connected in parallel with it.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the magnetic field $\vec{B}$, due to a circular coil of N turns, each of radius r carrying current I, at a distance 'x' from the centre along its axis.

answer.text: Magnetic field on the axis of a current-carrying circular loop, from the Biot–Savart law: $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{I\,dl}{r^2+x^2}$; the components perpendicular to the axis cancel, the axial components add: $B_x = \int dB\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2(x^2+r^2)^{3/2}}$. For $N$ turns, $B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI r^2}{2(x^2+r^2)^{3/2}}$ (along the axis).

questions.text: An alpha particle (mass $6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-27}$ kg and charge $3{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-19}$ C) having $8{\cdot}0$ MeV energy, enters a region of a uniform magnetic field of $0{\cdot}5$ T. If the field is directed perpendicular to the velocity of the particle, find the radius of the circular path described by the particle. Mention the condition under which the particle in this region (i) describes a helical path, and (ii) goes straight undeviated.

answer.text: Radius of the circular path, from the kinetic energy: $KE = \dfrac{q^2B^2r^2}{2m} \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{\sqrt{2\cdot KE\cdot m}}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2\times8\times1{\cdot}6\times10^{-19}\times10^{6}\times6{\cdot}4\times10^{-27}}}{3{\cdot}2\times10^{-19}\times0{\cdot}5} = 80\ \text{cm}$. Conditions: (i) helical path when the particle enters at an angle $0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$ (velocity has one component parallel and one perpendicular to $\vec{B}$); (ii) straight, undeviated path when its velocity is parallel or antiparallel to $\vec{B}$.

questions.text: A charged particle $+$q in an electric field $\vec{E}$ experiences a force in the direction of the electric field. As a result, its kinetic energy changes. Similarly, the charged particle also experiences a force when it moves in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. But this magnetic force is perpendicular to both velocity $\vec{v}$ of the charged particle and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$, so it cannot change the kinetic energy of the charged particle. Consider two charged particles 1 and 2 of masses m and $\dfrac{m}{2}$ having charges $-$ q and $+$2q respectively. They are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference V and acquire kinetic energy $K_1$ and $K_2$. Then they enter in a region of uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ perpendicular to their velocities. (i) The ratio of their kinetic energies $\left(\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}\right)$ is : (A) $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (B) $\dfrac{1}{4}$ (C) 4 (D) 1 (ii) The ratio of the radii of the circular paths described by them $\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)$ is : (A) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ (B) $\sqrt{2}$ (C) $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (D) 2 (iii) Suppose particles 1 and 2 enter the magnetic field $\vec{B} = B_0\,\hat{k}$ with velocities $\vec{v}_1 = v_1\,\hat{i}$ and $\vec{v}_2 = v_2\,\hat{i}$. Then : (A) both particles revolve clockwise (B) both particles revolve anticlockwise (C) particle 1 revolves clockwise while particle 2 revolves anticlockwise (D) particle 1 revolves anticlockwise while particle 2 revolves clockwise (iv)(a) If period of revolution for particle 1 is 4 s, then for particle 2, the period will be : (A) 1 s (B) 2 s (C) 4 s (D) 8 s  OR  (iv)(b) If the value of momentum for particles 1 and 2 are $p_1$ and $p_2$, then : (A) $p_1 = \dfrac{p_2}{2}$ (B) $p_1 = p_2$ (C) $p_1 = 2p_2$ (D) $p_1 = 4p_2$

answer.text: (i) (A) $\dfrac{1}{2}$. (ii) (D) $2$. (iii) (D) Particle 1 revolves anticlockwise while particle 2 revolves clockwise. (iv) (A) $1\ \text{s}$ [OR (B) $p_1 = p_2$].

questions.text: (a) The figure given below shows three straight long parallel conductors $\textcircled{1}$, $\textcircled{2}$ and $\textcircled{3}$ kept in x-y plane, carrying currents 2I, I and 3I respectively as shown in figure. Find the magnitude and direction of : (i) net magnetic field at a point on conductor $\textcircled{1}$ and (ii) net magnetic force acting on unit length of conductor $\textcircled{1}$, due to conductors $\textcircled{2}$ and $\textcircled{3}$.

(i) Net magnetic field at a point on conductor 1: due to conductor 2, $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}(+\hat{z})$; due to conductor 3, $B_2 = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(-\hat{z})$; net $= B_2 - B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}$, directed along $-\hat{z}$ (into the page). questions.text: Write the expression for the magnetic field due to a current element in vector form. Consider a 1 cm segment of a wire, centered at the origin, carrying a current of 10 A in positive x-direction. Calculate the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ at a point (1 m, 1 m, 0).
questions.topic: Magnetic Field due to a Current Element, Biot-Savart Law

answer.text: By the Biot–Savart law, $d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{I(d\vec{l}\times\hat{r})}{r^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\cdot\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$. With $I = 10\ \text{A}$, $dl = 10\ \text{cm}$, $r = \sqrt2\ \text{m}$ and $\theta = 45^\circ$, $dB = 10^{-7}\times\dfrac{10\times10\times10^{-2}\times\sin45^\circ}{2} = 3{\cdot}53\times10^{-9}\ \text{T}$, directed along $+\hat{z}$ (out of the plane).

questions.text: (a) (i) A rectangular loop of sides a and b carrying current I is placed in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ such that its area vector $\vec{A}$ makes an angle $\theta$ with $\vec{B}$. With the help of a suitable diagram, show that the torque $\vec{\tau}$ acting on the loop is given by $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}$, where $\vec{m}$ ($= $ I $\vec{A}$) is the magnetic dipole moment of the loop. (ii) A circular coil of 100 turns and radius $\left(\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)$ cm carrying current of $5{\cdot}0$ A is suspended vertically in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of $2{\cdot}0$ T. The field makes an angle $30^\circ$ with the normal to the coil. Calculate : (I) the magnetic dipole moment of the coil, and (II) the magnitude of the counter torque that must be applied to prevent the coil from turning.
questions.topic: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

answer.text: (a)(i) Torque on a rectangular current loop in a uniform field: forces on sides BC and DA are equal, opposite and collinear, so they cancel; forces on AB and CD (each $F = IbB$) are equal, opposite but non-collinear and form a couple, giving $\tau = F\cdot(a\sin\theta) = IbB\cdot a\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta$. With magnetic moment $m = IA$, $\tau = mB\sin\theta$, i.e. $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m}\times\vec{B}$. (ii)(I) $m = NIA = 100\times5\times\pi\left(\dfrac{10\times10^{-2}}{\sqrt\pi}\right)^2 = 5\ \text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2$. (II) Counter-torque to hold the coil at $30^\circ$ $= mB\sin\theta = 5\times2\times\sin30^\circ = 5\ \text{N}{\cdot}\text{m}$.

questions.text: (b) (i) Derive an expression for the force $\vec{F}$ acting on a conductor of length L and area of cross-section A carrying current I and placed in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. (ii) A part of a wire carrying $2{\cdot}0$ A current and bent at $90^\circ$ at two points is placed in a region of uniform magnetic field $\vec{B} = -(0{\cdot}50$ T$)\,\hat{k}$, as shown in the figure. Calculate the magnitude of the net force acting on the wire.

answer.text: (b)(i) Force on a current-carrying conductor: for $n$ free electrons per unit volume, the total charge in a conductor of length $L$ and area $A$ is $q = nALe$; the force on it, moving with drift velocity $\vec{v}_d$ in field $\vec{B}$, is $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}_d\times\vec{B}) = nALe(\vec{v}_d\times\vec{B})$; since $neAv_d = I$, $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L}\times\vec{B})$. (ii) For the bent wire ($\vec{B} = -0{\cdot}5\hat{k}\ \text{T}$, $I = 2\ \text{A}$): on the $50\ \text{cm}$ segment along $x$, $\vec{F}_1 = 2(50\times10^{-2}\hat{i}\times(-0{\cdot}5\hat{k})) = 0{\cdot}5\hat{j}\ \text{N}$; on the $20\ \text{cm}$ segment along $y$, $\vec{F}_2 = 2(20\times10^{-2}\hat{j}\times(-0{\cdot}5\hat{k})) = 0{\cdot}2\hat{i}\ \text{N}$. As $\vec{F}_1 \perp \vec{F}_2$, resultant $F = \sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2} = \sqrt{0{\cdot}25+0{\cdot}04} = \sqrt{0{\cdot}29} \approx 0{\cdot}54\ \text{N}$.

questions.text: (i) State and explain Ampere's circuital law. (ii) Two long straight parallel wires separated by 20 cm, carry 5 A and 10 A current respectively, in the same direction. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at a point midway between them.
questions.topic: Force between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

answer.text:
(i) Ampere's circuital law: the line integral of the magnetic field over a closed loop in vacuum equals $\mu_0$ times the total current threading the loop: $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_0 I$, the integral being over a closed loop coinciding with the boundary of the surface.
(ii) For two long parallel wires (currents $5\ \text{A}$ and $10\ \text{A}$) with $P$ at the midpoint, each at distance $r$, $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$. The two fields at $P$ are opposite, so the net field is
$B=B_2-B_1=\dfrac{\mu_0\times10^{2}}{20\pi}[10-5]=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times10^{2}\times5}{20\pi}=10^{-5}\ \text{T}$, directed along the field produced by the $10\ \text{A}$ conductor.

questions.text: Two long straight parallel conductors A and B carrying steady currents $I_a$ and $I_b$ in the same direction are separated by a distance d. Deduce the expressions for the force acting on length L of conductor B due to conductor A and show it in figure. Write the expression for the force acting on length L of conductor A due to conductor B and show that it follows Newton's third law.
questions.topic: Force between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

answer.text: Force between two long parallel current-carrying conductors: field of A at B is $\vec{B}_A = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_A}{2\pi d}(-\hat{k})$; force on a length $L$ of B: $\vec{F}_{BA} = I_B\vec{L}\times\vec{B}_A = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_AI_BL}{2\pi d}\hat{j}$; similarly $\vec{F}_{AB} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_AI_BL}{2\pi d}(-\hat{j}) = -\vec{F}_{BA}$ — equal and opposite, so Newton's third law is obeyed.

questions.text: A small magnetised needle P is placed at the origin of x-y plane with its magnetic moment pointing along the y-axis. Another identical magnetised needle Q is placed in two positions, one by one. Case 1 : at $(a, 0)$ with its magnetic moment pointing along x-axis. Case 2 : at $(0, a)$ with its magnetic moment pointing along y-axis. (a) In which case is the potential energy of P and Q minimum ? (b) In which case is P and Q not in equilibrium ? Justify your answers.

answer.text:
(a) In case 2 the potential energy is minimum, since the needle $Q$ is placed along the direction of $P$ (stable equilibrium). Since $U=-MB\cos\theta$ and $\theta=0^{\circ}$, the potential energy is minimum.
(b) In case 1, $P$ and $Q$ are not in equilibrium; here $Q$ lies on the perpendicular (normal) bisector of $P$. Since the two needles are mutually perpendicular they experience a torque $\tau=MB\sin\theta$, and for $\theta=90^{\circ}$, $\tau=MB$.

questions.text: What are ferromagnetic materials ? Explain ferromagnetism with the help of suitable diagrams, using the concept of magnetic domain.

answer.text:
Ferromagnetic substances are those which get strongly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field.
In the absence of an external field the domains are randomly oriented, giving weak (nearly zero) net magnetisation. In the presence of an external field the domains orient themselves along the field direction, giving strong magnetisation.

questions.text: (i) A rectangular coil of N turns and area of cross-section A is rotated at a steady angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field. Obtain an expression for the emf induced in the coil at any instant of time. (ii) Two coplanar and concentric circular loops $L_1$ and $L_2$ are placed coaxially with their centres coinciding. The radii of $L_1$ and $L_2$ are 1 cm and 100 cm respectively. Calculate the mutual inductance of the loops. (Take $\pi^2 = 10$)

answer.text:
(i) In an ac generator the flux through the coil at instant $t$ is $\phi=NBA\cos\theta=NBA\cos\omega t$. By Faraday's law:
$\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\phi_B}{dt}=-NBA\dfrac{d}{dt}(\cos\omega t)=NBA\,\omega\sin\omega t$.
(ii) Mutual inductance of the coaxial coils: $M=\dfrac{\mu_0\pi r_1^{2}}{2r_2}=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times\pi r_1^{2}}{2r_2}=\dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times\pi\times(10^{-2})^{2}}{100\times10^{-7}}=2\times10^{-10}\ \text{H}$.

questions.text: (b) A rectangular loop of sides $l$ and b and resistance 'R' is kept in a region in which the magnetic field varies as B $= B_0 \sin\omega t$. (i) Derive expression for the emf induced in the loop. (ii) Find the effective value of current that flows in the loop.

answer.text: (b) Rectangular loop (sides $l$, $b$) in a field $B = B_0\sin\omega t$. (i) Induced emf $\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(B_0\sin\omega t\cdot lb) = B_0\omega lb\cos\omega t$. (ii) Instantaneous current $= \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} = \dfrac{B_0\omega lb\cos\omega t}{R}$; effective (rms) value $I_{eff} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{B_0\omega lb}{R\sqrt2}$.

questions.text: A long solenoid of radius r consists of n turns per unit length. A current $I = I_0 \sin\omega t$ flows in the solenoid. A coil of N turns is wound tightly around it near its centre. What is : (a) the induced emf in the coil ? (b) the mutual inductance between the solenoid and the coil ?

answer.text:
(a) Magnetic field produced near the centre of the solenoid: $B = \mu_0 n I$.
Flux linked with the coil of $N$ turns wound over the solenoid:
$\phi = N B A = N \pi r^{2} B = N \pi r^{2} \mu_0 n I$.
Induced emf:
$e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = -\pi r^{2} N n \mu_0 \dfrac{dI}{dt} = -\mu_0 \pi r^{2} n N I_0 \omega \cos\omega t$  ...(i)
(b) Comparing (i) with $e = -M\dfrac{dI}{dt}$:
mutual inductance $M = \mu_0 \pi r^{2} n N$.

questions.text: (i) Define coefficient of self-induction. Obtain an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of length $l$, area of cross-section A having N turns. (ii) Calculate the self-inductance of a coil using the following data obtained when an AC source of frequency $\left(\dfrac{200}{\pi}\right)$ Hz and a DC source is applied across the coil.

answer.text:
(i) The coefficient of self-induction (self-inductance) $L$ is the magnetic flux linked with a coil when unit current flows through it (equivalently, the emf induced when the current changes at the rate of $1\ \text{A/s}$).
For a long solenoid the field is $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{l}$; the total flux linkage is
$N\phi_B=(N)\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{l}\right)A=\dfrac{\mu_0 N^{2} I A}{l}$,
so the self-inductance is $L=\dfrac{N\phi_B}{I}=\dfrac{\mu_0 N^{2} A}{l}$.
(ii) From the table $Z=6\ \Omega,\ R=4\ \Omega$: $X_L^{2}=Z^{2}-R^{2}=36-16=20$, so $X_L=2\sqrt{5}\approx4{\cdot}5\ \Omega$.
$2\pi\nu L=4{\cdot}5\ \Rightarrow\ L=\dfrac{4{\cdot}5}{2\pi\times\frac{200}{\pi}}=1{\cdot}1\times10^{-2}\ \text{H}=11\ \text{mH}$.

questions.text: (i) With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the principle and working of an ac generator. Hence, obtain an expression for the instantaneous value of the emf generated. (ii) The coil of an ac generator consists of 100 turns of wire, each of area 0·5 m$^2$. The resistance of the wire is 100 $\Omega$. The coil is rotating in a magnetic field of 0·8 T perpendicular to its axis of rotation, at a constant angular speed of 60 radian per second. Calculate the maximum emf generated and power dissipated in the coil.

answer.text:
Principle: an ac generator works on electromagnetic induction — when the magnetic flux linked with a coil changes, an emf is induced in it.
Working: when a rectangular coil is rotated in a magnetic field, the flux linked changes continuously, inducing an emf whose direction reverses periodically.
$\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}=-NBA\dfrac{d}{dt}(\cos\omega t)=NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, so the peak emf is $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega$.
(ii) $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega=100\times0{\cdot}8\times0{\cdot}5\times60=2400\ \text{V}$.
Power dissipated: $P=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{rms}^{2}}{R}=\dfrac{\left(2400/\sqrt{2}\right)^{2}}{100}=28{\cdot}8\ \text{kW}$.

questions.text: Consider the experimental set up shown in the figure. This jumping ring experiment is an outstanding demonstration of some simple laws of Physics. A conducting non-magnetic ring is placed over the vertical core of a solenoid. When current is passed through the solenoid, the ring is thrown off. Answer the following questions : (i) Explain the reason of jumping of the ring when the switch is closed in the circuit. (ii) What will happen if the terminals of the battery are reversed and the switch is closed ? Explain. (iii) Explain the two laws that help us understand this phenomenon.  OR  (b) Briefly explain various ways to increase the strength of magnetic field produced by a given solenoid.

answer.text:
(i) The induced current in the ring is in such a direction that the polarity developed on the ring's face is the same as that on the facing coil, so the ring is repelled and jumps up (Lenz's law).
(ii) On reversing the terminals of the battery, the polarity of the induced current in the ring also reverses, so the repulsion persists and the ring jumps again.
(iii) Lenz's law: the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that causes it.
Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: whenever the magnetic flux linked with a coil changes, an emf is induced; its magnitude equals the time rate of change of magnetic flux, $\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$.
OR — Two ways to increase the strength of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid: by inserting a soft-iron core inside the solenoid; by increasing the current through the solenoid.

questions.text: What is meant by the term 'mutual inductance' of a pair of coils ? Obtain an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids, each of length $l$ but having different number of turns $N_1$ and $N_2$ and radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ ($r_2 > r_1$).

answer.text:
Mutual inductance is the magnetic flux linked with the secondary coil due to unit current flowing in the primary coil (equivalently, the emf induced in the secondary when the rate of change of current in the primary is unity).
Let $N_1$ and $N_2$ be the turns of coils $S_1$ and $S_2$. A current $I_2$ in $S_2$ sets up a flux through $S_1$:
$N_1\phi_1=M_{12}I_2$  ...(1).
Field due to $I_2$ inside $S_2$: $B=\mu_0\left(\dfrac{N_2}{l}\right)I_2$, so
$N_1\phi_1=(N_1)(\pi r_1^{2})\left(\mu_0\dfrac{N_2}{l}I_2\right)$  ...(2).
From (1) and (2):
$M_{12}=\dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 \pi r_1^{2}}{l}$.

questions.text: (a) The figure shows the variation of induced emf as a function of rate of change of current for two identical solenoids X and Y. One is air cored and the other is iron cored. Which one of them is iron cored ? Why ? (b) Obtain an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of length L and cross-sectional area A having N turns.

answer.text:
(a) $X$ is iron-cored. Reason: the slope of the emf-vs-$\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right|$ graph equals the self-inductance, since $\varepsilon=L\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right|$, i.e. slope $=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{|dI/dt|}=L$. The slope of $X$ is greater than that of $Y$, and an iron-cored coil has a larger inductance than an air-cored one, so $X$ is iron-cored.
(b) Field on the axis of the solenoid: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{l}$.
Flux linkage: $\phi_B=N\phi=\dfrac{\mu_0 N^{2} A}{l}I$.
Self-inductance: $L=\dfrac{\phi_B}{I}=\dfrac{\mu_0 N^{2} A}{l}$.

questions.text: Two coils $C_1$ and $C_2$ are placed close to each other. The magnetic flux $\phi_2$ linked with the coil $C_2$ varies with the current $I_1$ flowing in coil $C_1$, as shown in the figure. Find (i) the mutual inductance of the arrangement, and (ii) the rate of change of current $\left(\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}\right)$ that will induce an emf of 100 V in coil $C_2$.

answer.text:
(i) $\phi_2=MI_1$, so the mutual inductance is the slope of the $\phi_2$-vs-$I_1$ graph:
$M=\dfrac{\phi_2}{I_1}=2{\cdot}5\ \text{H}$.
(ii) $|\varepsilon_2|=M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$, so
$\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}=\dfrac{|\varepsilon_2|}{M}=\dfrac{100}{2{\cdot}5}=40\ \text{A s}^{-1}$.

questions.text: State the basic principle behind the working of an a.c. generator. Briefly describe its working and obtain the expression for the instantaneous value of emf induced.

answer.text:
Principle: an ac generator works on electromagnetic induction — whenever the magnetic flux linked with a coil changes, an emf is induced.
Working: the coil (armature) is mechanically rotated in a uniform magnetic field; this continuously changes the flux linked with it, inducing an emf.
The flux at any instant is $\phi_B=BA\cos\omega t$, so
$\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{d\phi_B}{dt}=-NBA\dfrac{d}{dt}(\cos\omega t)$, giving the instantaneous emf
$\varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin\omega t$.

answer.text:
(i) Mutual inductance between two coils is the magnetic flux linked with one coil when unit current flows through the neighbouring coil (equivalently, the emf induced in one coil when the rate of change of current in the other is unity). Its SI unit is the henry (H).
(ii) When a current $I_2$ flows in the outer solenoid, the flux linked with the inner solenoid is $N_1\phi_1=N_1 B_2 A_1=N_1\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 N_2 I_2}{l}\right)\pi r_1^{2}=\dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2\pi r_1^{2} I_2}{l}$.

questions.text: (i) State Lenz's Law. In a closed circuit, the induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it as per the law of conservation of energy. Justify. (ii) A metal rod of length 2 m is rotated with a frequency 60 rev/s about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. A uniform magnetic field of 2T perpendicular to its plane of rotation is switched-on in the region. Calculate the e.m.f. induced between the centre and the end of the rod.

answer.text:
(i) Lenz's law: the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. Justification: if the induced current instead favoured the change in flux, the flux and current would grow without any external energy source, violating conservation of energy.
(ii) emf induced in a rod rotating about one end: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{1}{2}Bl^{2}\omega=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times(2)^{2}\times(2\pi\times60)=480\pi\ \text{V}=1{\cdot}51\times10^{3}\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: (a) Show that the energy required to build up the current I in a coil of inductance L is $\dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$. (b) Considering the case of magnetic field produced by air-filled current carrying solenoid, show that the magnetic energy density of a magnetic field B is $\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$.

answer.text: (a) Induced emf in an inductor $|\varepsilon| = L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$. Rate of work done at any instant $\dfrac{dW}{dt} = |\varepsilon|I$. Total work done in establishing current $I$: $W = \displaystyle\int dW = \int_0^I LI\,dI$, so the energy required to build up current $I$ is $W = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$. (b) The magnetic energy is $W = U_B = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}L\left(\dfrac{B}{n\mu_0}\right)^2$ (since $B = n\mu_0I$). Using $L = \mu_0n^2Al$: $U_B = \dfrac{1}{2}(\mu_0n^2Al)\left(\dfrac{B^2}{\mu_0^2n^2}\right)$. Energy density $= \dfrac{U_B}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\mu_0n^2Al\times\dfrac{B^2}{\mu_0^2n^2}\times\dfrac{1}{Al} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{B^2}{\mu_0}$.

questions.text: Two coils '1' and '2' are placed close to each other as shown in the figure. (c) The resistance connected with coil '2' is increased keeping both the coils stationary.

answer.text: (a) Induced current will be clockwise. Due to the direction of current flow in coil 2, the face approaching coil 1 behaves like a south pole; the induced polarity on coil 1 (viewed from the side of coil 2) will be a south pole. (b) Induced current will be anticlockwise. Due to the direction of current flow in coil 2, the face going away from coil 1 behaves like a south pole; the induced polarity on coil 1 (viewed from the side of coil 2) will be a north pole. (c) Induced current will be anticlockwise. While the resistance in coil 2 is increasing, the magnetic flux associated with coil 1 is decreasing. Hence, by Lenz's law, a current is induced in coil 1 momentarily, and after that there is no induced current in coil 1.

answer.text: (i) Lenz's law — the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it. When a magnet is moved closer to/away from the loop, the same/opposite pole develops on the approaching face of the loop; the mechanical work required to move the magnet gets converted into electrical energy, which is consistent with the law of conservation of energy. (ii)(I) Direction of induced current: anticlockwise as the loop enters the field, clockwise as the loop leaves the field. (II) Graphs: $\phi$ vs $t$ rises linearly between $t=\dfrac{l}{v}$ and $t=\dfrac{3l}{2v}$ to a plateau value, stays constant, then falls linearly to zero between $t=\dfrac{2l}{v}$ and $t=\dfrac{5l}{2v}$. Induced emf $\varepsilon$ vs $t$: a positive rectangular pulse of height $\dfrac{1}{2}Blv$ between $t=\dfrac{l}{v}$ and $\dfrac{3l}{2v}$ (entering), and a negative rectangular pulse of the same magnitude between $t=\dfrac{2l}{v}$ and $\dfrac{5l}{2v}$ (leaving).

(i) Define self-inductance of a coil. Derive the expression for the energy required to build up a current I in a coil of self-inductance L. (ii) The currents passing through two inductors of self-inductances 10 mH and 20 mH increase with time at the same rate. Draw graphs showing the variation of : (I) the magnitude of emf induced with the rate of change of current in each inductor. (II) the energy stored in each inductor with the current flowing through it.

answer.text: Self-inductance is the magnetic flux linked with a coil when the current through the coil is unity. (Alternatively: self-inductance is the induced emf in the coil when the rate of change of current through it is unity.) To maintain the growth of current, power must be supplied from an external source: $P = |e||I| = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = LI\dfrac{dI}{dt} \Rightarrow dW = LI\,dI \Rightarrow W = \displaystyle\int LI\,dI = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$. (I) $E = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$: graph of $|e|$ vs $\dfrac{di}{dt}$ is a straight line through the origin, steeper for the larger inductance (line 2, $20\ \text{mH}$) than the smaller (line 1, $10\ \text{mH}$). (II) $U = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$: a parabolic graph is obtained, again steeper for the larger inductance (curve 2, $20\ \text{mH}$) than the smaller (curve 1, $10\ \text{mH}$).

questions.text: (i) Define the term mutual inductance. Deduce the expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of the same length having different radii and different number of turns. (ii) The current through an inductor is uniformly increased from zero to 2 A in 40 s. An emf of 5 mV is induced during this period. Find the flux linked with the inductor at $t = 10$ s.

answer.text: (i) Mutual inductance is defined as the induced emf in the primary coil when the current in the secondary coil changes at unit rate. (Alternatively: the magnetic flux linked with the primary coil when the current in the secondary coil is unity.) Consider two long co-axial solenoids, each of length $l$: the inner solenoid $S_1$ has radius $r_1$ and $n_1$ turns per unit length; the outer solenoid $S_2$ has the corresponding quantities $r_2$ and $n_2$. When a current $I_2$ is set up through $S_2$, it sets up a magnetic flux through $S_1$: $N_1\phi_1 = M_{12}I_2 = (n_1l)\times(\pi r_1^2)\times(\mu_0n_2I_2) = \mu_0n_1n_2\pi r_1^2lI_2 \Rightarrow M_{12} = \mu_0n_1n_2\pi r_1^2l = M_{21}$. (ii) $|e| = L\dfrac{dI}{dt} \Rightarrow L = \dfrac{e}{dI/dt} = \dfrac{5\times10^{-3}}{2/40} = 0{\cdot}1\ \text{H}$. $\phi = LI = 0{\cdot}1\times\dfrac{2}{40}\times10 = 0{\cdot}05\ \text{Wb}$.

questions.text: State Lenz's law. A rod MN of length L is rotated about an axis passing through its end M perpendicular to its length, with a constant angular velocity $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ parallel to the axis. Obtain an expression for emf induced between its ends.

answer.text: Lenz's law: the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. Expression for induced emf: the magnitude of the emf generated across a length $dr$ of the rotating rod is $d\varepsilon = Bv\,dr$; $\varepsilon = \displaystyle\int d\varepsilon = \int_0^L Bv\,dr = \int_0^L B\omega r\,dr = \dfrac{1}{2}BL^2\omega$. (Alternatively: area of the sector QMN $=\dfrac{1}{2}L^2\theta$; induced emf $\varepsilon = B\times\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}L^2\theta\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}BL^2\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2}BL^2\omega$.)

questions.text: Define 'self-inductance' of a coil. Derive an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of cross-sectional area A and length $l$, having n turns per unit length.

answer.text: Self-inductance of a coil is the ratio of the flux linkage to the current flowing through it. (Alternatively: the flux linked with the coil when unit current flows through it; or the magnitude of the emf induced in the coil when the current changes at the rate of $1\ \text{A/s}$.) Expression for the self-inductance of a long solenoid: $B=\mu_0nI$; total flux linked, $N\phi_B = (nl)(\mu_0nI)A = \mu_0n^2AlI$; self-inductance $L = \dfrac{N\phi_B}{I} = \mu_0n^2Al$.

questions.text: (i) Define mutual inductance of a pair of coils. Write its SI unit. (ii) A long solenoid of radius R and length L has n turns per unit length. answer.text: (i) Mutual inductance of a pair of coils = the ratio of the magnetic flux linked with one coil to the current in the neighbouring coil (or the ratio of the induced emf to the rate of change of current in the neighbouring coil); SI unit: henry ($\text{H}$) [$= \text{T}\,\text{m}^2\text{A}^{-1} = \text{Wb}\,\text{A}^{-1} = \text{V}\,\text{s}\,\text{A}^{-1}$]. (ii) For a solenoid carrying current $I$, $B = \mu_0 nI$; flux through the inner loop of radius $r$: $\phi_B = BA = (\mu_0 nI)(\pi r^2)$; mutual inductance $M = \dfrac{\phi_B}{I} = \mu_0 n\pi r^2$.

questions.text: (i) With the help of a diagram, briefly explain the construction and working of ac generator. (ii) An electron is revolving around a proton in an orbit of radius r with a speed v. Obtain expression for magnetic moment associated with the electron.

answer.text:
(i) An ac generator consists of a coil mounted on a rotor shaft in a magnetic field, the coil ends being connected to an external circuit through slip rings and brushes. Working: the coil is rotated in the uniform magnetic field, so the flux through it changes and an emf $e=e_0\sin\omega t$ is induced.
(ii) For an electron revolving with speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$, the equivalent current is $I=\dfrac{q}{t}=\dfrac{e}{2\pi r/v}=\dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}$.
Magnetic moment $m=IA=\dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\times\pi r^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}evr$.

answer.text: (a) AC generator (labelled diagram: coil mounted on an axle between the poles N-S of a magnet, slip rings, carbon brushes). Principle: electromagnetic induction — a changing magnetic flux through the coil induces an emf. Working: as the coil rotates in the field, the flux linked with it changes and an emf is induced. (ii) $\phi_B = BA\cos\omega t \Rightarrow \varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\phi_B}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$. (iii) The emf is maximum at $t = \dfrac{T}{4}$ and $\dfrac{3T}{4}$.

questions.text: (b) (i) State Lenz's law and explain that it follows the law of conservation of energy. (ii) Write the dimensional formula for self-inductance. The current in a coil changes from $8{\cdot}0$ A to $2{\cdot}0$ A in $0{\cdot}6$ s. If an average emf induced in the coil is 50 V, calculate the self-inductance of the coil.

answer.text: (b)(i) Lenz's law: the induced emf drives a current in the direction that opposes the change in flux producing it (e.g. a magnet's N-pole approaching a coil makes the near face of the coil an N-pole, causing repulsion); this follows from the conservation of energy. (ii) Dimensional formula of self-inductance $= [ML^2T^{-2}A^{-2}]$; from $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$, $L = -\dfrac{\varepsilon}{dI/dt} = -\dfrac{50\times0{\cdot}6}{2-8} = 5\ \text{H}$.
