questions.text: (i) Differentiate between peak and rms values of alternating current. How are they related ? (ii) A current element X is connected across an ac source of emf $V = V_0 \sin 2\pi\nu t$. It is found that the voltage leads the current in phase by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radian. If element X was replaced by element Y, the voltage lags behind the current in phase by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radian. (I) Identify elements X and Y by drawing phasor diagrams. (II) Obtain the condition of resonance when both elements X and Y are connected in series to the source and obtain expression for resonant frequency. What is the impedance value in this case ?
questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit

answer.text: (i) Peak value — the maximum value of the alternating current. rms value — the equivalent dc current that would produce the same average power loss as the alternating current. (Alternatively: the effective value of an ac representing the equivalent dc that would produce the same heating effect in the same resistor over the same time period.) Relation: $I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2}$. (ii)(I) From the phasor diagrams: $X$ — Inductor ($L$, since $V$ leads $I$ by $90^\circ$); $Y$ — Capacitor ($C$, since $I$ leads $V$ by $90^\circ$). (II) Impedance of the circuit $Z = (X_L-X_C)$; at resonance $Z=0 \Rightarrow X_L=X_C \Rightarrow \omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} \Rightarrow \omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{LC} \Rightarrow \omega = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, so $\nu = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$. Impedance at resonance $Z=0$.

questions.text: (a) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer. State the principle on which it works and obtain the ratio of secondary voltage to primary voltage in terms of number of turns and currents in the two coils. (b) The ratio of the number of turns in the primary to the secondary of an ideal transformer is 1 : 5. If 5 kW power at 200 V is supplied to the primary, find (i) current in the primary, and (ii) output voltage.

answer.text: (a) Step-up transformer (labelled diagram: soft-iron core, primary and secondary windings). Principle: an alternating voltage across the primary sets up a changing flux that links the secondary and induces an emf (mutual induction). $\varepsilon_s = -N_s\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$, $\varepsilon_p = -N_p\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} \Rightarrow \dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$; for an ideal transformer $I_pV_p = I_sV_s \Rightarrow \dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{I_s}{I_p}$. (b)(i) $P = V_pI_p \Rightarrow 5000 = 200\,I_p \Rightarrow I_p = 25\ \text{A}$. (ii) $\dfrac{N_p}{N_s} = \dfrac{V_p}{V_s} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{200}{V_s} \Rightarrow V_s = 1000\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: How does the resistance differ from impedance ? With the help of a suitable phasor diagram, obtain an expression for impedance of a series LCR circuit, connected to a source $v = v_m \sin\omega t$.
questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit

answer.text:
Difference between resistance and impedance (any one):
1. Resistance opposes both alternating and direct current, while impedance opposes alternating current only.
2. Resistance is independent of frequency, while impedance depends on frequency.
Obtaining the impedance (from the phasor diagram):
$V_R = i_m R,\quad V_C = i_m X_C,\quad V_L = i_m X_L$  (where $i_m$ is the peak current).
$\vec{V}_L + \vec{V}_R + \vec{V}_C = \vec{V}_m$, so
$V_m^{2} = V_R^{2} + (V_C - V_L)^{2} = (i_m R)^{2} + (i_m X_C - i_m X_L)^{2} = i_m^{2}\,[R^{2} + (X_C - X_L)^{2}]$
$i_m = \dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt{R^{2} + (X_C - X_L)^{2}}} = \dfrac{V_m}{Z}$
$\therefore$ impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_C - X_L)^{2}}$.

questions.text: Find the condition for resonance in a series LCR circuit connected to a source $v = v_m \sin\omega t$, where $\omega$ can be varied. Give the factors on which the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit depends. Plot a graph showing the variation of electric current with frequency in a series LCR circuit.
questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit

answer.text:
$Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}}$. For maximum current $Z$ must be minimum, which requires
$X_L = X_C$.
Alternatively:
$X_L = X_C \ \Rightarrow\ \omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} \ \Rightarrow\ \omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.
The resonant frequency depends on the values of inductance $L$ and capacitance $C$ only. (The current $I$ is maximum at $\omega = \omega_r$ and falls off on either side.)

questions.text: A series CR circuit with R = 200 $\Omega$ and C = $\left(\dfrac{50}{\pi}\right)$ $\mu$F is connected across an ac source of peak voltage $\varepsilon_0$ = 100 V and frequency $\nu$ = 50 Hz. answer.text:
(a) $X_C=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\nu C}=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\times50\times\frac{50}{\pi}\times10^{-6}}=200\ \Omega$.
$Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+X_C^{2}}=\sqrt{(200)^{2}+(200)^{2}}=200\sqrt{2}\ \Omega\approx282\ \Omega$.
(b) $\tan\phi=\dfrac{X_C}{R}=\dfrac{200}{200}=1\ \Rightarrow\ \phi=45^{\circ}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\ \text{rad}$.
(c) $V_R=I_{rms}R=\dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z}\,R=\dfrac{100}{\sqrt{2}\times200\sqrt{2}}\times200=50\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: An ac source $v = v_m \sin\omega t$ is connected across an ideal capacitor. Derive the expression for the (i) current flowing in the circuit, and (ii) reactance of the capacitor. Plot a graph of current $i$ versus $\omega t$.
questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Capacitor

answer.text:
(i) For an ideal capacitor, $V_m\sin\omega t=\dfrac{q}{C}$, so
$I=\dfrac{dq}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}(C V_m\sin\omega t)=\omega C V_m\cos\omega t$.
$I=\dfrac{V_m}{1/\omega C}\cos\omega t=I_m\sin\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
(ii) Comparing with $I_m=\dfrac{V_m}{1/\omega C}$, the reactance of the capacitor is $X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$.
The graph of $i$ versus $\omega t$ leads the voltage by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.text: A series combination of an inductor L, a capacitor C and a resistor R is connected across an ac source of voltage in a circuit. Obtain an expression for the average power consumed by the circuit. Find power factor for (i) purely inductive circuit, and (ii) purely resistive circuit.
questions.topic: Power in AC Circuit: The Power Factor

answer.text:
Instantaneous power: $P=VI=(V_m\sin\omega t)\,(I_m\sin(\omega t+\phi))=\dfrac{V_m I_m}{2}\,[\cos\phi-\cos(2\omega t+\phi)]$.
The average over a cycle of the time-dependent term is zero, so the average power is
$P_{avg}=\dfrac{V_m I_m}{2}\cos\phi=\dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\dfrac{I_m}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\phi=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$.
(i) Purely inductive circuit: $\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ \cos\phi=0$.
(ii) Purely resistive circuit: $\phi=0\ \Rightarrow\ \cos\phi=1$.

questions.text: A resistor of 30 $\Omega$ and a capacitor of 250 $\mu$F are connected in series to a 200 V, 50 Hz ac source. Calculate (i) the current in the circuit, and (ii) voltage drops across the resistor and the capacitor. (iii) Is the algebraic sum of these voltages more than the source voltage ? If yes, solve the paradox.
questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor

answer.text:
$X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, with $\omega=2\pi\nu=100\pi$, so $X_C=\dfrac{1}{100\pi\times\frac{250}{\pi}\times10^{-6}}=40\ \Omega$.
Impedance: $Z=\sqrt{X_C^{2}+R^{2}}=\sqrt{(40)^{2}+(30)^{2}}=50\ \Omega$.
(i) Current: $I_{rms}=\dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z}=\dfrac{200}{50}=4\ \text{A}$.
(ii) $V_C=I_{rms}X_C=4\times40=160\ \text{V}$; $V_R=I_{rms}R=4\times30=120\ \text{V}$.
(iii) The algebraic sum $V_R+V_C=280\ \text{V}$ exceeds the source voltage of $200\ \text{V}$. The paradox is resolved because $V_R$ and $V_C$ are $90^{\circ}$ out of phase, so $V=\sqrt{V_R^{2}+V_C^{2}}=\sqrt{(120)^{2}+(160)^{2}}=200\ \text{V}$, equal to the source voltage.

questions.text: A series LCR circuit with R = 20 $\Omega$, L = 2 H and C = 50 $\mu$F is connected to a 200 volts ac source of variable frequency. What is (i) the amplitude of the current, and (ii) the average power transferred to the circuit in one complete cycle, at resonance ? (iii) Calculate the potential drop across the capacitor.

answer.text:
(i) At resonance $Z=R$, so $I_{rms}=\dfrac{200}{20}=10\ \text{A}$; amplitude of the current $I_0=\sqrt{2}\,I_{rms}=14{\cdot}14\ \text{A}$.
(ii) Average power at resonance: $P=I_{rms}^{2}R=(10)^{2}\times20=2000\ \text{W}$.
(iii) Resonant angular frequency $\omega_r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\times50\times10^{-6}}}=100\ \text{rad/s}$.
$V_C=I_{rms}X_C=I_{rms}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\omega_r C}=10\times\dfrac{1}{100\times50\times10^{-6}}=2000\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: An inductor, a capacitor and a resistor are connected in series with an ac source $v = v_m \sin\omega t$. Derive an expression for the average power dissipated in the circuit. Also obtain the expression for the resonant frequency of the circuit.
questions.topic: Power in AC Circuit: The Power Factor

answer.text:
With $v=v_m\sin\omega t$ and $i=i_m\sin(\omega t+\varphi)$, the instantaneous power is
$P=vi=(v_m\sin\omega t)\times[i_m\sin(\omega t+\varphi)]=\dfrac{v_m i_m}{2}[\cos\varphi-\cos(2\omega t+\varphi)]$  ...(1).
The average over a cycle of the time-dependent second term is zero, so
$P=\dfrac{v_m i_m}{2}\cos\varphi=VI\cos\varphi$ (or $P=I^{2}Z\cos\varphi$).
At resonance, $X_C=X_L$: $\dfrac{1}{\omega C}=\omega L\ \Rightarrow\ \omega=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, so the resonant frequency is
$\nu=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

questions.text: (i) A resistor and a capacitor are connected in series to an ac source $v = v_m \sin\omega t$. Derive an expression for the impedance of the circuit. (ii) When does an inductor act as a conductor in a circuit ? Give reason for it. (iii) An electric lamp is designed to operate at 110 V dc and 11 A current. If the lamp is operated on 220 V, 50 Hz ac source with a coil in series, then find the inductance of the coil.
questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor

answer.text:
(i) With $v=v_m\sin\omega t$ across a series $R$-$C$ circuit, from the phasor diagram $v_R+v_C=v$ (as vectors), so $v_m^{2}=v_{rm}^{2}+v_{cm}^{2}$ with $v_{rm}=i_mR$ and $v_{cm}=i_mX_C$:
$v_m^{2}=(i_mR)^{2}+(i_mX_C)^{2}=i_m^{2}[R^{2}+X_C^{2}]\ \Rightarrow\ i_m=\dfrac{v_m}{\sqrt{R^{2}+X_C^{2}}}$
$\therefore$ impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+X_C^{2}}$.
(ii) For direct current, an inductor behaves as a plain conductor. Reason: $X_L=\omega L=2\pi\nu L$; for dc, $\nu=0$, so $X_L=0$ (equivalently, the induced emf $\varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt}=0$ since $\dfrac{dI}{dt}=0$ for a steady current).
(iii) $R=\dfrac{110}{11}=10\ \Omega$. On $220\ \text{V}$, $50\ \text{Hz}$ ac with the coil in series and the lamp still drawing $11\ \text{A}$:
$i_{rms}=\dfrac{v_{rms}}{\sqrt{R^{2}+X_L^{2}}}\ \Rightarrow\ 11=\dfrac{220}{\sqrt{100+X_L^{2}}}\ \Rightarrow\ \sqrt{100+X_L^{2}}=20\ \Omega$
$100+X_L^{2}=400\ \Rightarrow\ X_L=10\sqrt{3}\ \Omega$.
$X_L=2\pi fL\ \Rightarrow\ 10\sqrt{3}=2\pi\times50\times L\ \Rightarrow\ L=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{10\pi}\ \text{H}$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer and describe its working principle. Explain any three causes for energy losses in a real transformer. (ii) A step-up transformer converts a low voltage into high voltage. Does it violate the principle of conservation of energy ? Explain. (iii) A step-up transformer has 200 and 3000 turns in its primary and secondary coils respectively. The input voltage given to the primary coil is 90 V. Calculate : (1) The output voltage across the secondary coil (2) The current in the primary coil if the current in the secondary coil is $2\cdot0$ A.

answer.text:
(i) A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary than the primary. Working principle: mutual induction — an alternating voltage in the primary produces an alternating flux in the soft-iron core, which links the secondary and induces an emf in it.
Three causes of energy loss in a real transformer (any three): flux leakage; resistance of the windings ($I^2R$ loss); eddy currents in the core; hysteresis loss in the core material.
(ii) No, it does not violate energy conservation — although the voltage increases, the current decreases correspondingly (since $I_PV_P=I_SV_S$ for an ideal transformer), so the input power equals the output power.
(iii)(1) $\dfrac{V_S}{V_P}=\dfrac{N_S}{N_P}\ \Rightarrow\ V_S=\dfrac{N_S}{N_P}\times V_P=\dfrac{3000}{200}\times90=1350\ \text{V}$.
(2) $\dfrac{I_P}{I_S}=\dfrac{N_S}{N_P}\ \Rightarrow\ I_P=\dfrac{3000}{200}\times2=30\ \text{A}$.

questions.text: (i) You are given three circuit elements X, Y and Z. They are connected one by one across a given ac source. It is found that V and I are in phase for element X. V leads I by $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ for element Y while I leads V by $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ for element Z. Identify elements X, Y and Z. (ii) Establish the expression for impedance of circuit when elements X, Y and Z are connected in series to an ac source. Show the variation of current in the circuit with the frequency of the applied ac source. (iii) In a series LCR circuit, obtain the conditions under which (1) impedance is minimum and (2) wattless current flows in the circuit.
questions.topic: Power in AC Circuit: The Power Factor

answer.text:
(i) X is a resistor; Y is an inductor (a real inductor whose reactance equals its resistance); Z is a capacitor (a real capacitor whose reactance equals its resistance).
(ii) From the phasor diagram, $V_m^{2}=V_{Rm}^{2}+(V_{Cm}-V_{Lm})^{2}=(i_m R)^{2}+(i_m X_C-i_m X_L)^{2}$, so the impedance $Z=\dfrac{V_m}{I_m}=\sqrt{R^{2}+(X_C-X_L)^{2}}$. The current is maximum at resonance (see the current-versus-$\omega$ graph).
(iii)(1) For minimum impedance, $Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+(X_C-X_L)^{2}}$ is least when $X_C=X_L$.
(2) Average power over a cycle $P=VI\cos\phi$; for wattless current $P=0$ with $V\neq0,\ I\neq0$, so $\cos\phi=0$, i.e. $\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.text: (i) Describe the construction and working of a transformer and hence obtain the relation for $\left(\dfrac{v_s}{v_p}\right)$ in terms of number of turns of primary and secondary. (ii) Discuss four main causes of energy loss in a real transformer.

answer.text:
(i) A transformer consists of two coils (primary and secondary), insulated from each other and wound on a soft-iron core. Working: an alternating voltage applied to the primary drives an alternating current that produces an alternating flux linking the secondary and inducing an emf in it. For an ideal transformer $\varepsilon_p=V_P=-N_P\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$ and $\varepsilon_s=V_S=-N_S\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$, giving $\dfrac{V_S}{V_P}=\dfrac{N_S}{N_P}$.
(ii) Causes of energy loss (any four): flux leakage; resistance of the windings (copper loss); eddy currents (iron loss); hysteresis; magnetostriction.

answer.text: (i) Principle: an AC generator works on the principle of electromagnetic induction. (Diagram: coil rotating between N-S magnet poles, connected via slip rings and carbon brushes to the external circuit.) Working: the coil is mechanically rotated in the uniform magnetic field; the rotation causes the magnetic flux through it to change, so an emf is induced in the coil. (ii) $Z = \sqrt{R^2+\left(\omega L-\dfrac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2} = 500\ \Omega$; $I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{140}{\sqrt2\times500} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt2}\ \text{A}$. $(V_{rms})_R = I_{rms}R = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt2}\times400 = \dfrac{112}{\sqrt2} = 56\sqrt2\ \text{V}$. $(V_{rms})_L = I_{rms}\omega L = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt2}\times500 = \dfrac{140}{\sqrt2} = 70\sqrt2\ \text{V}$. $(V_{rms})_C = I_{rms}\dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt2}\times200 = \dfrac{56}{\sqrt2} = 28\sqrt2\ \text{V}$. questions.text: (i) Write the principle of working of a transformer. With the help of a labelled diagram, explain the working of a step-up transformer. answer.text: (i) Principle: a transformer works on the principle of mutual induction. (Diagram: soft-iron core with primary and secondary windings.) Working: when an alternating voltage is applied to the primary, the resulting current produces an alternating magnetic flux which links the secondary and induces an emf in it. Since the number of turns is more in the secondary winding, the induced emf (proportional to the number of turns) is greater there — so more emf is developed across the secondary windings. (ii) $P_i=V_pI_p \Rightarrow 200=\dfrac{20}{\sqrt2}I_p \Rightarrow I_p=10\sqrt2\ \text{A}$. $\dfrac{V_o}{V_i}=\dfrac{250}{50}=5 \Rightarrow V_o = 100\sin(100\pi t)\ \text{V}$. $P_o=(V_o)_{rms}(I_o)_{rms} \Rightarrow 200=\dfrac{100}{\sqrt2}(I_o)_{rms} \Rightarrow (I_o)_{rms}=2\sqrt2\ \text{A}$. Therefore $I_o=(2\sqrt2)\sqrt2\sin(100\pi t) = 4\sin(100\pi t)\ \text{A}$.

questions.text: (a) (i) A light bulb and an open coil inductor are connected in series across an ac source of variable frequency. How will be the glow of the bulb be affected when : (I) an iron bar is inserted inside the coil, and (II) the frequency of the source is decreased ? Justify your answers. Assume that in each above case other factors remain unchanged. (ii) An ac voltage $V = 280 \sin(100\pi t)$ volt is connected across a series LCR circuit in which R $= 400\ \Omega$, L $= \dfrac{5}{\pi}$ H and C $= \dfrac{50}{\pi}\ \mu$F. Taking $\sqrt{2} = 1{\cdot}4$, calculate : (I) impedance of the circuit. (II) rms value of current that flows in the circuit. (III) power factor of circuit.

answer.text: (a)(i) Effect on the bulb: (I) inserting an iron bar raises the coil's inductive reactance ($L' = \mu_r L$, so $X_L = \omega L$ increases), so more voltage drops across the inductor and less across the bulb — the bulb dims. (II) Decreasing the frequency lowers $X_L$, so the current increases and the bulb brightens. (ii) $V = 280\sin(100\pi t)$: $X_L = 100\pi\times\dfrac{5}{\pi} = 500\ \Omega$, $X_C = \dfrac{10^6}{100\pi\times\frac{50}{\pi}} = 200\ \Omega$. (I) $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L-X_C)^2} = \sqrt{400^2+300^2} = 500\ \Omega$. (II) $I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_0}{Z\sqrt2} = \dfrac{280}{500\times1{\cdot}4} = 0{\cdot}4\ \text{A}$. (III) Power factor $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{400}{500} = 0{\cdot}8$.

questions.text: What is meant by the term 'displacement current' ? Briefly explain how this current is different from a conduction current.

answer.text:

$i_d=\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt}$, whereas the conduction current is $I=\dfrac{dq}{dt}$.

questions.text: (a) A parallel plate capacitor is charged by an ac source. Show that the sum of conduction current ($I_c$) and the displacement current ($I_d$) has the same value at all points of the circuit. answer.text: (a) Total current $I = I_c+I_d$. Outside the capacitor, $I_d=0 \Rightarrow I=I_c$. Inside the capacitor, $I_c=0 \Rightarrow I=I_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt} = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d}{dt}[EA] = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d}{dt}\left[\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}A\right] = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0}{\varepsilon_0}A\dfrac{d}{dt}\left[\dfrac{Q}{A}\right] = \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = I_c$. Hence $I_c+I_d$ has the same value at all points of the circuit. (b) Yes — the current entering the capacitor is $I_c$ and the current between the plates is $I_d$; $I_c=I_d$, which validates Kirchhoff's junction rule.

questions.text: Strontium titanate is a rare oxide $-$ a natural mineral found in Siberia. It is used as a substitute for diamond because its refractive index and critical angle are $2{\cdot}41$ and $24{\cdot}5^\circ$, respectively, which are approximately equal to the refractive index and critical angle of diamond. It has all the properties of diamond. Even an expert jeweller is unable to differentiate between diamond and strontium titanate. answer.text:
(a) The ray refracts into the prism and is incident on the second face at $\angle i = 60^{\circ}$. The critical angle is $\angle i_c = 24{\cdot}5^{\circ}$.
Since $\angle i > \angle i_c$, total internal reflection takes place at the second face (the ray emerges from the base).
(b) $n = \dfrac{c}{v} \ \Rightarrow\ v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{2{\cdot}41} = 1{\cdot}24\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$.
(c) Two applications of total internal reflection (any two): optical fibre, brilliance of diamond, mirage.
OR — Total internal reflection: when light travelling from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium at an interface is reflected back into the same (denser) medium.

answer.text:
Using the lens-maker's formula $\dfrac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$:
focal length of the plano-convex lens $=+30\ \text{cm}$, and of the plano-concave lens $=-30\ \text{cm}$.
For the plano-convex lens the object is at infinity, so its real image forms at the focus: $v_1=+30\ \text{cm}$.
For the plano-concave lens, $u_2=+(30-20)=+10\ \text{cm}$. Using $\dfrac{1}{f_2}=\dfrac{1}{v_2}-\dfrac{1}{u_2}$:
$\dfrac{1}{-30}=\dfrac{1}{v_2}-\dfrac{1}{10}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{1}{v_2}=\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{1}{15}$
$\therefore v_2=15\ \text{cm}$ (the final image forms $15\ \text{cm}$ from the plano-concave lens).

questions.text: Define critical angle for a given pair of media and total internal reflection. Obtain the relation between the critical angle and refractive index of the medium.

answer.text:
Critical angle: when a ray of light passes from a denser to a rarer medium, the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction becomes $90^{\circ}$ is called the critical angle for that pair of media.
Total internal reflection: when a ray of light passes from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, the ray is reflected back into the denser medium.
From Snell's law $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\mu_{rd}$; when $\angle i=\angle i_c$, $\angle r=90^{\circ}$:
$\dfrac{\sin i_c}{\sin 90^{\circ}}=\dfrac{1}{\mu_{dr}}\ \Rightarrow\ \mu_{dr}=\dfrac{1}{\sin i_c}$.

questions.text: The refractive indices of two media A and B are 2 and $\sqrt{2}$ respectively. What is the critical angle for their interface ?

answer.text:
From Snell's law at the critical angle, $\mu_A\sin i_c=\mu_B\sin 90^{\circ}$:
$2\times\sin i_c=\sqrt{2}\times1\ \Rightarrow\ \sin i_c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\therefore\ i_c=45^{\circ}$.
Alternatively, $\sin i_c=\dfrac{1}{{}_B\mu_A}=\dfrac{\mu_B}{\mu_A}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, giving $i_c=45^{\circ}$.

(i) From the similar right triangles $A'B'F$ and $MPF$: $\dfrac{B'A'}{PM}=\dfrac{B'F}{FP}$, i.e. $\dfrac{B'A'}{BA}=\dfrac{B'F}{FP}$ (since $PM=AB$)  ...(1).
Since $\angle APB=\angle A'PB'$, triangles $A'B'P$ and $ABP$ are similar: $\dfrac{B'A'}{BA}=\dfrac{B'P}{BP}$  ...(2).
Comparing (1) and (2): $\dfrac{B'F}{FP}=\dfrac{B'P-FP}{FP}=\dfrac{B'P}{BP}$.
Using the sign convention $B'P=-v,\ FP=-f,\ BP=-u$:
$\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{2}{R}$.
(ii) For the lens $\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$ with $u=-5\ \text{m},\ f=+1\ \text{m}$:
$\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{-5}=\dfrac{1}{+1}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\dfrac{5}{4}\ \text{m}=1{\cdot}25\ \text{m}$.
Magnification $m=\dfrac{v}{u}=\dfrac{+5/4}{-5}=-0{\cdot}25$, so the image height $I=m\times O=(-0{\cdot}25)\times(1{\cdot}8)=-0{\cdot}45\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a ray diagram showing refraction of a ray of light through a triangular glass prism. Hence, obtain the relation for the refractive index ($\mu$) in terms of angle of prism (A) and angle of minimum deviation ($\delta_m$). (ii) The radii of curvature of the two surfaces of a concave lens are 20 cm each. Find the refractive index of the material of the lens if its power is $-5\cdot0$ D.

answer.text:
(i) In quadrilateral $AQNR$ the angles at $Q$ and $R$ are right angles, so $\angle A+\angle QNR=180^{\circ}$; and in $\triangle QNR$, $r_1+r_2+\angle QNR=180^{\circ}$. Hence $r_1+r_2=A$  ...(1).
The total deviation $\delta=(i-r_1)+(e-r_2)=i+e-A$  ...(2).
At minimum deviation $\delta=\delta_m$, $i=e$ and $r_1=r_2=r$: from (1) $r=\dfrac{A}{2}$, and from (2) $i=\dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}$. Therefore
$\mu=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$.
(ii) Given $P=-5\ \text{D}$: $f=\dfrac{100}{-5}=-20\ \text{cm}$. Using the lens-maker's formula $\dfrac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right]$ with $R_1=-20\ \text{cm},\ R_2=+20\ \text{cm}$:
$\dfrac{1}{-20}=(\mu-1)\left[\dfrac{1}{-20}-\dfrac{1}{+20}\right]=(\mu-1)\left(-\dfrac{1}{10}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ \mu-1=\dfrac{1}{2}$
$\therefore\ \mu=\dfrac{3}{2}=1{\cdot}5$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a ray diagram to show how the final image is formed at infinity in an astronomical refracting telescope. Obtain an expression for its magnifying power. (ii) Two thin lenses $L_1$ and $L_2$, $L_1$ being a convex lens of focal length 24 cm and $L_2$ a concave lens of focal length 18 cm are placed coaxially at a separation of 45 cm. A 1 cm tall object is placed in front of the lens $L_1$ at a distance of 36 cm. Find the location and height of the image formed by the combination.

answer.text:
(i) For the final image at infinity, from the ray diagram $\beta=\dfrac{h}{f_e}$ and $\alpha=\dfrac{h}{f_o}$, so the magnifying power is
$M=\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}=\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$.
(ii) For lens $L_1$ ($f=24\ \text{cm},\ u=-36\ \text{cm}$): $\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{1}{24}-\dfrac{1}{36}=\dfrac{1}{72}$, so $v=72\ \text{cm}$.
For lens $L_2$ ($f'=-18\ \text{cm}$, object distance $u'=72-45=27\ \text{cm}$): $\dfrac{1}{v'}-\dfrac{1}{27}=\dfrac{1}{-18}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{1}{v'}=\dfrac{-3+2}{54}=\dfrac{-1}{54}$, so $v'=-54\ \text{cm}$.
Final image distance from the concave lens: $v_1'=-54-(-45)=-9\ \text{cm}$ (to the left of the concave lens).
Magnification: $\dfrac{h_i}{h_o}=\dfrac{v_1'}{u}=\dfrac{-9}{-36}\ \Rightarrow\ h_i=+\dfrac{1}{4}\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: (i) Explain the working principle of an optical fibre with the help of a diagram. Mention one use of a light pipe. (ii) A ray of light is incident at an angle of $60^\circ$ on one face of a prism with the prism angle A = $60^\circ$. The ray passes symmetrically through the prism. Find the angle of minimum deviation ($\delta_m$) and refractive index of the material of the prism. If the prism is immersed in water, how will $\delta_m$ be affected ? Justify your answer.

answer.text:
(i) Working principle of an optical fibre: it uses total internal reflection. Light entering the fibre undergoes repeated total internal reflection (the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding) and is confined to the core. Use: transmission of audio and video signals / examination of internal organs (endoscopy).
(ii) $\delta_m=i+e-A=2i-A=60^{\circ}$.
$\mu=\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}=\dfrac{\sin\frac{120^{\circ}}{2}}{\sin\frac{60^{\circ}}{2}}=\dfrac{\sin60^{\circ}}{\sin30^{\circ}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1/2}=\sqrt{3}$.
When the prism is immersed in water, $\mu$ decreases, and consequently the angle of minimum deviation $\delta_m$ also decreases.

questions.text: The lens maker's formula is useful to design lenses of desired focal lengths using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. The focal length also depends on the refractive index of the material of the lens and the surrounding medium. The refractive index depends on the wavelength of the light used. The power of a lens is related to its focal length. Answer the following questions based on the above : (a) How will the power of a lens be affected with an increase of wavelength of light ? (b) The radius of curvature of two surfaces of a convex lens is R each. For what value of $\mu$ of its material will its focal length become equal to R ? (c) The focal length of a concave lens of $\mu = 1\cdot5$ is 20 cm in air. It is completely immersed in water of $\mu = \dfrac{4}{3}$. Calculate its focal length in water.  OR  (c) An object is placed in front of a lens which forms its erect image of magnification 3. The power of the lens is 5 D. Calculate the distance of the object and the image from the lens.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text:
(a) $P=\dfrac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$; since $\mu\propto\dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, $P\propto\dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, so the power decreases as $\lambda$ increases.
(b) For an equiconvex lens ($R_1=R,\ R_2=-R$): $\dfrac{1}{R}=(\mu-1)\dfrac{2}{R}\ \Rightarrow\ \mu=\dfrac{3}{2}$.
(c) In air, $\dfrac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$, i.e. $\dfrac{1}{20}=\left(\dfrac{3}{2}-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
When immersed in water $\left(\mu_{rel}=\dfrac{3/2}{4/3}=\dfrac{9}{8}\right)$: $\dfrac{1}{f_{water}}=\left(\dfrac{9}{8}-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
Dividing, $\dfrac{1/20}{1/f_{water}}=\dfrac{1/2}{1/8}\ \Rightarrow\ f_{water}=80\ \text{cm}$.
OR — $m=3=\dfrac{v}{u}\ \Rightarrow\ v=3u$; $f=\dfrac{100}{+5}=+20\ \text{cm}$. Using $\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$:
$\dfrac{1}{3u}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{20}\ \Rightarrow\ u=-\dfrac{40}{3}\ \text{cm}$, and $v=3u=-40\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a ray diagram to show the working of a compound microscope. Obtain the expression for total magnification of the final image to be formed at the near point. (ii) In a compound microscope an object is placed at a distance of $1\cdot5$ cm from the objective of focal length $1\cdot25$ cm. If the eye-piece has a focal length of 5 cm and the final image is formed at the near point, find the magnifying power of the microscope.

answer.text:
(i) Linear magnification due to the objective: $\tan\beta=\dfrac{h}{f_0}=\dfrac{h'}{L}$, so $m_0=\dfrac{h'}{h}=\dfrac{L}{f_0}$ (where $L$ is the tube length).
Magnification due to the eyepiece: $m_e=\left(1+\dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$.
Total magnification: $m=m_0\times m_e=\dfrac{L}{f_0}\left(1+\dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$.
(ii) Given $u_0=-1{\cdot}5\ \text{cm},\ f_0=1{\cdot}25\ \text{cm},\ f_e=5\ \text{cm},\ D=25\ \text{cm}$:
$\dfrac{1}{v_0}=\dfrac{1}{f_0}+\dfrac{1}{u_0}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{v_0}=\dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}25}-\dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}5}=\dfrac{2}{15}$, so $v_0=\dfrac{15}{2}\ \text{cm}$.
$|m_0|=\dfrac{v_0}{u_0}=\dfrac{15}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}5}=5$; $|m_e|=1+\dfrac{25}{5}=6$.
$m=m_0\times m_e=5\times6=30$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a ray diagram for the formation of image of an object by an astronomical telescope, in normal adjustment. Obtain the expression for its magnifying power. (ii) The magnifying power of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment is $2\cdot9$ and the objective and the eyepiece are separated by a distance of 150 cm. Find the focal lengths of the two lenses.

answer.text:
(i) For an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment, $m\approx\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$, with $\beta=\dfrac{h}{f_e}$ and $\alpha=\dfrac{h}{f_0}$, so
$m=\dfrac{f_0}{f_e}$.
(ii) Given $m=2{\cdot}9$ and $d=f_0+f_e=150\ \text{cm}$: $\dfrac{f_0}{f_e}=\dfrac{29}{10}$.
Solving with $f_0+f_e=150\ \text{cm}$: $f_e=38{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}$ and $f_0=150-38{\cdot}5=111{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Considering image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, lens maker's formula is obtained. It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. This formula helps us obtain a relation between u, v and f for a lens. Lenses form images of objects and they are used in a number of optical devices, for example microscopes and telescopes. (i) An object AB is kept in front of a composite convex lens, as shown in figure. Will the lens produce one image ? If not, explain. (ii) A real image of an object formed by a convex lens is observed on a screen. If the screen is removed, will the image still be formed ? Explain. (iii) A double convex lens is made of glass of refractive index $1\cdot55$ with both faces of the same radius of curvature. Find the radius of curvature required if focal length is 20 cm.  OR  (iii) Two convex lenses A and B of focal lengths 15 cm and 10 cm respectively are placed coaxially $'d'$ distance apart. A point object is kept at a distance of 30 cm in front of lens A. Find the value of $'d'$ so that the rays emerging from lens B are parallel to its principal axis.

answer.text:
(i) No. The lens is made of two materials of different refractive indices, so it has two focal lengths.
(ii) Yes. The rays still intersect (converge) at the location of the image.
(iii) Using $\dfrac{1}{f}=(n-1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right]$ with $R_1=+R,\ R_2=-R$:
$\dfrac{1}{f}=(n-1)\dfrac{2}{R}\ \Rightarrow\ R=2(n-1)f=2(1{\cdot}55-1)\times20=22\ \text{cm}$.
OR — For lens A ($f=15\ \text{cm},\ u=-30\ \text{cm}$): $\dfrac{1}{v_1}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{1}{v_1}=\dfrac{1}{15}-\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v_1=30\ \text{cm}$. For the rays to emerge parallel from lens B, the image of A must lie at the focus of B, so the separation is $d=30+10=40\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: Monochromatic light of frequency $5\cdot0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz passes from air into a medium of refractive index $1\cdot5$. Find the wavelength of the light (i) reflected, and (ii) refracted at the interface of the two media.

answer.text:
(i) $v=\nu\lambda\ \Rightarrow\ 3\times10^{8}=5{\cdot}0\times10^{14}\times\lambda\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=600\ \text{nm}$ (wavelength of the reflected light, unchanged from the incident light).
(ii) $\lambda_{medium}=\dfrac{\lambda_{air}}{\mu}=\dfrac{600\ \text{nm}}{1{\cdot}5}=400\ \text{nm}$ (wavelength of the refracted light).

questions.text: A plano-convex lens of focal length 16 cm is made of a material of refractive index $1\cdot4$. Calculate the radius of the curved surface of the lens.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text:
Using the lens-maker's formula $\dfrac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$ for a plano-convex lens ($R_2=\infty$):
$\dfrac{1}{16}=(1{\cdot}4-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R}-\dfrac{1}{\infty}\right)=0{\cdot}4\times\dfrac{1}{R}$
$\therefore\ R=16\times0{\cdot}4=6{\cdot}4\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm. Find the (i) position of the image formed and (ii) magnification of the image.
questions.topic: Reflection of Light by Spherical Mirrors

answer.text:
(i) Using the mirror formula $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$ with $u=-30\ \text{cm},\ f=-20\ \text{cm}$:
$\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{-30}=\dfrac{1}{-20}$
On solving, $v=-60\ \text{cm}$ (the image is real, formed $60\ \text{cm}$ in front of the mirror).
(ii) $m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=-\left(\dfrac{-60}{-30}\right)=-2$ (the image is inverted and twice the size of the object).

questions.text: A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The focal length of a lens is determined by the radii of curvature of its two surfaces and the refractive index of its medium with respect to that of the surrounding medium. The power of a lens is reciprocal of its focal length. If a number of lenses are kept in contact, the power of the combination is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses. (i) A double-convex lens, with each face having same radius of curvature R, is made of glass of refractive index n. Its power is : (A) $\dfrac{2(n-1)}{R}$ (B) $\dfrac{(2n-1)}{R}$ (C) $\dfrac{(n-1)}{2R}$ (D) $\dfrac{(2n-1)}{2R}$ (ii) A double-convex lens of power P, with each face having same radius of curvature, is cut into two equal parts perpendicular to its principal axis. The power of one part of the lens will be : (A) 2P (B) P (C) 4P (D) $\dfrac{P}{2}$ (iii) The above two parts are kept in contact with each other as shown in the figure. The power of the combination will be : (A) $\dfrac{P}{2}$ (B) P (C) 2P (D) $\dfrac{P}{4}$ (iv)(a) A double-convex lens of power P, with each face having same radius of curvature, is cut along its principal axis. The two parts are arranged as shown in the figure. The power of the combination will be : (A) Zero (B) P (C) 2P (D) $\dfrac{P}{2}$  OR  (iv)(b) Two convex lenses of focal lengths 60 cm and 20 cm are held coaxially in contact with each other. The power of the combination is : (A) $6\cdot6$ D (B) 15 D (C) $\dfrac{1}{15}$ D (D) $\dfrac{1}{80}$ D
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text:
(i) Power of a double-convex lens (equal radii $R$, refractive index $n$): $P=\dfrac{2(n-1)}{R}$.
(ii) When cut perpendicular to the principal axis into two equal (plano-convex) halves, each half has power $\dfrac{P}{2}$.
(iii) When the two plano-convex halves are recombined in contact (curved surfaces together), the power of the combination is $P$ (the original lens power).
(iv)(a) When the lens is cut along its principal axis and the two halves are arranged as shown, the power of the combination remains $P$.
OR (iv)(b) For two convex lenses of focal length $60\ \text{cm}$ and $20\ \text{cm}$ in contact:
$P=P_1+P_2=\dfrac{100}{60}+\dfrac{100}{20}=1{\cdot}67+5=6{\cdot}67\ \text{D}\approx6{\cdot}6\ \text{D}$.

questions.text: (i) A ray of light passes through a triangular prism. Show graphically, how the angle of deviation varies with the angle of incidence ? Hence define the angle of minimum deviation. (ii) A ray of light is incident normally on a refracting face of a prism of prism angle A and suffers a deviation of angle $\delta$. Prove that the refractive index n of the material of the prism is given by $n = \dfrac{\sin(A + \delta)}{\sin A}$. (iii) The refractive index of the material of a prism is $\sqrt{2}$. If the refracting angle of the prism is $60^\circ$, find the (1) Angle of minimum deviation, and (2) Angle of incidence.

answer.text:
(i) As a ray passes through a triangular prism, the angle of deviation $\delta$ first decreases with increasing angle of incidence $i$, reaches a minimum value $\delta_m$ (at $i=e$), and then increases again — a graph of $\delta$ vs $i$ is a curve with a single minimum.
Angle of minimum deviation $\delta_m$ is the angle of deviation at which the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence (equivalently, the refracted ray inside the prism is parallel to the base).
(ii) For a ray incident normally on face $XY$ of a prism of angle $A$, refracting out through face $XZ$ with angle of incidence $i$ (inside the prism) and angle of refraction (emergence) $r$: at face $XZ$, Snell's law gives $\mu\sin i=\sin r$  ...(1); from the ray geometry, $r=i+\delta$  ...(2); and in $\triangle XMN$, $A+(90^{\circ}-i)+90^{\circ}=180^{\circ}\ \Rightarrow\ A=i$  ...(3).
Substituting (3) into (2): $r=A+\delta$; substituting into (1): $\mu\sin A=\sin(A+\delta)$, so
$\mu=\dfrac{\sin(A+\delta)}{\sin A}$.
(iii) With $\mu=\sqrt{2},\ A=60^{\circ}$: at minimum deviation, $\mu=\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$:
$\sqrt{2}=\dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{60+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin30^{\circ}}\ \Rightarrow\ \sin\left(\dfrac{60+\delta_m}{2}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\sin45^{\circ}\ \Rightarrow\ \delta_m=30^{\circ}$.
(2) Angle of incidence: $i=\dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}=\dfrac{60+30}{2}=45^{\circ}$.

questions.text: In the following question, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d).
questions.assertion: The magnifying power of a compound microscope is negative.
questions.reason: The final image formed is erect with respect to the object.
ar_options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

answer.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

questions.text: A convex lens (n = $1\cdot52$) has a focal length of $15\cdot0$ cm in air. Find its focal length when it is immersed in liquid of refractive index $1\cdot65$. What will be the nature of the lens ?
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text:
For the convex lens in air: $\dfrac{1}{f_a}=\left(\dfrac{n_g}{n_a}-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
For the same lens in the liquid: $\dfrac{1}{f_l}=\left(\dfrac{n_g}{n_l}-1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
Dividing: $\dfrac{f_l}{f_a}=\dfrac{\frac{n_g}{n_l}-1}{\frac{n_g}{n_a}-1}=\dfrac{1{\cdot}52-1}{\frac{1{\cdot}52}{1{\cdot}65}-1}=-6{\cdot}6$
$\therefore\ f_l=-6{\cdot}6\,f_a=-6{\cdot}6\times15=-99\ \text{cm}$.
Since $f_l$ is negative, the lens behaves as a diverging (concave) lens in this liquid.

questions.text: When a ray of light propagates from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal. When the incident angle is increased, the refracted ray deviates more from the normal. For a particular angle of incidence in the denser medium, the refracted ray just grazes the interface of the two surfaces. This angle of incidence is called the critical angle for the pair of media involved. (i) For a ray incident at the critical angle, the angle of reflection is : (A) $0^\circ$ (B) $< 90^\circ$ (C) $> 90^\circ$ (D) $90^\circ$ (ii) A ray of light of wavelength 600 nm is incident in water $\left(n = \dfrac{4}{3}\right)$ on the water-air interface at an angle less than the critical angle. The wavelength associated with the refracted ray is : (A) 400 nm (B) 450 nm (C) 600 nm (D) 800 nm (iii)(a) The interface AB between the two media A and B is shown in the figure. In the denser medium A, the incident ray PQ makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal. The refracted ray is parallel to the interface. The refractive index of medium B w.r.t. medium A is : (A) $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (B) $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ (C) $\dfrac{4}{3}$ (D) $\dfrac{3}{2}$  OR  (iii)(b) Two media A and B are separated by a plane boundary. The speed of light in medium A and B is $2 \times 10^8$ ms$^{-1}$ and $2\cdot5 \times 10^8$ ms$^{-1}$ respectively. The critical angle for a ray of light going from medium A to medium B is : (A) $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}$ (B) $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{4}{5}$ (C) $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{3}{5}$ (D) $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2}{5}$ (iv) The figure shows the path of a light ray through a triangular prism. In this phenomenon, the angle $\theta$ is given by : (A) $\sin^{-1}\sqrt{n^2 - 1}$ (B) $\sin^{-1}(n^2 - 1)$ (C) $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n^2 - 1}}$ (D) $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{(n^2 - 1)}$

answer.text:
(i) For a ray incident at the critical angle, the refracted ray grazes the interface; the reflected ray obeys the law of reflection, so the angle of reflection equals the critical angle — none of the listed options is strictly correct as stated, so full marks were awarded to all students for this part.
(ii) Since frequency (not wavelength) is preserved on refraction, and speed changes: the wavelength in air $\lambda_{air}=n\times\lambda_{water}=\dfrac{4}{3}\times600=800\ \text{nm}$.
(iii)(a) At the interface, the refracted ray is parallel to the interface, i.e. refracted at $90^{\circ}$; with the incident ray in denser medium A at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal (i.e. $60^{\circ}$ to the normal), by Snell's law:
$\mu_{BA}=\dfrac{\sin(\text{angle in A})}{\sin90^{\circ}}=\sin60^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
OR (iii)(b) Critical angle $\theta_c$: $\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}=\dfrac{2\times10^{8}}{2{\cdot}5\times10^{8}}=\dfrac{4}{5}$, so $\theta_c=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{4}{5}$.
(iv) For the given prism geometry, the angle $\theta$ (angle of incidence at the second face equal to the critical angle) is given by $\theta=\sin^{-1}\sqrt{n^{2}-1}$.

questions.text: The magnifying power of an astronomical telescope is 24. In normal adjustment, distance between its two lenses is 150 cm. Find the focal length of the objective lens.

answer.text:
Magnifying power $m=\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}=24$ and tube length $f_o+f_e=150\ \text{cm}$.
Solving these: $f_e=6\ \text{cm}$ and $f_o=144\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: Explain the following : (a) For a simple microscope, the angular size of the object equals the angular size of the image. Yet it offers magnification. (b) Both plane and convex mirrors produce virtual images of objects. Can they produce real images under some circumstances ?

answer.text:
(a) Yes, a simple microscope (magnifying glass) offers magnification: the small object can be kept much closer to the eye than $25\ \text{cm}$, so it subtends a larger angle at the eye and hence appears magnified.
(b) Yes. Rays converging towards a point behind a plane or convex mirror (a virtual object) are reflected so as to converge to a real point in front of the mirror, where the image can be obtained on a screen.

questions.text: (i) Trace the path of a ray of light showing refraction through a triangular prism and hence obtain an expression for angle of deviation ($\delta$) in terms of A, i and e, where symbols have their usual meanings. Draw a graph showing the variation of angle of deviation with the angle of incidence. (ii) In the figure, a ray of light is incident on a transparent liquid contained in a thin glass box at an angle of $45^\circ$ with its one face. The emergent ray passes along the face AB. Find the refractive index of the liquid.

answer.text:
(i) For the prism, in quadrilateral $AQNR$: $\angle A+\angle QNR=180^{\circ}$; in triangle $QNR$: $r_1+r_2+\angle QNR=180^{\circ}$. Comparing these gives $r_1+r_2=A$.
The angle of deviation $\delta=(i-r_1)+(e-r_2)=i+e-A$. The $\delta$–$i$ graph falls to a minimum (at $i=e$) and then rises.
(ii) Light incident at $45^{\circ}$ refracts into the medium: $\dfrac{\sin45^{\circ}}{\sin\theta}=\mu\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\mu\sin\theta$.
At the second (vertical) surface, total internal reflection gives $\dfrac{\sin(90^{\circ}-\theta)}{\sin90^{\circ}}=\dfrac{1}{\mu}$, i.e. $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=1\ \Rightarrow\ \tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
From triangle $GEF$, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, hence $\mu=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$.

questions.text: A ray of light is incident normally on one face of an equilateral glass prism. When the prism is completely immersed in a transparent medium, it is observed that the emergent ray just grazes the adjacent face. Find the refractive index of the medium.

answer.text:
At the first face, from Snell's law $\mu\sin i=\mu_m\sin r$. The ray inside strikes the second face at the critical angle so it emerges grazing it:
$\mu\sin60^{\circ}=\mu_m\sin90^{\circ}\ \Rightarrow\ \mu_m=\mu\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
Alternatively, using $\mu=\dfrac{1}{\sin C}$: $\dfrac{\mu}{\mu_m}=\dfrac{1}{\sin60^{\circ}}\ \Rightarrow\ \mu_m=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\mu$.

questions.text: An air bubble is trapped at point B (CB = 20 cm) in a glass sphere of radius 40 cm and refractive index $1{\cdot}5$ as shown in figure. Find the nature and position of the image of the bubble as seen by an observer at point P.

answer.text:
Using refraction at a spherical surface (denser to rarer medium): $\dfrac{n_1}{v}-\dfrac{n_2}{u}=\dfrac{n_1-n_2}{R}$, with $n_1=1$ (rarer), $n_2=1{\cdot}5$ (denser), $u=-20\ \text{cm}$, $R=-40\ \text{cm}$:
$\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{(-20)}=\dfrac{1-1{\cdot}5}{(-40)}\ \Rightarrow\ v=-16\ \text{cm}$.
The image is virtual.

questions.text: In normal adjustment, for a refracting telescope, the distance between objective and eye piece lens is $1{\cdot}00$ m. If the magnifying power of the telescope is 19, find the focal length of the objective and the eyepiece lens.

answer.text:
Distance between objective and eyepiece: $f_o+f_e=1{\cdot}00\ \text{m}=100\ \text{cm}$; magnifying power $|m|=\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}=19$.
Solving these: $f_o=95\ \text{cm}=0{\cdot}95\ \text{m}$ and $f_e=5\ \text{cm}=0{\cdot}05\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula of image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a thin lens, a formula known as lens maker's formula and hence the basic lens formula can be obtained. The focal length (or power) of a lens depends on the radii of its surfaces and the refractive index of its material with respect to the surrounding medium. The refractive index of a material depends on the wavelength of light used. Combination of lenses helps us to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired power and magnification. (i) A thin converging lens of focal length 20 cm and a thin diverging lens of focal length 15 cm are placed coaxially in contact. The power of the combination is : (A) $\dfrac{-5}{6}$ D (B) $\dfrac{-5}{3}$ D (C) $\dfrac{4}{3}$ D (D) $\dfrac{3}{2}$ D (ii) The radii of curvature of two surfaces of a convex lens are R and 2R. If the focal length of this lens is $\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$R, the refractive index of the material of the lens is : (A) $\dfrac{5}{3}$ (B) $\dfrac{4}{3}$ (C) $\dfrac{3}{2}$ (D) $\dfrac{7}{5}$ (iii) The focal length of an equiconvex lens : (A) increases when the lens is dipped in water. (B) increases with the wavelength of incident light decreases. (C) increases with decrease in radius of curvature of its surface. (D) decreases when the lens is cut into two identical parts along its principal axis. (iv)(a) A thin convex lens L of focal length 10 cm and a concave mirror M of focal length 15 cm are placed coaxially 40 cm apart as shown in figure. A beam of light coming parallel to the principal axis is incident on the lens. The final image will be formed at a distance of : (A) 10 cm, left of lens (B) 10 cm, right of lens (C) 20 cm, left of lens (D) 20 cm, right of lens  OR  (iv)(b) A beam of light coming parallel to the principal axis of a convex lens $L_1$ of focal length 10 cm is incident on it. Another convex lens $L_2$ of focal length 12 cm is placed coaxially at a distance 40 cm from $L_1$. The nature and distance of the final image from $L_2$ will be : (A) real, 24 cm (B) virtual, 12 cm (C) real, 32 cm (D) virtual, 18 cm

(i) (B) $-\dfrac{5}{3}D$.
(ii) (C) $\dfrac{3}{2}$.
(iii) (A) increases when a lens is dipped in water.

OR (iv)(b) (A) real, $24\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a ray diagram for the formation of the image of an object by a convex mirror. Hence, obtain the mirror equation. (ii) Why are multi-component lenses used both for the objective and the eyepiece in optical instruments ? (iii) The magnification of an object placed in front of a compound microscope is 200. The focal length of the eyepiece is 2 cm and the final image is formed at infinity. Find the magnification of the eyepiece.

answer.text:
(i) For image formation by a concave mirror, taking paraxial rays $MP$ as nearly a straight line perpendicular to the axis, triangles $A'B'F$ and $MPF$ are similar: $\dfrac{B'A'}{PM}=\dfrac{B'F}{FP}$, i.e. $\dfrac{B'A'}{BA}=\dfrac{B'F}{FP}$  ...(1).
Since $\angle APB=\angle A'PB'$, triangles $A'PB'$ and $APB$ are similar: $\dfrac{B'A'}{BA}=\dfrac{B'P}{BP}$  ...(2).
Comparing (1) and (2): $\dfrac{PF-PB'}{FP}=\dfrac{B'P}{BP}$. Using the sign convention $PF=-f,\ PB'=-v,\ PB=-u$ and simplifying: $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$.
(ii) Multi-component lenses are used to improve image quality by minimising the various optical aberrations.
(iii) Magnification of a compound microscope $m=m_0\times m_e$, so $m_0=\dfrac{m}{m_e}=\dfrac{m}{\left|\dfrac{D}{f_e}\right|}=\dfrac{200}{\frac{25}{2}}=16$.

questions.text: The focal lengths of the objective and the eyepiece of a compound microscope are 1 cm and 2 cm respectively. If the tube length of the microscope is 10 cm, the magnification obtained by the microscope for most suitable viewing by relaxed eye is :

A telescope has an objective lens of focal length 150 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. Calculate its magnifying power in normal adjustment and the distance of the image formed by the objective.

answer.text:
Magnifying power $|m|=\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}=\dfrac{150}{5}=30$.
For the image distance of the objective, using $\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}$ with $f=150\ \text{cm}$ and a distant object ($u\to\infty$): $\dfrac{1}{150}=\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{\infty}\ \Rightarrow\ v=150\ \text{cm}$ (the image forms at the focus of the objective).

questions.text: A transparent solid cylindrical rod (refractive index $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$) is kept in air. A ray of light incident on its face travels along the surface of the rod, as shown in figure. Calculate the angle $\theta$.

answer.text: For the critical angle, $\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta_c}$; with $n_1=1$, $n_2=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ (given), $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta_c} \Rightarrow \sin\theta_c = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \Rightarrow \theta_c = 60^\circ$, so $r = 90^\circ-\theta_c = 30^\circ$. From Snell's law at the air–rod interface, $n_1\sin\theta = n_2\sin r \Rightarrow \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin30^\circ} \Rightarrow \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\times\dfrac{1}{2} = \sin\theta \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \Rightarrow \theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$.

A thin lens has two foci $-$ called 'first focal point' and 'second focal point' of the lens, one on each side. (i) Consider the arrangement shown in figure. The focal length of each part will be : (A) f (B) 2 f (C) $\dfrac{f}{2}$ (D) $\dfrac{f}{4}$  OR  (iii)(b) If an object in case (i) above is 20 cm from the lens and the screen is 50 cm away from the object, the focal length of the lens used is : (A) 10 cm (B) 12 cm (C) 16 cm (D) 20 cm (iv) The distance of an object from first focal point of a biconvex lens is $X_1$ and distance of the image from second focal point is $X_2$. questions.text: (i) A thin pencil of length $\left(\dfrac{f}{4}\right)$ is placed coinciding with the principal axis of a mirror of focal length f. The image of the pencil is real and enlarged, just touches the pencil. Calculate the magnification produced by the mirror. (ii) A ray of light is incident on a refracting face AB of a prism ABC at an angle of $45^\circ$. The ray emerges from face AC and the angle of deviation is $15^\circ$. The angle of prism is $30^\circ$. Show that the emergent ray is normal to the face AC from which it emerges out. Find the refractive index of the material of the prism.

answer.text: (i) As the pencil lies between $f$ and $2f$ such that one end coincides with $2f$: position of the other end $u = -\left(2f-\dfrac{f}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{7f}{4}$. Magnification $m = \dfrac{f}{f-u} = \dfrac{-f}{-f-\left(-\frac{7f}{4}\right)} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$. (Alternatively: $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{4}{7f} = -\dfrac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{f}+\dfrac{4}{7f} \Rightarrow v=-\dfrac{7f}{3}$, so $m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=-\dfrac{4}{3}$.) (ii) For the prism: $i+e = A+\delta \Rightarrow 45^\circ+e = 30^\circ+15^\circ \Rightarrow e=0^\circ$, hence $r_2=0^\circ$; the emergent ray is perpendicular to face AC. (If shown using a diagram, full credit is given.) $r_1+r_2=A$; as $r_2=0$, $r_1=30^\circ$. Refractive index $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\sin45^\circ}{\sin30^\circ} = \sqrt2$.

questions.text: (i) An object is placed 30 cm from a thin convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The lens forms a sharp image on a screen. If a thin concave lens is placed in contact with the convex lens, the sharp image on the screen is formed when the screen is moved by 45 cm into its initial position. Calculate the focal length of the concave lens. (ii) Calculate the angle of minimum deviation of an equilateral prism. The refractive index of the prism is $\sqrt{3}$. Calculate the angle of incidence in this case of minimum deviation also.

answer.text: For the real image formed by the convex lens: $\dfrac{1}{f_1} = \dfrac{1}{v_1}-\dfrac{1}{u_1} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{v_1}-\dfrac{1}{(-30)} \Rightarrow v_1=15\ \text{cm}$. For the combination of lenses, letting the combined focal length be $f_3$: $\dfrac{1}{f_3} = \dfrac{1}{v_3}-\dfrac{1}{u_3} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{f_3} = \dfrac{1}{(15+45)}+\dfrac{1}{30} \Rightarrow f_3=20\ \text{cm}$. Letting the focal length of the concave lens be $f_2$: $\dfrac{1}{f_3}=\dfrac{1}{f_1}+\dfrac{1}{f_2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{f_2}=\dfrac{1}{20}-\dfrac{1}{10} \Rightarrow f_2=-20\ \text{cm}$. (ii) Angle of minimum deviation: $\mu = \dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)} \Rightarrow \sqrt3 = \dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{60^\circ+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin30^\circ}$, solving $\delta_m = 60^\circ$. Angle of incidence: $i+e=A+\delta \Rightarrow 2i=A+\delta_m \Rightarrow i=\dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}=60^\circ$.

questions.text: A compound microscope has an objective and an eyepiece of focal lengths $f_0$ and $f_e$ respectively. To obtain a large magnification of a small object, the microscope should have :

answer.text: $f_0$ and $f_e$ small, and $f_0 > f_e$

questions.text: A point object is placed in air at a distance $\dfrac{R}{3}$ in front of a convex surface of radius of curvature R, separating air from a medium of refractive index n ($< 4$). Find the nature and position of the image formed.

answer.text: For refraction at the convex surface: $\dfrac{n_1}{-u}+\dfrac{n_2}{v}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R} \Rightarrow \dfrac{n}{v} = \dfrac{[n-1-3]}{R} \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{nR}{n-4}$. For all values of $n<4$, the value of $v$ is negative and greater than $R$; therefore the image is virtual, formed in front of the convex surface.

questions.text: A rectangular glass slab ABCD (refractive index $1{\cdot}5$) is surrounded by a transparent liquid (refractive index $1{\cdot}25$) as shown in the figure. A ray of light is incident on face AB at an angle i such that it is refracted out grazing the face AD. Find the value of angle i.

answer.text: For the glass–liquid interface: $\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{n_{21}} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}25}{1{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{5}{6}$. Since $i_c+r=90^\circ$: $\sin r = \sqrt{1-\cos^2 r} = \dfrac{\sqrt{11}}{6}$. Since $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n$: therefore $\sin i = \dfrac{\sqrt{11}}{4}$, i.e. $i = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{11}}{4}\right)$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a ray diagram of a reflecting telescope (Cassegrain) and explain the formation of image. State two important advantages that a reflecting telescope has over a refracting telescope. (ii) In a refracting telescope, the focal length of the objective is 50 times the focal length of the eyepiece. When the final image is formed at infinity, the length of the tube is 102 cm. Find the focal lengths of the two lenses.

answer.text: (i) Diagram of a reflecting telescope: objective mirror (large concave), secondary mirror (small convex), eyepiece. The parallel rays from a distant object are reflected by the large concave mirror; these rays are then reflected by the convex mirror placed just before the focus of the concave mirror, converging to a point outside the hole; the final image is viewed through the eyepiece. Advantages (any two): no chromatic aberration; less spherical aberration; less mechanical support required; brighter image; high resolving power; high magnifying power. (ii) For the image at infinity, $|f_0|+|f_e|=L$. Given $f_0=50f_e$: $f_e+50f_e=102 \Rightarrow f_e=2\ \text{cm}$, $f_0=100\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: (i) Write any two advantages of a compound microscope over a simple microscope. Draw a ray diagram for the image formation at the near point by a compound microscope and explain it. (ii) A thin planoconcave lens with its curved face of radius of curvature R is made of glass of refractive index $n_1$. It is placed coaxially in contact with a thin equiconvex lens of same radius of curvature of refractive index $n_2$. Obtain the power of the combination lens.

answer.text: (i) Two advantages of a compound microscope over a simple microscope (any two): larger magnification; brighter image. Ray diagram: the lens nearest the object (objective) forms a real, inverted, magnified image; this serves as the object for the second lens (eyepiece), which functions like a simple microscope and produces the final image, enlarged and virtual. (ii) Power of the plano-concave lens $P_1 = -\dfrac{(n_1-1)}{R}$; power of the convex lens $P_2 = (n_2-1)\left(\dfrac{2}{R}\right)$; $P = P_1+P_2 = \dfrac{2n_2-n_1-1}{R}$.

answer.text: Ray diagram of a concave mirror (object AB beyond C forming real image A'B'). Mirror-formula derivation: in similar triangles $\triangle A'B'F$ and $\triangle MPF$: $\dfrac{A'B'}{MP}=\dfrac{B'F}{FP}$, i.e. $\dfrac{A'B'}{AB}=\dfrac{B'F}{FP}$ (since $MP=AB$) $\ldots(1)$. In similar triangles $\triangle A'B'P$ and $\triangle ABP$: $\dfrac{A'B'}{AB}=\dfrac{PB'}{PB}\ \ldots(2)$. From (1) and (2): $\dfrac{B'F}{FP}=\dfrac{PB'}{PB} \Rightarrow \dfrac{PB'-PF}{FP}=\dfrac{PB'}{PB} \Rightarrow \dfrac{(-v)-(-f)}{(-f)}=\dfrac{(-v)}{(-u)}$; solving, $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$.

questions.text: (i) Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation by a compound microscope. Obtain the expression for the total magnification of the microscope when the final image is formed at infinity. (ii) In a compound microscope, an object is placed at a distance of $1{\cdot}5$ cm from the objective of focal length $1{\cdot}25$ cm. The eyepiece has a focal length of 5 cm. The final image is formed at infinity. Calculate the distance between the objective and the eyepiece.

answer.text: (i) Ray diagram of a compound microscope (objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image; eyepiece further magnifies it). Magnification by the objective, $m_0 = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{L}{f_0}$. Magnification by the eyepiece, $m_e = 1+\dfrac{D}{f_e}$; if the final image is at infinity, $m_e = \dfrac{D}{f_e}$. Total magnification $m = m_0\times m_e = \left(\dfrac{L}{f_0}\right)\left(\dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$. (ii) $\dfrac{1}{v_o}-\dfrac{1}{u_o}=\dfrac{1}{f_0} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v_o}-\dfrac{1}{(-1{\cdot}5)}=\dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}25} \Rightarrow v_o=7{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}$. $L = |v_o|+|f_e|$ (as the final image is at infinity, $v_e=\infty$, $u_e=f_e$): $L=7{\cdot}5+5=12{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: Using the mirror equation and the formula of magnification, deduce that \"the virtual image formed by a convex mirror is always diminished in size and is located between the pole and the focus.\"
