answer.text: Let $u=nf$. From the mirror formula: $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{1}{f}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}+\dfrac{1}{nf} \Rightarrow v=\dfrac{nf}{n+1}$. Since $n=+ve$, $v<f$. $m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=\dfrac{1}{n+1}$, which is always positive and less than 1.

questions.text: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm, a concave lens of focal length 15 cm and a third lens of unknown focal length are placed coaxially in contact. If the focal length of the combination is $+12$ cm, find the nature and focal length of the third lens, if all lenses are thin. Will the answer change if the lenses were thick ?
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: $\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{f_1}+\dfrac{1}{f_2}+\dfrac{1}{f_3} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{12}=\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{15}+\dfrac{1}{f_3} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{f_3}=\dfrac{5-6+4}{60} \Rightarrow f_3=20\ \text{cm}$. Nature: convex. Yes — changing the thickness of the lens changes its focal length.

questions.text: When light travels from an optically denser medium to an optically rarer medium, at the interface it is partly reflected back into the same medium and partly refracted to the second medium. The angle of incidence corresponding to an angle of refraction $90^\circ$ is called the critical angle ($i_c$) for the given pair of media. This angle is related to the refractive index of medium 1 with respect to medium 2. Refraction of light through a prism involves refraction at two plane interfaces. A relation for the refractive index of the material of the prism can be obtained in terms of the refracting angle of the prism and the angle of minimum deviation. For a thin prism, this relation reduces to a simple equation. Laws of refraction are also valid for refraction of light at a spherical interface. When an object is placed in front of a spherical surface separating two media, its image is formed. A relation between object and image distance, in terms of refractive indices of two media and the radius of curvature of the spherical surface can be obtained. Using this relation for two surfaces of a lens, 'lens maker formula' is obtained. (i) A small bulb is placed at the bottom of a tank containing a transparent liquid (refractive index n) to a depth H. The radius of the circular area of the surface of liquid, through which light from the bulb can emerge out, is R. Then $\left(\dfrac{R}{H}\right)$ is : (A) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n^2-1}}$ (B) $\sqrt{n^2-1}$ (C) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n^2+1}}$ (D) $\sqrt{n^2+1}$ (ii)(a) A parallel beam of light is incident on a face of a prism with refracting angle $60^\circ$. The angle of minimum deviation is found to be $30^\circ$. The refractive index of the material of the prism is close to : (A) $1{\cdot}3$ (B) $1{\cdot}4$ (C) $1{\cdot}5$ (D) $1{\cdot}6$  OR  (ii)(b) The angle of minimum deviation for a ray of light incident on a thin prism, made of crown glass (n = $1{\cdot}52$) is $D_m$. If the prism was made of dense flint glass (n = $1{\cdot}62$) instead of crown glass, the angle of minimum deviation will : (A) decrease by 4% (B) increase by 4% (C) decrease by 19% (D) increase by 19% (iii) An object is placed in front of a convex spherical glass surface (n = $1{\cdot}5$ and radius of curvature R) at a distance of 4R from it. As the object is moved slowly close to the surface, the image formed is : (A) always real (B) always virtual (C) first real and then virtual (D) first virtual and then real (iv) A double-convex lens, made of glass of refractive index $1{\cdot}5$, has focal length 10 cm. The radius of curvature of its each face, is : (A) 10 cm (B) 15 cm (C) 20 cm (D) 40 cm

answer.text: (i) (A) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n^2-1}}$. (ii)(a) (B) $1{\cdot}4$ [OR (b) (D) increase by 19%]. (iii) (C) first real and then virtual. (iv) (A) $10\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: (i) Explain with the help of a labelled ray diagram the formation of final image in a compound microscope at infinity. Write the expression for its magnifying power. (ii) The total magnification produced by a compound microscope is 20. The magnification produced by the eyepiece is 5. When the microscope is focussed on a certain object, the distance between the objective and eyepiece is observed to be 14 cm. Calculate the focal lengths of the objective and the eyepiece. (Given that the least distance of distinct vision = 25 cm)

answer.text: Light from a distant object enters the objective lens and forms a real image $A'B'$ at $f_0$. This image acts as the object for the eyepiece, which forms a magnified image at infinity. Magnifying power $= \dfrac{f_0}{f_e}$. (ii) The image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision: $20=m_o\times m_e$; $m_o=\dfrac{20}{5}=4$; $m_e=1+\dfrac{D}{f_e} \Rightarrow f_e=\dfrac{25}{4}\ \text{cm}$. $\dfrac{1}{v_e}-\dfrac{1}{u_e}=\dfrac{1}{f_e} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{-25}-\dfrac{1}{u_e}=\dfrac{4}{25} \Rightarrow u_e=-5\ \text{cm}$. $L=v_0+|u_e|$, with $v_0=9\ \text{cm}$. Given $\dfrac{v_0}{u_0}=4$: $\dfrac{1}{v_0}-\dfrac{1}{u_0}=\dfrac{1}{f_0} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{f_0}=\dfrac{1}{9}-\left(-\dfrac{4}{9}\right) \Rightarrow f_0=\dfrac{9}{5}\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: A concave lens of focal length 10 cm is cut into two identical plano-concave lenses. The focal length of each lens will be
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: 20 cm

questions.text: (a) Draw the ray diagram to show the image formation by a refracting telescope and write the expression for angular magnification in normal adjustment. (b) Give two reasons to explain why a reflecting telescope is preferred over a refracting telescope.

answer.text: (a) Ray diagram of a refracting (astronomical) telescope; angular magnification $|m| = \dfrac{f_0}{f_e}$. (b) Two advantages of a reflecting telescope over a refracting one (any two): no chromatic aberration; needs less mechanical support; brighter and clearer image; more cost-effective; little to no spherical aberration.

questions.text: (a) State the two conditions under which total internal reflection occurs. (b) A transparent container contains layers of three immiscible transparent liquids A, B and C of refractive indices n, $\dfrac{3}{4}$n and $\dfrac{2}{3}$n, respectively. A laser beam is incident at the interface between A and B at an angle $\theta$ as shown in figure. Prove that the beam does not enter region C at all for $\sin\theta \geq \dfrac{2}{3}$.

answer.text: (a) Two conditions for total internal reflection: (i) light must travel from a denser to a rarer medium; (ii) the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle ($i > i_c$). (b) At face AB: $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin\theta_1} = \dfrac{3n/4}{n} \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}\sin\theta_1\ \ldots(1)$. At face BC: $\dfrac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin r} = \dfrac{2n/3}{3n/4} \Rightarrow \sin\theta_1 = \dfrac{8}{9}\sin r\ \ldots(2)$. Combining (1) and (2): $\dfrac{3}{2}\sin\theta = \sin r$; for $\sin\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$, $\sin r = 1 \Rightarrow r = 90^\circ$, so the ray just grazes face BC. Hence for $\sin\theta \ge \dfrac{2}{3}$ the beam does not enter region C at all.

questions.text: (a) Using the relation for refraction at a curved spherical surface, derive the expression for lens maker's formula. (b) Three lenses $L_1$, $L_2$ and $L_3$, each of focal length 40 cm, are placed coaxially. The distance between $L_1$ and $L_2$ and between $L_2$ and $L_3$ are 120 cm and 20 cm respectively. An object is kept at a distance of 80 cm to the left of lens $L_1$. Find the distance of the final image formed from the object.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: (a) Lens maker's formula: refraction at the first surface gives $\dfrac{n_1}{OB} + \dfrac{n_2}{BI_1} = \dfrac{n_2-n_1}{BC_1}\ \ldots(1)$ and at the second surface $-\dfrac{n_2}{DI_1} + \dfrac{n_1}{DI} = \dfrac{n_2-n_1}{DC_2}\ \ldots(2)$; for a thin lens ($BI_1 = DI_1$), adding (1) and (2) gives $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \left(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$, and for an object at infinity $\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$. (b) Three lenses, $f = 40\ \text{cm}$ each, object $80\ \text{cm}$ from $L_1$: for $L_1$, $v_1 = 80\ \text{cm}$; for $L_2$ ($u_2 = 120-80 = 40\ \text{cm}$), $v_2 = \infty$; for $L_3$ ($u_3 = \infty$), $v_3 = 40\ \text{cm}$. Distance of the final image from the object $= 80+120+20+40 = 260\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: (a) Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation by a concave mirror when the object is kept between its focus and the centre of curvature. Using this diagram, derive the mirror formula. (b) A concave mirror produces a two times magnified virtual image of an object kept 10 cm in front of it. Calculate the focal length of the mirror.
questions.topic: Reflection of Light by Spherical Mirrors

answer.text: (a) Mirror formula for a concave mirror, derived from the ray diagram using similar triangles: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u}$. (b) For a two-times magnified virtual image: $m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = 2 \Rightarrow v = -2u = -2(-10) = 20\ \text{cm}$; then $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{10} \Rightarrow f = -20\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: A ray of light in air is incident at angle $\angle i$ on a face of an equilateral glass prism and is refracted through the prism. As $\angle i$ is varied, it is observed that the ray undergoes minimum deviation, when the $\angle i$ is three-fourth of the angle of the prism. Calculate the speed of light in the prism.

answer.text: Speed of light in the prism: angle of incidence $i = \dfrac{3}{4}A = 45^\circ$; at minimum deviation $r = \dfrac{A}{2} = 30^\circ$; refractive index $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{\sin45^\circ}{\sin30^\circ} = \sqrt{2}$. Since $n = \dfrac{c}{v}$, $v = \dfrac{c}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\times10^{8} = 2{\cdot}12\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.text: A 5 cm long pencil is placed along the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm such that its nearest end is at a distance of 25 cm from the mirror. Calculate the length of the image of the pencil.
questions.topic: Reflection of Light by Spherical Mirrors

answer.text: Length of the image of a pencil placed on the axis of a concave mirror: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u}$. Near end: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{-20} - \dfrac{1}{-25} \Rightarrow v_1 = -100\ \text{cm}$; far end: $\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{-20} - \dfrac{1}{-30} \Rightarrow v_2 = -60\ \text{cm}$. Length of image $L = |v_1| - |v_2| = 40\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: In an experiment with convex lens of focal length f, the screen is fixed at a distance D from the object. A student slowly moves the lens away from the object towards the screen and finds that she is able to form sharp image of the object for two positions of the lens. The distance between these two positions of the lens is d. (i) The value of d is : (A) $\sqrt{D(D-4f)}$ (B) $\sqrt{D(D-2f)}$ (C) $2\sqrt{Df}$ (D) $\sqrt{D(D-f)}$ (ii) Compared to the size of the object, the images formed in the two positions of the lens are respectively (A) reduced, enlarged (B) reduced, reduced (C) enlarged, enlarged (D) enlarged, reduced (iii) If the distance between object and screen is $80{\cdot}00$ cm and the lens forms sharp images at two positions separated by $20{\cdot}00$ cm., the focal length of convex lens is (A) $15{\cdot}50$ cm (B) $18{\cdot}75$ cm (C) $20{\cdot}50$ cm (D) $22{\cdot}75$ cm (iv)(a) Consider a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. For which of the following values of object-screen distance, two positions of the object can be found to obtain sharp image on the screen ? (A) 45 cm (B) 50 cm (C) 55 cm (D) 65 cm  OR  (iv)(b) A thin convex lens of focal length 10 cm and another thin lens of focal length 'f' are placed coaxially in contact. If the power of their combination is $\dfrac{10}{3}$ D, the value of 'f' is (A) $-15$ cm (B) $-10$ cm (C) $-20$ cm (D) $-30$ cm.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: (i) (A) $\sqrt{D(D-4f)}$. (ii) (D) Enlarged, reduced. (iii) (B) $18{\cdot}75\ \text{cm}$. (iv) (D) $65\ \text{cm}$ [OR (A) $-15\ \text{cm}$].

questions.text: A thin plano-convex lens and a thin equi-concave lens are kept coaxially in contact as shown in the figure. Assuming both the lenses are made of glass of refractive index $\mu$, and R is the radius of curvature of each curved surface, the focal length of the combination is :
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: $-\dfrac{R}{\mu-1}$

questions.text: A telescope has an objective lens of focal length 144 cm and an eyepiece of focal length $6{\cdot}0$ cm. The magnifying power and the length of telescope tube will be respectively :
In which of the following, total internal reflection does $\textbf{not}$ occur ?

answer.text: Twinkling of stars

questions.text: A ray of light is travelling through a rectangular glass slab (refractive index $\dfrac{3}{2}$) and is incident on the horizontal glass-air surface at the critical angle for the two media. The slab is then brought in contact with water (refractive index $\dfrac{4}{3}$) such that a thin horizontal layer of water is formed on the surface of the slab. Find the angle at which the ray will emerge into air from the water-air surface.

answer.text: Angle of emergence at the water–air surface: $\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{2}{3}$. At the glass–water surface, $\dfrac{3}{2}\sin i_c = \dfrac{4}{3}\sin r \Rightarrow \sin r = \dfrac{3}{4}$. At the water–air surface, $\dfrac{4}{3}\sin r = \sin e \Rightarrow \dfrac{4}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{4} = \sin e = 1 \Rightarrow e = 90^\circ$.

questions.text: (a) (i) A point object is kept in front of a convex spherical surface of radius of curvature R. Draw the ray diagram to show the formation of image and derive the relation between the object and image distance (u and v) in terms of refractive index of the medium and R. (ii) A convex lens of focal length 20 cm is used to form the image of an object placed 30 cm away from the lens. Find the position and nature of the image formed.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: (a) Refraction at a single convex spherical surface (ray diagram, small angles): $i = \angle NOM + \angle NCM$, $r = \angle NCM - \angle NIM$, and by Snell's law $1\cdot i = n\cdot r$; this gives $\dfrac{1}{MO} + \dfrac{n}{MI} = \dfrac{n-1}{MC}$, and with Cartesian sign convention ($MO = -u$, $MI = +v$, $MC = +R$): $\dfrac{n}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{n-1}{R}$. (ii) For the given data the image is formed at $v = 60\ \text{cm}$ and is real and inverted.

questions.text: (b) (i) Two thin converging lenses of focal length $f_1$ and $f_2$ are placed coaxially in contact. Derive expression for the focal length of the combination. (ii) A beam of coherent light of wavelength 550 nm is incident normal to the plane of a pair of two slits $S_1$ and $S_2$ each of width $1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-6}$ m separated by $1{\cdot}1$ mm. Dark and bright fringes are observed on a screen $2{\cdot}2$ m away from the plane of the slits. Calculate : (I) fringe width. (II) distance of the second dark fringe from the central maximum. (III) what will happen when the entire apparatus is immersed in water.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: (b)(i) Two thin lenses in contact: for lens A, $\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}$; for lens B, $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$; adding, $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2} = \dfrac{1}{f}$, so $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$. (ii) YDSE: (I) fringe width $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{550\times10^{-9}\times2{\cdot}2}{1{\cdot}1\times10^{-3}} = 1{\cdot}1\ \text{mm}$. (II) Distance of the 2nd dark fringe, $x = \dfrac{(2n-1)\lambda D}{2d}$ with $n=2 \Rightarrow x = 1{\cdot}65\ \text{mm}$. (III) On immersing the set-up in water the fringe width decreases ($\beta' = \dfrac{\beta}{n}$).

questions.text: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given $-$ one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.
questions.assertion: When a convex lens made of glass is immersed in water, its converging power increases.
questions.reason: The focal length of a lens depends only on the radii of curvature of its two faces.
ar_options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

questions.text: A small bulb is placed at the bottom of a tank, containing a transparent liquid of refractive index $\sqrt{2}$, to a depth of 1 m. Calculate the area of the surface of the liquid through which light from the bulb emerges.

answer.text: Area of the circle of light emerging from the water surface: only rays within the critical angle escape, so radius $r = h\tan i_c$; $\sin i_c = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \Rightarrow i_c = 45^\circ$, hence $r = h$. Area $= \pi r^2 = 3{\cdot}14\times(1)^2 = 3{\cdot}14\ \text{m}^2$.

questions.text: An astronomical telescope consists of two converging lenses. One of them of large aperture and large focal length is called objective lens and the other one, of smaller focal length and smaller aperture is called the eyepiece. It is used to see distant objects which are not seen clearly with naked eyes. The image formed by the objective lens acts as an object for the eyepiece and the final image produced by the eyepiece is magnified. (i) The images formed by the objective lens and the eyepiece are respectively : (A) virtual, real (B) real, virtual (C) virtual, virtual (D) real, real (ii) The magnification produced by the telescope does $\textbf{not}$ depend upon the : (A) colour of light (B) focal length of objective lens (C) focal length of eyepiece (D) apertures of objective lens and eyepiece (iii) Which of the following statements is $\textbf{not}$ correct for this telescope ? (A) The focal length of objective lens ($f_o$) is larger than the focal length of eyepiece ($f_e$). (B) Its magnifying power can be increased by increasing the focal length of objective lens ($f_o$). (C) The distance between two lenses is more than ($f_o + f_e$). (D) The magnifying power can be decreased by increasing the focal length of eyepiece. (iv)(a) An astronomical telescope has objective lens and eyepiece of focal lengths 80 cm and 4 cm respectively. To view the image in normal adjustment, the lenses must be separated by a distance of : (A) 84 cm (B) 76 cm (C) 20 cm (D) 320 cm  OR  (iv)(b) Consider the telescope described in question (iv)(a). Its magnifying power in normal adjustment will be : (A) 320 (B) 84 (C) 76 (D) 20

answer.text: (i) (B) real, virtual. (ii) (D) apertures of the objective lens and the eyepiece. (iii) (C) the distance between the two lenses is more than $(f_0+f_e)$. (iv) (A) $84\ \text{cm}$ [OR (D) $20$].

questions.text: (a) (i) Define refractive index of a medium in terms of speed of light. (ii) Derive the relation for the refractive index ($\mu$) of a prism in terms of angle of minimum deviation ($\delta_m$) and angle of prism (A). (iii) A ray of light QP is incident normally on the face BC of a triangular prism ABC of refractive index $1{\cdot}5$ kept in air, as shown in the figure. Trace the path of the ray as it passes through the prism and give relevant explanation.

answer.text: (a)(i) Refractive index of a medium = the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium ($n = \dfrac{c}{v}$). (ii) For a prism, $r_1+r_2 = A$ and total deviation $\delta = i+e-A$; at minimum deviation $i = e$ and $r_1 = r_2$, giving $r = \dfrac{A}{2}$ and $i = \dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}$, so $n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$. (iii) For the given prism the ray strikes face BC normally and goes undeviated; as $i > i_c$ it undergoes total internal reflection and then exits the other face normally, undeviated.

questions.text: A tank is filled with a liquid to a height of $12{\cdot}5$ m. The apparent depth of a needle lying at the bottom of the tank is measured to be $9{\cdot}0$ m. Calculate the speed of light in the liquid.

answer.text: Refractive index $n = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$. With real depth $12{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}$ and apparent depth $9\ \text{cm}$, $n = \dfrac{12{\cdot}5}{9}$; hence speed of light in the liquid $v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}\times9}{12{\cdot}5} = 2{\cdot}16\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.text: Two thin lenses of focal length $f_1$ and $f_2$ are placed in contact with each other coaxially. Prove that the focal length f of the combination is given by $f = \dfrac{f_1 f_2}{f_1 + f_2}$.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text: For two thin lenses in contact, the combination behaves as a single lens of focal length $f$ given by $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$, i.e. $f = \dfrac{f_1f_2}{f_1+f_2}$ (equivalently, power $P = P_1 + P_2$).

questions.text: Why is a reflecting telescope preferred over a refracting telescope ? Justify your answer giving two reasons.

answer.text:
A reflecting telescope is preferred over a refracting telescope. Reasons (any two):
1. No chromatic aberration — a mirror reflects light and does not refract it.
2. No spherical aberration — a parabolic reflector is used.
3. Easy mechanical support — mirrors are lighter and can be supported over their entire back surface.
4. High resolving power — a mirror of large diameter can be used.
5. Brighter image — large mirrors gather more light.

questions.text: (i) A spherical surface of radius of curvature R separates two media of refractive indices $n_1$ and $n_2$. A point object is placed in front of the surface at distance u in medium of refractive index $n_1$ and its image is formed by the surface at distance v, in the medium of refractive index $n_2$. Derive a relation between u and v. (ii) A solid glass sphere of radius $6{\cdot}0$ cm has a small air bubble trapped at a distance $3{\cdot}0$ cm from its centre C as shown in the figure. The refractive index of the material of the sphere is $1{\cdot}5$. Find the apparent position of this bubble when seen through the surface of the sphere from an outside point E in air.
questions.topic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

answer.text:
For a spherical refracting surface, using small-angle geometry: for $\triangle NOC$, $i$ is the exterior angle, so
$i = \angle NOM + \angle NCM = \dfrac{MN}{OM} + \dfrac{MN}{MC}$  ...(i)
$r = \angle NCM - \angle NIM = \dfrac{MN}{MC} - \dfrac{MN}{MI}$  ...(ii)
By Snell's law $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$; for small angles $n_1 i = n_2 r$. Substituting (i) and (ii):
$\dfrac{n_1}{OM} + \dfrac{n_2}{MI} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{MC}$.
Applying the Cartesian sign convention ($OM = -u,\ MI = +v,\ MC = +R$):
$\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$.
(ii) With $R = -6\ \text{cm},\ u = -3\ \text{cm},\ n_1 = 1{\cdot}5,\ n_2 = 1$:
$\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{3} = \dfrac{1 - 1{\cdot}5}{-6}$
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{6} - \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{3} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5 - 3}{6} = \dfrac{-2{\cdot}5}{6}$
$v = -2{\cdot}4\ \text{cm}$  (the image is $2{\cdot}4\ \text{cm}$ from the surface, inside the sphere).

questions.text: (i) Draw a labelled ray diagram showing the image formation by a refracting telescope. Define its magnifying power. Write two limitations of a refracting telescope over a reflecting telescope. (ii) The focal lengths of the objective and the eye-piece of a compound microscope are 1·0 cm and 2·5 cm respectively. Find the tube length of the microscope for obtaining a magnification of 300.

answer.text:
Magnifying power (of a telescope) is the ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle subtended by the object at the unaided eye.
Two limitations of a refracting telescope (over a reflecting one, any two): less resolving power; difficult mechanical support; less bright image; it suffers from chromatic aberration; it suffers from spherical aberration.
(ii) For the compound microscope, $f_o=1{\cdot}0\ \text{cm},\ f_e=2{\cdot}5\ \text{cm},\ m=300,\ D=25\ \text{cm}$:
$|m|=\dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}\ \Rightarrow\ 300=\dfrac{L}{1{\cdot}0}\cdot\dfrac{25}{2{\cdot}5}$
$\therefore L=30\ \text{cm}$ (tube length).

questions.text: (i) Draw a labelled ray diagram of a compound microscope showing image formation at least distance of distinct vision. Derive an expression for its magnifying power. (ii) A telescope consists of two lenses of focal length 100 cm and 5 cm. Find the magnifying power when the final image is formed at infinity.

answer.text:
(i) The magnification by the eyepiece is $m_e=\left(1+\dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$; by the objective, $m_0=\dfrac{v_0}{-u_0}$.
Total magnifying power: $m=m_0\times m_e=\dfrac{v_0}{-u_0}\left(1+\dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)$.
(ii) For a telescope with the final image at infinity, $m=\left|\dfrac{f_0}{f_e}\right|$; with $f_0=100\ \text{cm}$ and $f_e=5\ \text{cm}$:
$m=\left|\dfrac{100}{5}\right|=20$.

questions.text: A point source of light in air is kept at a distance of 12 cm in front of a convex spherical surface of glass of refractive index $1{\cdot}5$ and radius of curvature 30 cm. Find the nature and position of the image formed.

answer.text: $\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v}-\dfrac{1}{(-12)}=\dfrac{1{\cdot}5-1}{30} \Rightarrow v=-22{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}$. The image is virtual and erect.

questions.text: (a) Draw a labelled ray diagram of a refracting telescope when it forms image of a distant object at infinity. Derive expression for its magnifying power. (b) (i) In a telescope the objective has much larger aperture than the eye piece. Why ? (ii) Write two advantages of reflecting telescope over refracting telescope.

(b)(i) The objective is given a larger aperture so that fainter objects can be seen clearly (greater light-gathering power and resolving power). (ii) Two advantages of a reflecting telescope (any two): no chromatic aberration; spherical aberration removed using a parabolic mirror; needs less mechanical support; more cost-effective; brighter and sharper image.

The objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image of the object; this image acts as the object for the eyepiece, which forms the final image, virtual and further enlarged. (Draw and label the ray diagram; final magnification $m = m_0\times m_e$.) (ii)(I) Yes — a real image is still formed even if the screen is removed, since it is produced by the actual intersection of the refracted rays. (II) Such a real image forms when the object presented to the lens is a virtual object.

questions.text: (i) State Huygens' principle. A plane wave is incident at an angle i on a reflecting surface. Construct the corresponding reflected wavefront. Using this diagram, prove that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. (ii) What are the coherent sources of light ? Can two independent sodium lamps act like coherent sources ? Explain. (iii) A beam of light consisting of a known wavelength 520 nm and an unknown wavelength $\lambda$, used in Young's double-slit experiment produces two interference patterns such that the fourth bright fringe of unknown wavelength coincides with the fifth bright fringe of known wavelength. Find the value of $\lambda$.

answer.text:
(i) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets spreading out with the speed of the wave; their common tangent gives the new wavefront.
For a plane wave $AB$ incident at angle $i$ on a reflecting surface $MN$: drawing a sphere of radius $v\tau$ from $A$ (where $v$ is the wave speed and $\tau$ the time for the wavefront to travel from $B$ to $C$), the tangent $CE$ gives the reflected wavefront.
In $\triangle EAC$ and $\triangle BAC$: $AE=BC=v\tau$, $\angle AEC=\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$, $AC$ common, so $\triangle EAC\cong\triangle BAC$, giving $\angle i=\angle r$ (the law of reflection).
(ii) Two sources are coherent if the phase difference between them does not change with time. No, two independent sodium lamps cannot act as coherent sources, because the phase difference between light from two independent sources varies randomly with time.
(iii) The fourth bright fringe of the unknown wavelength coincides with the fifth bright fringe of the known wavelength: $4\beta_2=5\beta_1\ \Rightarrow\ 4\times\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}=5\times\dfrac{\lambda_{known}D}{d}$
$\lambda=\dfrac{5}{4}\times\lambda_{known}=\dfrac{5}{4}\times520=650\ \text{nm}$.

questions.text: (i) The displacement of two light waves, each of amplitude a and frequency $\omega$, emanating from two coherent sources of light, are given by $y_1 = a\cos\omega t$ and $y_2 = a\cos(\omega t + \phi)$. $\phi$ is the phase difference between the two waves. These light waves superpose at a point. Obtain the expression for the resultant intensity at that point. (ii) In Young's double-slit experiment, find the ratio of intensities at two points on a screen when waves emanating from two slits reaching these points have path differences (i) $\dfrac{\lambda}{6}$ and (ii) $\dfrac{\lambda}{12}$.
questions.topic: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

answer.text:
(i) Superposition of $y_1=a\cos\omega t$ and $y_2=a\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ gives $y=a\cos\omega t(1+\cos\phi)-a\sin\phi\sin\omega t$; writing the amplitude as $A$, $A^{2}=a^{2}(1+\cos\phi)^{2}+a^{2}\sin^{2}\phi=2a^{2}(1+\cos\phi)=4a^{2}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}$.
Since $I\propto A^{2}$ (i.e. $I=kA^{2}$): $I=4ka^{2}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}=4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}$.
(ii) For path difference $\dfrac{\lambda}{6}$: $\phi_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $I_1=4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{6}=3I_0$.
For path difference $\dfrac{\lambda}{12}$: $\phi_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $I_2=4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{12}=4I_0\cos^{2}15^{\circ}$.
$\therefore\ \dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\dfrac{3}{4\cos^{2}15^{\circ}}$.

questions.text: (i) Differentiate between a wavefront and a ray. (ii) State Huygen's principle and verify laws of reflection using suitable diagram. (iii) In Young's double slit experiment, the slits $S_1$ and $S_2$ are 3 mm apart and the screen is placed $1{\cdot}0$ m away from the slits. It is observed that the fourth bright fringe is at a distance of 5 mm from the second dark fringe. Find the wavelength of light used.

answer.text:
(i) A wavefront is a surface of constant phase (locus of points oscillating in phase); a ray is the straight-line path along which light travels and is normal to the wavefront.
(ii) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; the common tangent to these wavelets gives the new wavefront. For reflection, triangles $EAC$ and $BAC$ are congruent, hence $\angle i=\angle r$.
(iii) Position of the 4th bright fringe $x_{4(bright)}=\dfrac{4D\lambda}{d}$; position of the 2nd dark fringe $x_{2(dark)}=\dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{D\lambda}{d}$.
Given $x_{4(bright)}-x_{2(dark)}=5\ \text{mm}$: $\dfrac{4D\lambda}{d}-\dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{D\lambda}{d}=5\times10^{-3}\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=6\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: (i) Light consisting of two wavelengths 600 nm and 480 nm is used to obtain interference fringes in a double slit experiment. The screen is placed $1{\cdot}0$ m away from slits which are $1{\cdot}0$ mm apart. (1) Calculate the distance of the third bright fringe on the screen from the central maximum for wavelength 600 nm. (2) Find the least distance from the central maximum where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide. (ii) (1) Draw the variation of intensity with angle of diffraction in single slit diffraction pattern. Write the expression for value of angle corresponding to zero intensity locations. (2) In what way diffraction of light waves differs from diffraction of sound waves ?

answer.text: (i)(1) Distance of the $n$th bright fringe from the central maximum, $x_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}$; for $n=3$: $x_3 = \dfrac{3\times600\times10^{-9}\times1}{1\times10^{-9}} = 1800\ \text{m}$. (2) $n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2 \Rightarrow n_1\times600 = n_2\times480 \Rightarrow \dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{480}{600} = \dfrac{4}{5}$. Position of the 4th bright fringe of $600\ \text{nm}$ $= 4\times600 = 2400\ \text{m}$. (Alternatively: position of the 5th bright fringe of $480\ \text{nm}$ $= 5\times480 = 2400\ \text{m}$.) (Alternatively: $(n-1)\lambda_1 = n\lambda_2 \Rightarrow (n-1)\times600 = n\times450$, solving $n=4$; position of the 4th bright fringe of $600\ \text{nm}$ $=4\times600=2400\ \text{m}$; position of the 5th bright fringe of $480\ \text{nm}$ $=5\times480=2400\ \text{m}$.) (ii)(1) Graph of intensity vs angle of diffraction for a single slit (central maximum flanked by weaker secondary maxima). Angle of diffraction for zero intensity, $\theta = \dfrac{n\lambda}{a}$; $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. (2) Diffraction of light waves is not generally observed as easily as diffraction of sound waves, because light waves have a much shorter wavelength.

questions.text: (i) A physics teacher wants to demonstrate interference with the help of double slit experiment using a laser beam of 633 nm wavelength. Since the hall is large enough, interference pattern is formed on the wall $5{\cdot}0$ m from the slits. For clear and comfortable view by all the students they want the fringe width 5 mm. (I) Find the slit separation for obtaining the desired interference pattern. (II) How far will the first minimum be from the central maximum ? (ii) A parallel beam of light of wavelength 650 nm passes through a slit of width $0{\cdot}6$ mm. The diffraction pattern is obtained on a screen kept 60 cm away from the slit. Find the distance between first order minima on both sides of the central maximum.

answer.text: (i)(I) Slit separation: $\beta = \dfrac{D\lambda}{d} \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{D\lambda}{\beta} = \dfrac{633\times10^{-9}\times5}{5\times10^{-3}} = 633\times10^{-6}\ \text{m} = 633\ \mu\text{m}$. (II) Distance of the first minimum from the central maximum: $x_n = \dfrac{(2n-1)\lambda D}{2d}$; for $n=1$: $x = \dfrac{633\times10^{-9}\times5}{2\times5\times10^{-3}} = 316{\cdot}5\times10^{-6}\ \text{m} = 316{\cdot}5\ \mu\text{m}$. (ii) Distance between the first-order minima on both sides of the central maximum: $W = \dfrac{2D\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{2\times650\times10^{-9}}{0{\cdot}6\times10^{-3}}\times60\times10^{-2} = 1{\cdot}3\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: In Young's double slit experimental set-up, the intensity of the central maximum is $I_0$. Calculate the intensity at a point where the path difference between two interfering waves is $\dfrac{\lambda}{3}$.

answer.text: $\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. $I' = 4I\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$; given $4I=I_0$: $I' = I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{I_0}{4}$. (If attempted using $I=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi$, full credit is given for the correct answer.)

questions.text: (i) Using Huygens' principle, explain the refraction of a plane wavefront, propagating in air, at a plane interface between air and glass. Hence verify Snell's law. (ii) Use mirror formula to deduce that a convex mirror always produces a virtual image of an object kept in front of it.
questions.topic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves using Huygens Principle

answer.text: (i) Refraction of a plane wavefront (diagram: incident wavefront AB in medium 1, refracted wavefront in medium 2 with $v_2<v_1$): $\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_1\tau}{AC}$; $\sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_2\tau}{AC}$; so $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{c/n_1}{c/n_2} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$, i.e. $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$ (Snell's law verified). (ii) $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$, with $u<0$, $f>0$: $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{(-u)}=\dfrac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{1}{f}+\dfrac{1}{u}$, which is positive; therefore $v$ is positive $\Rightarrow$ the image is virtual (a convex mirror always produces a virtual image of an object).

questions.text: (i) Two coherent light waves, each of intensity $I_0$ superpose each other and produce interference pattern on a screen. Obtain the expression for the resultant intensity at a point where the phase difference between the waves is $\phi$. Write its maximum and minimum possible values. (ii) In a single slit diffraction experiment, the aperture of the slit is 3 mm and the separation between the slit and the screen is $1{\cdot}5$ m. A monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm is normally incident on the slit. Calculate the distance of (I) first order minimum, and (II) second order maximum, from the centre of the screen.

answer.text: (i) $y_1=a\cos\omega t$; $y_2=a\cos(\omega t+\phi)$. By the principle of superposition: $y=y_1+y_2=a[\cos\omega t+\cos(\omega t+\phi)] = 2a\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right) = A\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$, where $A=2a\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}$; $I=kA^2=k\left(4a^2\cos^2\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right) = 4I_0\cos^2\dfrac{\phi}{2}$. (Alternatively, if written as $I=I_1+I_1+2\sqrt{I_1I_1}\cos\phi$, one mark is awarded.) Maximum value $I=4I_0$; minimum value $I=0$. (ii)(I) Position of the first-order minimum: $y=\dfrac{n\lambda D}{a} \Rightarrow y_1=\dfrac{\lambda D}{a} = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}\times1{\cdot}5}{3\times10^{-3}} = 3\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$. (II) Position of the second-order maximum: $y_n=(2n+1)\dfrac{\lambda D}{2a}$; for $n=2$: $y_2=\dfrac{5\lambda D}{2a} = \dfrac{5\times600\times10^{-9}\times1{\cdot}5}{2\times3\times10^{-3}} = 7{\cdot}5\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, a beam of light consisting of two wavelengths 500 nm and 600 nm is incident at a screen placed $1{\cdot}8$ m away from the plane of slits (slit separation $0{\cdot}3$ mm). Calculate the least distance from the central maximum where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide.

answer.text: Least distance at which bright fringes of the two wavelengths coincide: $n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{600}{500} = \dfrac{6}{5}$, so $n_1 = 6$. $y_{max} = \dfrac{n_1\lambda_1 D}{d} = \dfrac{6\times500\times10^{-9}\times1{\cdot}8}{0{\cdot}3\times10^{-3}} = 18\ \text{mm}$.

questions.text: (b) (i) What is the difference between a ray and a wavefront ? (ii) A plane wave is incident on a reflecting surface. Using Huygens principle, show how it is reflected from the surface. Hence, verify the law of reflection. (iii) Depict refraction of a plane wave by a convex lens.
questions.topic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves using Huygens Principle

answer.text: (b)(i) Ray = a straight line showing the rectilinear propagation of light; wavefront = the locus of points oscillating in the same phase. (ii) Using Huygens' construction, $BC = v\tau$ and $AE = v\tau$, so triangles EAC and BAC are congruent, giving angle of incidence = angle of reflection (law of reflection verified). questions.text: Using Huygens' principle, draw a ray diagram showing the propagation of a plane wave refracting at a plane surface separating two media. Also verify Snell's law of refraction.
questions.topic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves using Huygens Principle

answer.text:
$AB$ is the incident wavefront reaching the surface at angle $i$. Let $\tau$ be the time taken by the wavefront to travel the distance $BC$.
$BC = v_1\tau$, where $v_1$ is the speed of the wave in medium 1.
To find the refracted wavefront, draw a sphere of radius $v_2\tau$ (speed in medium 2) about $A$; the tangent $CE$ from $C$ is the refracted wavefront, so $AE = v_2\tau$.
$\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_1\tau}{AC}, \qquad \sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_2\tau}{AC}$
$\therefore\ \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = n_{21}$  (Snell's law of refraction).

questions.text: Two coherent monochromatic light beams of intensities I and 4 I superpose each other. Find the ratio of maximum and minimum intensities in the resulting beam.
questions.topic: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

answer.text:
$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2})^{2}}{(\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2})^{2}} = \dfrac{I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1 I_2}}{I_1 + I_2 - 2\sqrt{I_1 I_2}}$
With $I_1 = 4I$ and $I_2 = I$:
$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \dfrac{5I + 4I}{5I - 4I} = \dfrac{9}{1}$
$\therefore\ I_{max}:I_{min} = 9:1$.
Alternatively (amplitude method):
$\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{a^{2}}{b^{2}} = \dfrac{4I}{I} = \dfrac{4}{1} \ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{2}{1}$
$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \dfrac{(a+b)^{2}}{(a-b)^{2}} = \dfrac{(2+1)^{2}}{(2-1)^{2}} = \dfrac{9}{1}$.

questions.text: (i) (1) Write two points of difference between an interference pattern and a diffraction pattern. (2) Name any two factors on which the fringe width in a Young's double-slit experiment depends. (ii) In Young's double-slit experiment, the two slits are separated by a distance equal to 100 times the wavelength of light that passes through the slits. Calculate : (1) the angular separation in radians between the central maximum and the adjacent maximum. (2) the distance between these two maxima on a screen 50 cm from the slits.

answer.text:
(i)(1) Differences between interference and diffraction (any two):
(a) Interference has equally spaced bright and dark bands; diffraction has a central bright maximum twice as wide as the others.
(b) Interference is the superposition of two waves from two narrow slits; diffraction is the superposition of a continuous family of waves from each point of a single slit.
(c) In interference the bright fringes have the same intensity; in diffraction the intensity falls off for successive maxima away from the centre.
(2) Factors affecting fringe width (any two): wavelength $\lambda$, distance of the screen from the slits $D$, separation between the slits $d$.
(ii)(1) $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$; for the first maximum $n = 1$, $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d}$.
For a small angle, with $d = 100\lambda$:  $\sin\theta \approx \theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{100\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{100}\ \text{rad}$.
(2) $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \theta D = \dfrac{1}{100}\times50\times10^{-2} = 50\times10^{-4}\ \text{m} = 5\ \text{mm}$.

questions.text: What happens to the interference pattern when two coherent sources are (a) infinitely close, and (b) far apart from each other ?
questions.topic: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

answer.text:
(a) When the two coherent sources are infinitely close, $d$ is very small. Since the fringe width $\beta\propto\dfrac{1}{d}$, $\beta$ becomes very large — a single bright patch occupies the whole field of view and the interference pattern cannot be observed (equivalently, the fringe width increases so much that fringes are not seen).
(b) When the sources are far apart, $d$ is very large, so $\beta$ becomes so small that the fringes are not resolved and cannot be seen separately (the fringe width decreases).

questions.text: (i) State Huygen's principle. With the help of a diagram, show how a plane wave is reflected from a surface. Hence verify the law of reflection. answer.text:
(i) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; the common tangent (envelope) to these secondary wavelets gives the new position of the wavefront at a later time.
Verification of the law of reflection: in $\triangle AEC$ and $\triangle CBA$, $EC=AB$ (each $=c\tau$), $\angle AEC=\angle CBA=90^{\circ}$, and $AC$ is common; by RHS congruency $\triangle AEC\cong\triangle CBA$, hence $\angle i=\angle r$.
(ii) Given $m=+3,\ f=-12\ \text{cm}$: $m=-\dfrac{v}{u}=3\ \Rightarrow\ v=-3u$.
Using the mirror formula $\dfrac{1}{v}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{f}$:
$\dfrac{1}{-3u}+\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{-12}\ \Rightarrow\ u=-8\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: State Huygens' principle. How did Huygens explain the absence of the backwave ?

answer.text:
Statement: every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; the common tangent to all the secondary wavelets gives the new position of the wavefront.
Absence of the backwave: the intensity of the secondary wavelets varies as $I=\dfrac{1}{2}(1+\cos\theta)$; in the backward direction $\theta=180^{\circ}$, so the contribution is zero. Hence light energy cannot travel in the backward direction (the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction).

questions.text: Use Huygens' principle to show reflection/refraction of a plane wave by (i) concave mirror, and (ii) a convex lens.

(ii) Convex lens — an incident plane wavefront emerges as a spherical (converging) wavefront of radius $f$, converging towards the focus.

If both light and sound waves can bend around obstacles, how is it that the students are unable to see each other even though they can converse easily ?

answer.text:

(b) Condition for the first minimum: the path difference $a\theta=\lambda$, i.e. it occurs at an angle $\theta\approx\dfrac{\lambda}{a}$.
(c) Differences (any two): in an interference pattern all maxima are equally spaced and of equal intensity, and the dark fringes have zero intensity; in a diffraction pattern the central maximum is twice as wide as the others, the intensity of the maxima decreases sharply after the central one, and the dark fringes are not completely dark. Interference is obtained by superposing waves from two slits/sources, whereas diffraction is obtained by superposing waves from points on a single slit.
OR — Reason: the opening (slit) is $3\ \text{m}$, which is of the order of the wavelength of sound but very large compared with the wavelength of light; hence sound can bend (diffract) around the obstacle while light cannot.

questions.text: (i) In diffraction due to a single slit, the phase difference between light waves reaching a point on the screen is $5\pi$. Explain whether a bright or a dark fringe will be formed at the point. (ii) What should the width (a) of each slit be to obtain eight maxima of two double-slit patterns (slit separation d) within the central maximum of the single slit pattern ? (iii) Draw the plot of intensity distribution in a diffraction pattern due to a single slit.

answer.text:
(i) For a bright fringe (maximum) the phase difference is $\phi=(2n+1)\pi$; here $\phi=5\pi$ corresponds to $n=2$.
The corresponding path difference is $\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi}\,\Delta\phi=\dfrac{5}{2}\lambda$.
(ii) For the first minimum $a\theta=\lambda$, i.e. $\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{a}$. Given the condition $8\dfrac{\lambda}{d}=2\dfrac{\lambda}{a}$, we get $a=\dfrac{d}{4}$.
(iii) The intensity distribution in the diffraction pattern shows a broad, intense central maximum with much weaker secondary maxima falling off symmetrically on either side.

questions.text: (i) In a Young's double-slit experiment $SS_2 - SS_1 = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$, where $S_1$ and $S_2$ are the two slits as shown in the figure. Find the path difference $(S_2P - S_1P)$ for constructive and destructive interference at P. (ii) What is the effect on the interference fringes in a Young's double-slit experiment, if the monochromatic source S is replaced by a source of white light ?
questions.topic: Interference of Light Waves and Young's Experiment

answer.text:
(i) The net path difference of the two waves reaching a point $P$ on the screen is
$SS_2P-SS_1P=(SS_2-SS_1)+(S_2P-S_1P)=\dfrac{\lambda}{4}+(S_2P-S_1P)$.
For constructive interference $\Delta x=n\lambda$: $(S_2P-S_1P)=n\lambda-\dfrac{\lambda}{4}=\lambda\left(n-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$.
For destructive interference $\Delta x=(2n-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$: $(S_2P-S_1P)=(2n-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}-\dfrac{\lambda}{4}=\dfrac{\lambda}{4}(4n-3)$.
(ii) If the monochromatic source is replaced by white light, the central bright fringe is white.

options: equal in both the forward and the backward directions.

questions.text: A plane wave-front propagating in a medium of refractive index $'\mu_1'$ is incident on a plane surface making an angle of incidence (i). It enters into a medium of refractive index $\mu_2$ $(\mu_2 > \mu_1)$. Use Huygen's construction of secondary wavelets to trace the refracted wave-front. Hence verify Snell's law of refraction.
questions.topic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves using Huygens Principle

answer.text:
$AB$ is the incident wavefront meeting the surface at angle $i$; let $\tau$ be the time taken to travel $BC$.
$BC=v_1\tau$, where $v_1$ is the speed in medium 1. Drawing a sphere of radius $v_2\tau$ (with $v_2$ the speed in medium 2), the tangent $CE$ is the refracted wavefront, so $AE=v_2\tau$.
$\sin i=\dfrac{BC}{AC}=\dfrac{v_1\tau}{AC}, \qquad \sin r=\dfrac{AE}{AC}=\dfrac{v_2\tau}{AC}$
$\therefore\ \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=\dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}$, i.e. $\mu_1\sin i=\mu_2\sin r$ (Snell's law).

questions.text: Using Huygen's construction, show how a plane wave is reflected from a surface. Hence verify the law of reflection.
questions.topic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves using Huygens Principle

answer.text:
A plane wave $AB$ is incident at angle $i$ on the reflecting surface $MN$. If $v$ is the wave speed and $\tau$ the time to advance from $B$ to $C$, then $BC=v\tau$.
Drawing a sphere of radius $v\tau$ about $A$, the tangent $CE$ is the reflected wavefront, so $AE=v\tau$.
In $\triangle AEC$ and $\triangle ABC$: $AE=BC=v\tau$, $\angle CEA=\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$, and $AC$ is common; hence $\triangle AEC\cong\triangle ABC$.
$\therefore\ \angle i=\angle r$ (law of reflection).

questions.text: Two waves, each of amplitude $'a'$ and frequency $'\omega'$ emanating from two coherent sources of light superpose at a point. If the phase difference between the two waves is $\phi$, obtain an expression for the resultant intensity at that point.
questions.topic: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

answer.text:
$x_1=a\cos\omega t,\ x_2=a\cos(\omega t+\phi)$; resultant displacement
$x=x_1+x_2=a(\cos\omega t+\cos(\omega t+\phi))=2a\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$.
Since intensity $I=K(\text{amplitude})^{2}$:
$I=K\left(2a\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)^{2}=4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}$, where $I_0=Ka^{2}$ is the intensity of each wave.

questions.text: What is the effect on the interference pattern in Young's double-slit experiment when (i) the source slit is moved closer to the plane of the slits, and (ii) the separation between the two slits is increased ? Justify your answers.
questions.topic: Interference of Light Waves and Young's Experiment

answer.text:
(i) When the source slit is moved closer to the plane of the two slits, the sharpness of the interference pattern decreases, since $\dfrac{s}{S}<\dfrac{\lambda}{d}$ is violated; interference patterns from different parts of the (now less point-like) source overlap, and eventually the fringes disappear (the screen is uniformly illuminated).
(ii) $\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$; as the slit separation $d$ increases, $\beta$ decreases, and eventually the fringes become too closely spaced to be resolved and disappear.

questions.text: (i) Give any two differences between the interference pattern obtained in Young's double-slit experiment and a diffraction pattern due to a single slit. (ii) Draw an intensity distribution graph in case of a double-slit interference pattern. (iii) In Young's double-slit experiment using monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$, the intensity of light at a point on the screen, where path difference is $\lambda$, is K units. Find the intensity of light at a point on the screen where the path difference is $\dfrac{\lambda}{6}$.

answer.text:
(i) The interference and diffraction patterns differ as shown in the table below.
(ii) The intensity distribution graph for double-slit interference shows a series of equally-spaced maxima of equal (uniform) intensity, separated by zero-intensity minima.
(iii) For path difference $\lambda$, phase difference $\phi=\dfrac{2\pi\Delta}{\lambda}=2\pi$, and $I=4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}$, so $K=4I_0\cos^{2}\pi=4I_0$.
For path difference $\dfrac{\lambda}{6}$: $\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so
$I=4I_0\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{6}=4I_0\times\dfrac{3}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4}K$.

questions.text: Diffraction and interference are closely related phenomena that occur together. Diffraction is the phenomenon of bending of light around the edges of the obstacle, while interference is the combination of waves that results in a new wave pattern. In order to get interference, there must be at least two waves that are diffracting. So while diffraction can occur without interference, interference cannot occur without diffraction. Two slits of width $2\ \mu$m each in an opaque material are separated by a distance of $6\ \mu$m. Monochromatic light of wavelength 450 nm is incident normally on the slits. One finds a combined interference and diffraction pattern on the screen. (i) The number of peaks of the interference fringes formed within the central peak of the envelope of the diffraction pattern will be : (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 6 (ii) The number of peaks of the interference formed if the slit width is doubled while keeping the distance between the slits same will be : (A) 1 (B) 2 (C) 3 (D) 4 (iii)(a) If instead of 450 nm light, another light of wavelength 680 nm is used, number of peaks of the interference formed in the central peak of the envelope of the diffraction pattern will be : (A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) 9  OR  (iii)(b) Consider the diffraction of light by a single slit described in this case study. The first minimum falls at an angle $\theta$ equal to : (A) $\sin^{-1}(0.12)$ (B) $\sin^{-1}(0.225)$ (C) $\sin^{-1}(0.32)$ (D) $\sin^{-1}(0.45)$ (iv) The number of bright fringes formed due to interference on 1 m of screen placed at $\dfrac{4}{3}$ m away from the slits is : (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 6 (D) 10

questions.text: (i) A plane light wave propagating from a rarer into a denser medium, is incident at an angle i on the surface separating two media. Using Huygen's principle, draw the refracted wave and hence verify Snell's law of refraction. (ii) In a Young's double slit experiment, the slits are separated by $0{\cdot}30$ mm and the screen is kept $1{\cdot}5$ m away. The wavelength of light used is 600 nm. Calculate the distance between the central bright fringe and the $4^{\text{th}}$ dark fringe.
questions.topic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves using Huygens Principle

answer.text:
(i) Using Huygens' construction the refracted wavefront $AE$ is drawn. Considering triangles $ABC$ and $AEC$: $\sin i=\dfrac{BC}{AC}=\dfrac{v_1\tau}{AC}$  ...(1) and $\sin r=\dfrac{AE}{AC}=\dfrac{v_2\tau}{AC}$  ...(2).
Dividing, $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}$  ...(3). With $n_1=\dfrac{c}{v_1}$ and $n_2=\dfrac{c}{v_2}$: $n_1\sin i=n_2\sin r$, which is Snell's law of refraction.
(ii) Position of the 4th dark fringe: $X_4=\dfrac{(2n-1)\lambda D}{2d}=\dfrac{(2\times4-1)\times600\times10^{-9}\times1{\cdot}5}{2\times0{\cdot}3\times10^{-3}}=1{\cdot}05\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: (i) Discuss briefly diffraction of light from a single slit and draw the shape of the diffraction pattern. (ii) An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. Using mirror formula, prove mathematically that it produces a virtual and an enlarged image.

answer.text:
(i) Diffraction: when a beam of light falls normally on a narrow single slit, it bends around the edges of the slit. On a screen the diffracted light forms a pattern whose central maximum is the brightest, the intensity of successive maxima decreasing on moving away from the centre on either side.
(ii) The minima of the single-slit pattern occur where $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$ ($n=1,2,3,\dots$); the first minimum is at $a\sin\theta=\lambda$.

questions.text: In a diffraction experiment, the slit is illuminated by light of wavelength 600 nm. The first minimum of the pattern falls at $\theta = 30^\circ$. Calculate the width of the slit.

answer.text: Condition for minima: $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$. For the first minimum, $n=1$: $a\sin30^\circ = 600\times10^{-9}\ \text{m} \Rightarrow a\times\dfrac{1}{2} = 600\times10^{-9}\ \text{m} \Rightarrow a = 1200\times10^{-9}\ \text{m} = 1{\cdot}2\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$.

questions.text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, two light waves, each of intensity $I_0$, interfere at a point, having a path difference $\dfrac{\lambda}{8}$ on the screen. Find the intensity at this point.
questions.topic: Interference of Light Waves and Young's Experiment

answer.text: Phase difference $= \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\text{path difference}$: $\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$; since $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{8}$ (given), $\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{8} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. $I = I_0 + I_0 + 2\sqrt{I_0I_0}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2I_0 + 2I_0\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = 2I_0\left(1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) = I_0(2+\sqrt2) = 3{\cdot}414\,I_0$. (Alternatively, $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right) = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right)$.)

questions.text: (i) (1) What are coherent sources ? Why are they necessary for observing a sustained interference pattern ? (2) Lights from two independent sources are not coherent. Explain. (ii) Two slits $0{\cdot}1$ mm apart are arranged $1{\cdot}20$ m from a screen. Light of wavelength 600 nm from a distant source is incident on the slits. (1) How far apart will adjacent bright interference fringes be on the screen ? (2) Find the angular width (in degree) of the first bright fringe.
questions.topic: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

answer.text: (i)(1) If the phase difference between the displacements produced by each of two waves does not change with time, the two sources are said to be coherent. (Alternatively: two sources are coherent if they emit light continuously of the same frequency/wavelength with zero or constant phase difference.) Coherent sources are required to get a constant (sustained) interference pattern. (2) Two independent sources will never be coherent because the phase difference between them will not remain constant. (ii)(1) Distance between adjacent bright fringes = fringe width: $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}\times1{\cdot}2}{0{\cdot}1\times10^{-3}} = 7{\cdot}2\ \text{mm}$. (2) $\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}}{0{\cdot}1\times10^{-3}} = 6\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad} = 0{\cdot}34^\circ$. (Full marks if given in radians only.)

questions.text: (i) Define a wavefront. An incident plane wave falls on a convex lens and gets refracted through it. Draw a diagram to show the incident and refracted wavefront. (ii) A beam of light coming from a distant source is refracted by a spherical glass ball (refractive index $1{\cdot}5$) of radius 15 cm. Draw the ray diagram and obtain the position of the final image formed.

answer.text: (i) A wavefront is the locus of all the points which oscillate in phase. Diagram: an incident plane wave falling on a convex lens produces a converging spherical wavefront of radius $f$, meeting at the focus F. (ii) Refraction at the 1st surface (rarer to denser medium, object at $\infty$): $n_1=1$, $n_2=1{\cdot}5$, $R=15\ \text{cm}$, $u=\infty$: $\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} - \dfrac{1}{\infty} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5-1}{15} \Rightarrow v=45\ \text{cm}$. Refraction at the 2nd surface (denser to rarer medium, object at $15\ \text{cm}$): $n_1=1$, $n_2=1{\cdot}5$, $R=-15\ \text{cm}$, $u=15\ \text{cm}$: $\dfrac{n_1}{v} - \dfrac{n_2}{u} = \dfrac{n_1-n_2}{R} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{15} = \dfrac{1-1{\cdot}5}{-15} \Rightarrow v = 7{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}$.

questions.text: In a double-slit experiment, $6^{\text{th}}$ dark fringe is observed at a certain point of the screen. A transparent sheet of thickness t and refractive index n is now introduced in the path of one of the two interfering waves to increase its phase by $2\pi(n-1)t/\lambda$. The pattern is shifted and $8^{\text{th}}$ bright fringe is observed at the same point. Find the relation for thickness t in terms of n and $\lambda$.
questions.topic: Interference of Light Waves and Young's Experiment

answer.text: Phase difference for the 6th dark fringe $= 11\pi$; phase difference for the 8th bright fringe $= 16\pi$. Since $\Delta\phi + \phi_6 = \phi_8$: $2\pi(n-1)\dfrac{t}{\lambda} + 11\pi = 16\pi \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{5\lambda}{2(n-1)}$. Alternatively: path difference for the 6th dark fringe $x_6 = \dfrac{11\lambda}{2}$; path difference for the 8th bright fringe $x_8 = 8\lambda$; increase in path difference on introducing the sheet, $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi}\times2\pi(n-1)\dfrac{t}{\lambda} = (n-1)t$; since $x_6+\Delta x = x_8$: $\dfrac{11\lambda}{2} + (n-1)t = 8\lambda$, giving on solving $t = \dfrac{5\lambda}{2(n-1)}$.

questions.text: In Young's double slit experiment, the separation between the two slits is $1{\cdot}0$ mm and the screen is $1{\cdot}0$ m away from the slits. A beam of light consisting of two wavelengths 500 nm and 600 nm is used to obtain interference fringes. Calculate : (a) the distance between the first maxima for the two wavelengths. (b) the least distance from the central maximum, where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide.

answer.text: (a) Distance $= \dfrac{n\lambda_1D}{d} - \dfrac{n\lambda_2D}{d}$; for $n=1$: distance $= \dfrac{(600-500)\times10^{-9}\times1}{10^{-3}} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}$. (b) $n\lambda_1\dfrac{D}{d} = (n+1)\lambda_2\dfrac{D}{d} \Rightarrow n\times600\times10^{-9} = (n+1)\times500\times10^{-9} \Rightarrow n=5$; $x = 5\times\dfrac{\lambda_1D}{d} = \dfrac{5\times600\times10^{-9}\times1}{10^{-3}} = 3\ \text{mm}$. (Alternatively: $n_1\lambda_1=n_2\lambda_2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{n_1}{n_2}=\dfrac{5}{6}$, so $n=5$; position of the 5th bright fringe for $\lambda_1$ ($600\ \text{nm}$), $x=5\times\dfrac{\lambda_1D}{d}=3\ \text{mm}$.)

(ii) $\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \pi$; $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0$.

questions.text: (a) What are coherent sources ? Why they are necessary for observing stable interference pattern ? Draw a graph showing the variation of intensity of light with the position on the screen in Young's double-slit experiment. (b) Find the intensity of light at a point on the screen when two interfering waves of the same intensity ($I_0$) have a path difference of (i) $\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$ and (ii) $\dfrac{\lambda}{3}$.

answer.text: (a) Coherent sources: two sources emitting waves of the same frequency with a constant (or zero) phase difference. They are needed because with incoherent sources the phase difference varies rapidly with time, so the maxima/minima keep shifting and only a time-averaged intensity is observed; coherence gives a stable interference pattern (graph of intensity vs position with equal-height maxima). (b) $I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)$: (i) $\Delta p = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} \Rightarrow \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2I_0$; (ii) $\Delta p = \dfrac{\lambda}{3} \Rightarrow \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \Rightarrow I = 4I_0\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = I_0$.

questions.text: Explain why diffraction of sound is more common in daily experience than that of light.

answer.text: Diffraction of sound is more common than that of light because diffraction is appreciable only when the size of the obstacle is comparable to the wavelength. Sound wavelengths are comparable to everyday obstacles, whereas the wavelength of light is far smaller than most obstacles, so light diffraction is rarely noticed.

questions.text: (a) State Huygens principle. How did Huygens justify the absence of the backwave on a spherical wavefront ?

answer.text: (a) Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread out at the wave speed; the common tangent (envelope) to these wavelets gives the new wavefront. Absence of the back wave: the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction ($A \propto (1+\cos\theta)$; for $\theta = 180^\circ$, amplitude $= 0$).

questions.text: (b) In a single-slit diffraction experiment, light of wavelength $\lambda$ illuminates the slit of width 'a'. questions.text: (a) (i) A parallel beam of monochromatic light falls normally on a single slit of width 'a' and a diffraction pattern is observed on a screen placed at distance D from the slits. Explain : (I) the formation of maxima and minima in the diffraction pattern, and (II) why the maxima go on becoming weaker and weaker with its increasing number (n). (ii) Write any two points of difference between interference pattern due to double-slit and diffraction pattern due to single-slit.

answer.text: (a)(i)(I) Single-slit diffraction — the path difference between waves from the two edges of a slit of width $a$ reaching a point at angle $\theta$ is $a\sin\theta$. Secondary minima occur where $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$ ($n = \pm1,\pm2,\ldots$) and secondary maxima where $a\sin\theta = \dfrac{(2n+1)\lambda}{2}$ ($n = \pm1,\pm2,\ldots$), the central maximum being the brightest. (II) Successive maxima become weaker as $n$ increases because only light from a small fraction of the slit (one-third, one-fifth, one-seventh, …) contributes to a secondary maximum, the remainder cancelling in pairs. (ii) Interference vs diffraction (any two): interference bands are equally spaced and of equal intensity with good contrast, whereas in diffraction the central maximum is twice as wide as the others, the intensity of the bright fringes decreases with distance from the centre, and the contrast is poorer.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text: How does Einstein's photoelectric equation explain the emission of electrons from a metal surface ? Explain briefly. Plot the variation of photocurrent with : (a) collector plate potential for different intensity of incident radiation, and (b) intensity of incident radiation.
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation: Energy Quantum of Radiation

answer.text:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, an electron absorbs a quantum of energy $h\nu$ of the incident radiation. If the absorbed energy exceeds the minimum energy needed to escape the metal surface (work function $\varphi_0$), the electron is emitted:
$K_{max} = h\nu - \varphi_0$.
(a) Variation of photocurrent with collector-plate potential for different intensities (same frequency): the saturation current increases with intensity ($I_3 > I_2 > I_1$), but the stopping potential $-V_0$ is the same for all three intensities.
(b) Variation of photocurrent with intensity of incident radiation: the photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity — a straight line through the origin.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text: Figure shows the variation of photoelectric current measured in a photo cell circuit as a function of the potential difference between the plates of the photo cell when light beams A, B, C and D of different wavelengths are incident on the photo cell. Examine the given figure and answer the following questions : (i) Which light beam has the highest frequency and why ? (ii) Which light beam has the longest wavelength and why ? (iii) Which light beam ejects photoelectrons with maximum momentum and why ?  OR  (b) What is the effect on threshold frequency and stopping potential on increasing the frequency of incident beam of light ? Justify your answer.
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation: Energy Quantum of Radiation

answer.text:
(i) The light beam $B$ has the highest frequency, because it requires the maximum retarding (stopping) potential to reduce the photoelectric current to zero.
(ii) The light beam $C$ has the longest wavelength, because it requires the minimum retarding potential to reduce the photoelectric current to zero.
(iii) The light beam $B$ ejects photoelectrons with the maximum momentum, because the highest-frequency beam ejects photoelectrons with the highest kinetic energy and hence the highest momentum.
OR — There is no effect on the threshold frequency, since it is a characteristic of the metal.
With an increase in the frequency of the incident light the stopping potential increases, because a larger retarding potential is needed to stop the higher-kinetic-energy photoelectrons; this follows from $eV_0=h(\nu-\nu_0)$.

Using this graph and Einstein's photoelectric equation, obtain the expression for Planck's constant and work function of the surface.
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation: Energy Quantum of Radiation

answer.text:
By Einstein's photoelectric equation, $\dfrac{1}{2}mv_m^{2}=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi_0$, so
$v_m^{2}=\left(\dfrac{2hc}{m}\right)\dfrac{1}{\lambda}-\dfrac{2}{m}\phi_0$.
Hence a plot of $v_m^{2}$ versus $\dfrac{1}{\lambda}$ is a straight line with slope $\dfrac{2hc}{m}$ and intercept $\dfrac{2}{m}\phi_0$.
From the graph, $h=\dfrac{m}{2c}\times\text{slope}$ and $\phi_0=\dfrac{m}{2}\times\text{intercept}$.

Here, K is the energy of the moving particles. (a) What does the slope of a line represent ? (b) Which of the two particles is heavier ? (c) Is this graph also valid for a photon ? answer.text:
(a) Since $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m}}\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$, the slope of $\lambda$ vs $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$ is $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m}}$.

(c) No — the graph is not valid for a photon, since a photon's momentum is $p=\dfrac{E}{c}$ (not $\sqrt{2mK}$, which requires a rest mass and non-relativistic kinetic energy).

De Broglie wavelength of a proton: $\lambda_p=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_p q_p V_1}}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV_1}}$.

questions.text: The ground state energy of hydrogen atom is $-13{\cdot}6$ eV. What is the potential energy and kinetic energy of an electron in the third excited state ?

Total energy in the $n$-th state: $E_n = \dfrac{-13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}$.

Alpha-particles emitted by a radioactive source were allowed to fall on a thin gold foil. The scattered $\alpha$-particles were observed through a rotatable detector consisting of a zinc-sulphide screen and a microscope; on striking the screen they produced scintillations (light flashes).

questions.text: (i) State three postulates of Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom. (ii) Find the angular momentum of an electron revolving in the second orbit in Bohr's hydrogen atom.

answer.text:
(i) Bohr's postulates: (1) an electron revolves in certain stable orbits without emitting radiant energy; (2) the electron revolves only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; (3) when an electron makes a transition from a higher to a lower energy orbit, a photon is emitted whose energy equals the difference between the two energy levels.
(ii) Angular momentum $=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$; for $n=2$,
$=\dfrac{2h}{2\pi}=\dfrac{h}{\pi}=\dfrac{6{\cdot}63\times10^{-34}}{\pi}=2{\cdot}1\times10^{-34}\ \text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.text: Write the drawbacks of Rutherford's atomic model. How did Bohr remove them ? Show that different orbits in Bohr's atom are not equally spaced.
questions.topic: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

answer.text:
Drawbacks of Rutherford's model: (i) an accelerating charged particle (the orbiting electron) should, by classical electromagnetic theory, continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom would not be stable; (ii) since the electron's frequency would change continuously as it spirals in, it should emit a continuous spectrum, contrary to the line spectrum actually observed.
Bohr removed these by postulating that an electron revolves only in certain stable orbits without radiating energy, where the angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; radiation is emitted only when the electron transitions between such orbits.
The radius of the $n$-th orbit is $r_n=\left(\dfrac{n^{2}}{m}\right)\left(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\right)^{2}\dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_0}{e^{2}}$, i.e. $r_n\propto n^{2}$.
Since the difference $r_{n+1}-r_n=k[(n+1)^{2}-n^{2}]=k(2n+1)$ depends on $n$, successive orbits are not equally spaced.

Also, the Coulomb force provides the centripetal force (for $Z=1$): $\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}=\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\dfrac{e}{\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_0 mr}}$.

questions.text: State Bohr's first and second postulates. Use them to derive an expression for the radius of the $n^{th}$ orbit in a hydrogen atom.
questions.topic: DE Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

answer.text:
Bohr's first postulate: an electron in an atom revolves in certain stable orbits without the emission of radiant energy.
Bohr's second postulate: the electron revolves only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$, i.e. $mv_n r_n=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$  ...(ii).
The electrostatic force between the electron and the nucleus provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv_n^{2}}{r_n}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r_n^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ v_n=\dfrac{e}{\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_0 m r_n}}$  ...(i).
Using (i) and (ii): $r_n=\left(\dfrac{n^{2}}{m}\right)\left(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\right)^{2}\dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_0}{e^{2}}=\dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m e^{2}}$.

questions.text: Prove that, in Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the time period of revolution of an electron in $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit is proportional to $n^3$.

answer.text: $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}\ \ldots(1)$. From Bohr's quantisation condition, $mvr = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi} \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}\ \ldots(2)$. From (1) and (2): $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{nh/2\pi mr} = \dfrac{2\pi r(2\pi mr)}{nh} = \dfrac{4\pi^2mr^2}{nh}$. Using $r = \dfrac{n^2h^2}{4\pi^2mke^2}$: $T = \dfrac{4\pi^2m}{nh}\left(\dfrac{n^2h^2}{4\pi^2mke^2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{n^3h^3}{4\pi^2mk^2e^4} \Rightarrow T \propto n^3$. Alternatively: $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$; since $r\propto n^2$ and $v\propto\dfrac{1}{n}$, $T \propto n^3$.

questions.text: How is the necessary force provided to an electron to keep it moving in a circular orbit according to Bohr model of hydrogen atom ? Derive an expression for the total energy of an electron moving in an orbit of radius r in hydrogen atom. Give the significance of negative sign in this expression.

answer.text: The electrostatic force of attraction between the electron and the nucleus provides the necessary centripetal force for the electron to revolve in its orbit: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\ \ldots(1)$ ($Z=1$ for the hydrogen atom). Kinetic energy of the electron: $K=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r}$ (from eq. 1). Potential energy: $U = -\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$ (since $U=\dfrac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$). Total energy of the electron: $E=K+U=-\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r}$. The negative sign signifies that the electron is bound to the nucleus (the force is attractive).

(ii) $L=mvr=n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$. (iii) $h\nu=E_f-E_i$. (a) $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{Ze^2}{r^2}\ \ldots(1)$; $mvr=n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\ \ldots(2)$. (b) Since the energy in the orbit is $E_n = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r}$, using eq. (3): $E_n = -\dfrac{me^4}{8n^2\varepsilon_0^2h^2}$, i.e. $E_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n^2}$.

answer.text: (a) Bohr's second (quantisation) postulate: the electron revolves only in those orbits for which its angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$, i.e. $L = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$; significance — it defines the stable/stationary orbits (angular momentum is quantised). questions.text: (i) Draw a graph to show the variation of the number of scattered particles detected (N) in Geiger-Marsden experiment as a function of scattering angle ($\theta$). (ii) Discuss briefly two conclusions that can be drawn from this graph and how they lead to the discovery of nucleus in an atom.
questions.topic: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

answer.text:
(i) In the Geiger-Marsden experiment, the graph of the number of scattered $\alpha$-particles $N$ against the scattering angle $\theta$ falls very steeply — most particles are scattered through small angles and only a very few through large angles.
(ii) Conclusions (any two): the entire positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small space; most $\alpha$-particles pass straight through the foil (so they suffer no collision — the atom is largely empty).
To deflect an $\alpha$-particle backward, a large repulsive force is required, which is possible only if the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated tightly at the centre — this led to the discovery of the nucleus.

questions.text: (b) (i) Draw the number of scattered particles versus the scattering angle graph for scattering of alpha particles by a thin foil. answer.text: (i) From the Geiger–Marsden $\alpha$-scattering graph (scattered particles vs scattering angle) one concludes that most of the atom is empty space (most $\alpha$-particles pass almost undeflected) and that the entire positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus (a few $\alpha$-particles are deflected through large angles). (ii) Bohr's quantisation $L = mvr = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$ is not noticed for planetary motion because a planet's angular momentum is enormous, giving a huge quantum number $n$; successive energy levels are then so closely spaced that the quantisation is imperceptible (the motion appears continuous).
