questions.text: Draw a diagram to show the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number for different nuclei and mention its two features. Why do lighter nuclei usually undergo nuclear fusion ?

answer.text:
The graph of binding energy per nucleon $E_{bn}$ versus mass number $A$ rises steeply for light nuclei, is nearly flat (about $8{\cdot}75\ \text{MeV}$, peak near $A = 56$) for $30 < A < 170$, and then falls slowly to about $7{\cdot}6\ \text{MeV}$ at $A = 238$.
Features (any two):
1. $E_{bn}$ is practically independent of atomic number for middle-mass nuclei ($30 < A < 170$).
2. The curve has a maximum of about $8{\cdot}75\ \text{MeV}$ for $A = 56$ and a value of about $7{\cdot}6\ \text{MeV}$ for $A = 238$.
3. $E_{bn}$ is lower for both light nuclei ($A < 30$) and heavy nuclei ($A > 170$).
Reason for fusion: two lighter nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus because the binding energy per nucleon of the fused nucleus is greater, so the final system is more tightly bound (more stable) and energy is released.

questions.text: Define the term, mass defect. How is it related to stability of the nucleus ?

answer.text:
Mass defect is the difference between the sum of the masses of the individual nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus.
The greater the mass defect, the greater the binding energy and the more stable the nucleus (i.e. mass defect $\propto$ stability of the nucleus).

questions.text: (i) Distinguish between nuclear fission and fusion giving an example of each. (ii) Explain the release of energy in nuclear fission and fusion on the basis of binding energy per nucleon curve.

answer.text:
Nuclear fission: a heavy nucleus, when excited (e.g. by a slow-moving neutron), splits into two lighter nuclei of nearly comparable masses with the release of a large amount of energy.
Example: ${}^{1}_{0}n+{}^{235}_{92}U\to{}^{236}_{92}U\to{}^{144}_{56}Ba+{}^{89}_{36}Kr+3\,{}^{1}_{0}n+Q$.
Nuclear fusion: two lighter nuclei fuse (at extremely high temperature) to form a heavier nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy.
Example: ${}^{2}_{1}H+{}^{2}_{1}H\to{}^{3}_{2}He+{}^{1}_{0}n+Q$.
(ii) In both processes the binding energy per nucleon of the products is greater than that of the reactants, so energy is released.

questions.text: (i) How is the size of a nucleus found experimentally ? Write the relation between the radius and mass number of a nucleus. (ii) Prove that the density of a nucleus is independent of its mass number.

answer.text:
(i) The size of a nucleus is determined experimentally by scattering experiments (fast particles/electrons are used to bombard target nuclei).
Relation between radius and mass number: $R=R_0\,A^{1/3}$.
(ii) Density of the nucleus:
$\rho=\dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}=\dfrac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}=\dfrac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi\left(R_0 A^{1/3}\right)^{3}}=\dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^{3}}$,
which is independent of the mass number $A$.

questions.text: Draw a graph showing the variation of binding energy per nucleon as a function of mass number A. The binding energy per nucleon for heavy nuclei (A > 170) decreases with the increase in mass number. Explain.

answer.text:
The binding energy per nucleon rises steeply for light nuclei, is nearly constant (about $8{\cdot}75\ \text{MeV}$, peak near $A=56$) for $30<A<170$, and falls slowly for heavy nuclei.
Explanation: nuclear forces are short-range and show saturation, whereas the electrostatic (Coulomb) force is neither short-range nor saturating. Hence for heavier nuclei ($A>170$) the electrostatic force of repulsion becomes predominant, decreasing the binding energy per nucleon (as the size of the nucleus increases it becomes less stable).

(ii) On the potential-energy-vs-separation graph for a pair of nucleons, $U$ is large and positive at very small $r$, has a minimum at $r=r_0$, and tends to zero for large $r$.
Inferences (any two): the nuclear force is attractive for distances greater than $r_0$; it is repulsive for distances less than $r_0$.

questions.text: Briefly explain how the diffusion and drift currents contribute to the formation of potential barrier in a p-n junction diode.

answer.text:
When a p-n junction is formed, the diffusion current due to the concentration gradient causes majority carriers to cross the junction, forming a space-charge (depletion) region of immobile ionised atoms.
Because of this an electric field is set up at the junction, which gives rise to a drift current in the direction opposite to the diffusion current.
The potential at which the diffusion current becomes equal to the drift current is called the potential barrier.

questions.text: Explain the roles of diffusion current and drift current in the formation of the depletion layer in a p-n junction diode.

answer.text:
During the formation of a p-n junction, because of the concentration gradient, holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side ($p\to n$) and electrons from the n-side to the p-side ($n\to p$).
A diffusing electron leaves behind an immobile ionised donor (positive charge) on the n-side, and a diffusing hole leaves behind an immobile ionised acceptor (negative charge) on the p-side. This space-charge region on either side of the junction together forms the depletion region.
As a result an electric field is set up across the junction. Due to this field an electron on the p-side moves to the n-side and a hole on the n-side moves to the p-side — this motion of carriers is the drift current, opposite to the diffusion current.
Initially the diffusion current is large and the drift current is small; as diffusion continues the field strength (and hence the drift current) increases, until the diffusion and drift currents become equal.

questions.text: Explain the property of a p-n junction which makes it suitable for rectifying alternating voltages. Differentiate between a half-wave and a full-wave rectifier.

answer.text:
A p-n junction conducts (offers a low resistance) only in forward bias and blocks conduction in reverse bias, i.e. it is a unidirectional device; this property makes it suitable for rectifying an alternating voltage.
Difference: a half-wave rectifier gives an output only for half of each input cycle, whereas a full-wave rectifier gives an output for both halves of each input cycle.

With proper doping, the number of conduction electrons becomes much larger than the number of holes; the donor level lies just below the conduction band (about $0{\cdot}01\ \text{eV}$ below $E_C$), so the conductivity of the doped (n-type) crystal increases.
(ii) Two processes: Diffusion — due to the concentration gradient, majority carriers move (electrons $n\to p$ and holes $p\to n$). Drift — due to the junction field, an electron on the p-side moves to the n-side and a hole on the n-side moves to the p-side.

questions.text: (i) With the help of a circuit diagram, briefly explain the working of a full-wave rectifier using p-n junction diodes. (ii) Draw V$-$I characteristics of a p-n junction diode. Explain how these characteristics make a diode suitable for rectification. (iii) Carbon and silicon have the same lattice structure. Then why is carbon an insulator but silicon a semiconductor ?
questions.topic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

answer.text:
(i) A full-wave rectifier uses a centre-tapped transformer with two diodes $D_1,D_2$ and a load $R_L$.
Working: when the voltage at $A$ (w.r.t. the centre tap) is positive, that at $B$ is negative, so $D_1$ is forward-biased and conducts while $D_2$ is reverse-biased; during the next half-cycle the polarity reverses and only $D_2$ conducts. Thus current flows through $R_L$ in the same direction in both halves.
(ii) The V-I characteristics show that the diode conducts when forward-biased and does not conduct when reverse-biased, which makes it suitable for rectification.
(iii) The four valence electrons of C and Si lie in the second and third orbits respectively; hence the energy needed to free an electron in Si is much less than in C. So at room temperature Si has a significant number of free electrons for conduction, while for C it is negligibly small.

questions.text: Junction Diode as a Rectifier : The process of conversion of an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification and the device which performs this conversion is called a rectifier. The characteristics of a p-n junction diode reveal that when a p-n junction diode is forward biased, it offers a low resistance and when it is reverse biased, it offers a high resistance. Hence, a p-n junction diode conducts only when it is forward biased. This property of a p-n junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier. Thus, when an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during those alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only half cycle of an ac voltage is called a half-wave rectifier and one that rectifies both the half cycles is known as a full-wave rectifier. (i) The root mean square value of an alternating voltage applied to a full-wave rectifier is $\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$. Then the root mean square value of the rectified output voltage is : (A) $\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$ (B) $\dfrac{V_0^2}{\sqrt{2}}$ (C) $\dfrac{2V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$ (D) $\dfrac{V_0}{2\sqrt{2}}$ (ii) In a full-wave rectifier, the current in each of the diodes flows for : (A) Complete cycle of the input signal (B) Half cycle of the input signal (C) Less than half cycle of the input signal (D) Only for the positive half cycle of the input signal (iii) In a full-wave rectifier : (A) Both diodes are forward biased at the same time. (B) Both diodes are reverse biased at the same time. (C) One is forward biased and the other is reverse biased at the same time. Identify the output across resistance $R_L$ (options A, B, C, D shown in the figure) :
questions.topic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

answer.text:
(i) For a full-wave rectifier, if the rms value of the alternating input is $\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$, the rms value of the rectified output voltage is still $\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$.
(ii) In a full-wave rectifier, the current in each diode flows for half a cycle of the input signal.
(iii) In a full-wave rectifier, at any instant one diode is forward-biased and the other is reverse-biased.
(iv)(a) For a half-wave rectifier with a $50\ \text{Hz}$ input, the ripple frequency of the output is $50\ \text{Hz}$ (equal to the input frequency).
OR (iv)(b) A p-n junction diode conducts (passes the signal to $R_L$) only during the half-cycle for which it is forward-biased; the output across $R_L$ is a clipped/rectified version of the input square-wave signal.

questions.text: With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a p-n junction diode as a full wave rectifier. Draw its input and output waveforms.
questions.topic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

answer.text:
A full-wave rectifier uses a centre-tapped transformer with two diodes $D_1,D_2$ and a load $R_L$. When the voltage at $A$ (w.r.t. the centre tap) is positive, $B$ is negative, so $D_1$ is forward-biased and conducts while $D_2$ does not; we get an output current and voltage across $R_L$.
During the second half-cycle, $A$ is negative and $B$ is positive, so $D_1$ does not conduct but $D_2$ does, again giving output across $R_L$.
Thus an output voltage is obtained during both halves of the input cycle — the output waveform (across $R_L$) consists of a series of positive pulses, alternately due to $D_1$ and $D_2$.

questions.text: On the basis of energy band diagrams, distinguish between (i) an insulator, (ii) a semiconductor, and (iii) a conductor.

answer.text:

(i) Insulator: a large forbidden energy gap $E_g>3\ \text{eV}$ separates the filled valence band from the empty conduction band.
(ii) Semiconductor: a small energy gap $E_g<3\ \text{eV}$, so electrons can be thermally excited from the valence band to the conduction band.
(iii) Metal (conductor): the conduction and valence bands overlap ($E_g\approx0$), providing a large number of free electrons.

questions.text: Explain the following, giving reasons : (a) A doped semiconductor is electrically neutral. (b) In a p-n junction under reverse bias, there is no net current. (c) In a diode, the reverse current is practically not dependent on the applied voltage.

(a) The charge of the additional (mobile) charge carriers is just equal and opposite to that of the ionised cores fixed in the lattice, so the semiconductor as a whole is electrically neutral.
(b) Under equilibrium (no applied bias) the diffusion current is exactly equal to the drift current.

questions.text: (a) What are majority and minority charge carriers of p-type and n-type semiconductors ? (b) Explain briefly the formation of diffusion current and drift current in a p-n junction diode.

In an $n$-type semiconductor: majority charge carriers — electrons; minority charge carriers — holes. (b) Diffusion current — during the formation of a $p$-$n$ junction, due to the concentration gradient across the $p$ and $n$ sides, holes diffuse from the $p$-side to the $n$-side ($p\to n$) and electrons diffuse from the $n$-side to the $p$-side ($n\to p$); this motion of charge carriers gives rise to the diffusion current across the junction. questions.text: Differentiate between half-wave and full-wave rectification. With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of a full-wave rectifier.
questions.topic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

answer.text: In half-wave rectification there is output in only one half of the input cycle, whereas in full-wave rectification output is obtained for both half cycles of the input (positive and negative). Working of a full-wave rectifier (centre-tap transformer with diodes $D_1$, $D_2$): suppose the input voltage at A, with respect to the centre tap, is positive at some instant. At that instant, the voltage at B (out of phase) will be negative, so diode $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts (while $D_2$, being reverse biased, does not conduct). During this positive half cycle we get an output current (and output voltage across the load resistor $R_L$). During the course of the ac cycle, when the voltage at A becomes negative with respect to the centre tap, the voltage at B becomes positive; $D_1$ would not conduct but $D_2$ would, giving an output current and output voltage during the negative half cycle of the input ac.

questions.text: Draw energy band diagrams of n-type and p-type semiconductors at temperature $T > 0$ K. Show the donor/acceptor energy levels with the order of difference of their energies from the bands.

answer.text: Energy-band diagrams: for an $n$-type semiconductor, the donor energy level $E_D$ lies just below the conduction band $E_C$ (gap $E_D$ to $E_C$ $\approx 0{\cdot}01\ \text{eV}$), with the valence band $E_V$ well below. For a $p$-type semiconductor, the acceptor energy level $E_A$ lies just above the valence band $E_V$ (gap $E_V$ to $E_A$ $\approx 0{\cdot}01$–$0{\cdot}05\ \text{eV}$), with the conduction band $E_C$ well above.

questions.text: Explain the process of formation of 'depletion layer' and 'potential barrier' in a p-n junction region of a diode, with the help of a suitable diagram. Which feature of junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier ?
questions.topic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

answer.text: When an electron diffuses from the $n$-side to the $p$-side, it leaves behind an ionised donor on the $n$-side. Similarly, when a hole diffuses from the $p$-side to the $n$-side, it leaves behind an ionised acceptor on the $p$-side. This space-charge region of immobile ions on either side of the junction is known as the depletion layer. As the diffusion process continues, the width of the depletion layer increases, and consequently the electric field strength across the junction increases, and so does the drift current. The potential that prevents further movement of electrons from the $n$-region into the $p$-region is called the potential barrier. Feature enabling its use as a rectifier: a diode allows current to pass only when it is forward biased (its resistance is small), whereas in reverse bias its resistance is very large. (Alternatively: a diode is unidirectional.)

questions.text: Briefly explain the two important processes that occur during the formation of a p-n junction.

answer.text: Two important processes in the formation of a $p$-$n$ junction: (i) \textit{Diffusion} — due to the concentration gradient across the junction, holes diffuse from the $p$-side to the $n$-side and electrons from the $n$-side to the $p$-side, giving a diffusion current. (ii) \textit{Drift} — the space-charge region sets up an electric field across the junction; this field drives an electron on the $p$-side to the $n$-side and a hole on the $n$-side to the $p$-side, constituting a drift current (opposite in sense to the diffusion current).

questions.text: How are charge carriers created in an intrinsic semiconductor ? Explain.

answer.text: Creation of charge carriers in an intrinsic semiconductor: at low temperature all covalent bonds are intact; as temperature rises, thermal energy frees some electrons (available for conduction), and each vacated site leaves a vacancy with an effective positive charge called a hole — so electron-hole pairs (charge carriers) are created.

questions.text: The hole concentration in an intrinsic semiconductor is $5 \times 10^8$ m$^{-3}$. When it is doped with certain impurity, the electron concentration becomes $4 \times 10^{12}$ m$^{-3}$. Find the new value of the hole concentration. Also identify the type of new semiconductor formed after doping.

answer.text: New hole concentration: $n_en_h = n_i^2$; $n_h = \dfrac{n_i^2}{n_e} = \dfrac{5\times10^{8}\times5\times10^{8}}{4\times10^{12}} = 6{\cdot}25\times10^{4}\ \text{m}^{-3}$. Since $n_e > n_h$, the doped semiconductor is $n$-type.

answer.text: Full-wave rectifier (centre-tap transformer with diodes $D_1$, $D_2$ and load $R_L$): when terminal A is positive with respect to the centre tap, $D_1$ is forward biased and conducts ($D_2$ is off); in the next half cycle B is positive so $D_2$ conducts ($D_1$ is off).
